units.la: Christum itaque mihi propositum, placamentum per fidem in sanguine ejus, & pro peccatis meis propitiationem merito retineo & adoro, ut suo Merito, & corporis sui Sacrificio Reconciliatorem meum.
units.tr: Therefore I hold fast and adore Christ set before me as the placation through faith in his blood and as the propitiation for my sins, as my Reconciler by his merit and by the sacrifice of his body.

units.la: CAPITIS IV. SECTIO III.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. SECTION III.

units.la: Vivere & proprie, verum pretium redemtionis nostra persolvendo nos redemit, is utiq;[?] nobis satis fecit. Atqui Christus Jesus vere & proprie, verum pretium redemtio-nis nonis nostræ perfolvêdo, nos redemit, licet pretium hoc à Deo fuerit procuratum. Quod ipsum jam demonstrandum. Agitur hic de redemtione priori, jam peracta à Christo, quatenus ipse nos pretioso suo sanguine redemit, vel seipsum pretium redemtionis pro nobis dedit.
units.tr: He who truly and properly redeemed us by paying the true price of our redemption has certainly satisfied for us. But Christ Jesus truly and properly redeemed us by paying the true price of our redemption, although this price was provided by God. This is what has yet to be demonstrated. We are speaking here of the earlier redemption, already accomplished by Christ, insofar as he redeemed us with his precious blood, or gave himself as the price of our redemption on our behalf.

units.la: In vera autem redemtione (ut ipsi Adversarii docent) peragenda requiruntur quinq;. 1. Captivus, hic in liberatione, de qua agimus, est Homo. 2. Is qui eum captivum detineat, alioqui captivus non esset. Ea multa sunt, Peccatum, Diabolus, Mundus & mortis æternæ decreta pœna. 3. Is qui redimat: Hic autem est Deus, sive Christus, per quem redemtionem nostram confecit. 4. Pretium Redemtionis: hoc autem est ipse Christus à Deo Patre datus (ut ajunt) seu vita ejus, qui seipsum seu vitam suam dedit, ut tantæ redemtionis effectus sequeretur. 5. Hic ajunt nihil desiderari, ut omnino vere Redemtioni respondeat, nisi quintum, ut is, qui captivum detinebat, pretium accipiat. Hinc concludunt, non veram, sed Metaphoricam esse hanc nostram Redemtionem.
units.tr: In a true redemption (as our opponents themselves teach) five things are required. 1. The captive: in the liberation we are discussing, this is man. 2. The one who holds him captive, since otherwise he would not be a captive. This is manifold: sin, the Devil, the world, and the sentence of eternal death. 3. The redeemer: this is God, or Christ, through whom he accomplished our redemption. 4. The price of redemption: this is Christ himself, given by God the Father (as they say), or his life, since he gave himself, or his life, so that the effect of so great a redemption would follow. 5. They say that nothing more is needed, in order that the redemption should fully and truly correspond, except a fifth thing: that the one who held the captive should receive the price. From this they conclude that our redemption is not true but metaphorical.

units.la: 1. Quoniam in ea[?] nemo fit, qui pretium accipiat. Si enim id, quod in ipsa pretii loco est, acceptum (ab eo scilicet, qui captivum hominem detinebat) fuisset: iam non metaphoricum, sed verum pretium intervenisset, uti inquiunt.
units.tr: 1. Because in this case there is no one who receives the price. For if what stands in the place of the price had been received (namely, by him who held the man captive), then a real and not a metaphorical price would have intervened, as they put it.

units.la: 2. Quoniam Redimendi verbum, non-aliquando, non etiam saepe, sed plerumque & fere semper apud sacros Scriptores metaphoricam prorsus significationem obtineat, adeo ut nihil aliud sit Redimere, quam liberare, aut sibi afferere, quamvis veri pretii verasolutio aliquando non interveniat.
units.tr: 2. Because the verb "to redeem" does not sometimes, nor often, but for the most part and almost always, carry a purely metaphorical sense in the sacred writers, so that "to redeem" means nothing other than "to free" or "to claim for oneself," even though a true payment of a real price sometimes does not intervene.

units.la: 1. Sicut dicitur in Veteri Testamento Deus Redemisse populum Israeliticum, quem ex Ægyptiorum, & Pharaonis servitute liberaverat, & sibi quodammodo asserverat, quamvis nullum pretium pro eo liberando solvisset. 2. Sicut Moses a Stephano Actor, 7. λυτρωτὴς sive Redemtor est appel-latus. latus. Abrahamus dicitur è manibus Chaldæorum redemtus, Jes. 29.
units.tr: 1. Thus in the Old Testament God is said to have redeemed the Israelite people, whom he had freed from the servitude of the Egyptians and of Pharaoh, and in a sense claimed for himself, although he had paid no price for their liberation. 2. Thus Moses is called by Stephen in Acts 7 a redeemer [λυτρωτής], or Redeemer. Abraham is said to have been redeemed from the hands of the Chaldeans, Isa. 29.

units.la: Ita autem Metaphoricam hanc redemtionem exponunt, ut eam dupliciter considerent. 1. Quatenus ab ipso peccato in hac vita liberamur, 2. Quatenus ab æterna morte vindicati sempiterna vita donamur. Utrā-que dicunt primo residere in Deo, qui nos à tantis malis liberare & constituit & curat. Deinde in nobis, qui eam re ipsa adipiscimur. Christum vero pretium fuisse autumant, non quo liberatio ex parte Dei, qui eam procuravit & ipsum dedit, compararetur nobis: sed quo nos eam reipsa conseque-remur.
units.tr: They explain this metaphorical redemption in such a way as to consider it in two respects. 1. Insofar as we are freed from sin itself in this life; 2. Insofar as, delivered from eternal death, we are given everlasting life. They say that both belong first to God, who both resolved and takes care to free us from such great evils; and then to us, who actually obtain it. But they maintain that Christ was the price, not in the sense that liberation was procured for us on the part of God, who obtained it and gave him, but in the sense that we actually attain it through him.

units.la: Priorem igitur redemtionem, hoc est, à peccato in hac vita liberationem nos adipisci, spe nobis facta vitæ immortalis, atq; æternæ beatitatis, quam fide ipsius Christi verbis adhibita concipimus, qui nos pœnitentiam agere iussit, & novos homines fieri, præmio cœlestis hæreditatis, voluit. Fidem autem hanc potissimũ gignere ipsius Resurrectione, ad quam non nisi per mortem pervenire poterat, & ipsius in cœ-lis Majestatem & æternam beatamque vitam, ad quam, ita Deo statuente, per ignominiam & mortem acerbissimam eum perduci, necesse erat. Sed his re-lictis [?], nostram subjiciamus declarationem & demonstrationem Assumti ex Verbo Dei.
units.tr: They therefore hold that we obtain the former redemption, that is, liberation from sin in this life, through the hope of immortal life and eternal blessedness, which is set before us, and which we conceive by faith, using the words of Christ himself, who commanded us to repent and to become new men, and who willed the reward of the heavenly inheritance. This faith is chiefly produced by his resurrection, to which he could not come except through death, and by his majesty in heaven and his eternal and blessed life, to which, since God so decreed, he had to be brought through shame and most bitter death. But setting these aside, let us subjoin our own statement and demonstration of the assumption from the Word of God.

units.la: Nostra hæc redemtio, de qua agitur hoc loco, non est aliqua Metaphorica re-demtio, h. e. simplex tantum liberatio, vel assertio in libertatem, sed vera & propria, in qua omnes partes veræ redemtionis apparent.
units.tr: This redemption of ours, which is under discussion here, is not some merely metaphorical redemption, that is, a simple liberation or assertion into freedom, but a true and proper one, in which all the parts of a true redemption appear.

units.la: I. Captivis est homo, qui venit in potestatem Diaboli per peccatum: quatenus primi nostri parentes sese ab illo decipi passi sunt, ut transgrederentur Mandatum Dei, atq; ita a Deo ad ipsum deficerent. Unde ipse tum in eos, tum in posteros ipsorum, tanquam in lumbis eorum inclusos 1. Corinth, 15. v. 10, potestatem nactus est, quasi jure belli, vincens nimirum eos, non quidem armis, sed dolo, videlicet mendaci promissiomissione æqualitatis cum Deo adipiscendæ. Quo accedit & alius juris atque dominii titulus, videlicet jus judicialis traditionis, qua homines lapsi à Deo judice traditi sunt Diabolo tanquam carnifici ad puniendum eos propter crimen læsæ majestatis; hac tamen conditione; nisi pro illis satisfieret judicio Dei.
units.tr: I. The captive is man, who came under the power of the Devil through sin, insofar as our first parents allowed themselves to be deceived by him so that they transgressed God's command, and thus fell away from God to him. Hence he obtained power over them, and over their posterity, as though they were enclosed in their loins (1 Cor. 15:10), as by a right of war, conquering them indeed not by arms but by guile, namely by the lying promise of attaining equality with God. To this is added another title of right and dominion, namely the right of judicial surrender, by which fallen men were handed over by God the judge to the Devil as an executioner, to punish them for the crime of treason against majesty; yet on this condition: unless satisfaction were made to the judgment of God on their behalf.

units.la: Hic sibi dictum ait Paulus Actor. 26. ver. 18. Quod mittat ipsum ad populum Israëliticum, & ad Gentes, ut aperiat oculos eorum, ut se convertant à tenebris ad lucem, & à potestate Satanæ ad Deum. Coloss. 1. verf. 13. de Deo Patre loquens ait: Qui liberavit nos à potestate tenebrarum, ac transtulit in Regnum Filii sibi dilecti. 2. Timoth. 2. v. 26. Ut mentis sanitatem recipiant elapsi ex Diaboli laqueo, ut qui captivi tenentur ab ipso. Apocal. 20. v. 6. Beatus & Sanctus, qui habet partem in Resurrectione prima: in hac secunda mors non habet potestatem.
units.tr: Paul says that this was said to him, Acts 26:18: "that he should send him to the people of Israel and to the Gentiles, to open their eyes, that they might turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God." Speaking of God the Father, Col. 1:13 says: "who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son." 2 Tim. 2:26: "that they may recover their senses, having escaped from the snare of the Devil, who are held captive by him." Rev. 20:6: "Blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection; over such the second death has no power."

units.la: II. Manifestum hinc est, quis sit ille, qui captivum hominem teneat, nempe Potestas tenebrarum, Servitus peccatis & Mortis, & is qui mortis habebat imperium Diabolus. ut jam probatum constat. Non igitur Redemtio nostri est temporalis à servitute aut tyrannide aliqua corporali, qualis fuit redemtio Israëlis ex Ægypto, è domo servitutis, & manu Pharaonis per Mosen, & postea è manu Cananæorum & Midiani-tarum, aliorumque inimicorum su-orum per Gideonem, aliosque judi-ces, & præsertim è tristissima & septu-agenaria captivitate Babylonica, per Cyrum Persarum Regem & Monar-cham: sed est Redemtio hæc spiritualis atque æterna, corporalibus illis libe-rationibus olim adumbrata; è potesta-te scilicet tenebrarum, servitute peccati & mortis, & diaboli, qui mortis ha-bebat imperium.
units.tr: II. It is clear from this who it is that holds man captive: namely, the power of darkness, the servitude of sin and of death, and the Devil, who had the power of death, as has now been established. Our redemption is therefore not a temporal liberation from some bodily servitude or tyranny, such as the redemption of Israel from Egypt, out of the house of bondage and from the hand of Pharaoh through Moses, and afterwards from the hand of the Canaanites and Midianites and their other enemies through Gideon and the other judges, and especially from the most sorrowful Babylonian captivity of seventy years, through Cyrus, king and monarch of the Persians. Rather, this redemption is spiritual and eternal, foreshadowed long ago by those bodily liberations: from the power of darkness, the servitude of sin and death, and the Devil, who had the power of death.

units.la: Atque hi sunt inimici, quorum Za-charias pater Baptistæ in cantico suo meminit, hanc ipsam Redemtionem celebrans: Benedictus (inquit Lucæ 1.) Dominus noster Deus Israël, quod inviserit & redemerit populum suum, & erexerit cornu salutis no-bis in domo David Pueri sui, prout locutus est per os sanctorum Prophetarum, fore ut nos servaret ex inimicis nostris, & e manu omnium, qui oderunt nos, ut sine metu, e manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati servitemus ipsi, cum sanctitate & justitia coram ipso, omnibus diebus vitæ nostræ.
units.tr: These are the enemies of whom Zacharias, the father of the Baptist, speaks in his canticle, celebrating this very redemption: "Blessed" (he says, Luke 1) "be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people, and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, so that, delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life."

units.la: 3. Is, qui hominem captivum redimit ex servitute & potestate peccati, mortis & diaboli, est idem ipse pro sua ineffabili Misericordia & gratia Deus, a quo defeceramus, qui omnium nostrum peccata fecit incurrere in filium suum: q. filium suum, qui nō novit peccatū, fecit peccatum, qui erat in Christo mundū sibi reconcilians per mortē ejus: hic redemtionem misit populo suo. Hic autem nos redemit per filium suum, quem mediatorem inter se & nos esse voluit, qui Christus nobis datus & natus, nos a servitute peccati & mortis, ac dominatu Satanæ liberavit.
units.tr: 3. He who redeems the captive man from the servitude and power of sin, death, and the Devil is the same God, by his unspeakable mercy and grace, from whom we had fallen away, who made the sins of us all fall upon his Son; or, who made him who knew no sin to be sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21), who was in Christ reconciling the world to himself through his death. He sent redemption to his people. He redeemed us through his Son, whom he willed to be the mediator between himself and us, who, given and born as Christ, freed us from the servitude of sin and death and from the dominion of Satan.

units.la: In hoc facta est Redemtio, qui nobis factus est a Deo Sapientia, Iustitia, Sanctificatio & Redemtio, qui est apud Deum propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi: nec in alio quoquam est salus, nec aliud nomen sub cœlo datum est inter homines, per quod oportet nos servari. Hic propter nos & nostram salutem ipse se exinanivit forma servi accepta, & habitu compertus ut homo; & submisit sese factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, ut sua passione & morte, & sacratissimi sanguinis effusione, tanquam unico sacrificio propitiatorio corpus & anima nostram ab æterna damnatione redimeret, nobisq; gratiam Dei, iustitiam ac vitam æternam acquireret.
units.tr: In him the redemption was made, who was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, who is with God the propitiation for the sins of the whole world; nor is there salvation in any other, nor is there any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. For our sake and for our salvation he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in fashion as a man; and he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, the death of the cross, so that by his suffering and death, and by the shedding of his most sacred blood, as the one propitiatory sacrifice, he might redeem our body and soul from eternal damnation, and acquire for us the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life.

units.la: 4. Λύτρον[?] sive pretium redemptionis, quo satisfactum est, est sanguis & mors Jesu Christi. Matth. 20[?]. v. 8. Itemq; Mar. 10. v. 45. Filius hominis non venit, ut sibi ministrari sineret; sed ut ministraret, daretq; animam suam redemptionis pretium (λύτρον) pro multis. Coloss. 1. vers. 14. In Christo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum. 1. Timoth. 2. v. 6. Christus semetipsum dedit redemptionis pretium (ἀντίλυτρον) pro omnibus. 1. Tim. 2. v. 14. Qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate. Heb. 9. v. 12. Per proprium sanguinem ingressus est Christus semel in Sacrarium aeternam redemptionem nactus.
units.tr: 4. The ransom or price of redemption, by which satisfaction was made, is the blood and death of Jesus Christ. Matt. 20 [?] v. 8. Likewise Mark 10 v. 45: The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom (λύτρον) for many. Col. 1 v. 14: In Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. 1 Tim. 2 v. 6: Christ gave himself a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) for all. 1 Tim. 2 v. 14: Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity. Heb. 9 v. 12: By his own blood he entered once into the Sanctuary, having obtained eternal redemption.

units.la: Ut autem passio, effusus sanguis & mors Christi esset pretium sufficiens ꝑ[?] redemtione generis humani, fecit spotanea obedientia filii ad mortem usq; crucis, fecit summa innocentia, ut qui peccatum non fecit, & in cujus ore dolus non est inventus: fecit ipsa hominis innocentis & justi divinitas, siquidem persona patiens, moriens & pretium persolvens non tantum homo, verum etiam Deus erat.
units.tr: That the passion, the shed blood and the death of Christ should be a sufficient price for the redemption of mankind, it was the voluntary obedience of the Son, even unto death, the death of the cross, it was his supreme innocence, since he who did not sin, and in whose mouth no guile was found; it was the very divinity of the innocent and just man, since the person who suffered, died and paid the price was not only man but also God.

units.la: V. Pretium redemptionis accepit Deus, cui se Christus obtulit redemptionem pro nobis in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ, cui nos etiam reconciliavit. Tradidit enim semetipsum pro nobis oblationem & hostiam Deo, in odorem suavitatis. Eph. 5. & 1. Et per Spiritum æternum semetipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, ut purgaret conscientiam nostram ab operibus mortuis, ad serviendum Deo vivo. Hebr. 9. Pretium hoc non Diabolo, sed Deo est persolutum, qui jus damnationis in nos habebat, & Diaboli potestati juste suo judicio nos obnoxios reddiderat. Nam quantum ad Diabolum, injuste hominem tenebat; sed homo interim juste tenebatur, sic prævaricatione ipsius, & justo Dei judicio postulantib", ut Satanæ manciparetur. Deo itaq; satisfecit & reconciliavit nos Christus, ei sese offerens per Spiritum æter-num: atq; ita jam nobis Deo reconcili-atis, cui peccaveramus, Regnum Sata-næ necessario destructum fuit.
units.tr: V. The price of redemption was received by God, to whom Christ offered himself for us as a sweet-smelling savour, to whom he also reconciled us. For he gave himself for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God, for a sweet smell. Eph. 5, and 1: And through the eternal Spirit he offered himself without spot to God, to purge our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God. Heb. 9. This price was paid not to the Devil but to God, who held the right of condemnation over us and had justly, by his judgment, made us liable to the power of the Devil. For as far as the Devil was concerned, he held man unjustly; but man was meanwhile justly held, by his own transgression and the just judgment of God, so that he was delivered over to Satan. Christ therefore satisfied God and reconciled us to him, offering himself to him through the eternal Spirit; and so, now that we have been reconciled to God, whom we had offended, the kingdom of Satan was of necessity destroyed.

units.la: Christus itaq; Servator noster pretioso sanguine suo nos redimens, & dans seipsum ꝑ nobis pretium redemtionis à nobis Deo Patri satisfecit, Satisfecit inquam vera & proprie dicta redemtione, in qua verum λύτρον[?] intervenit.
units.tr: Christ therefore, our Saviour, redeeming us with his precious blood, and giving himself as the price of redemption, satisfied God the Father on our behalf. He satisfied, I say, by a true and properly so-called redemption, in which a true ransom intervened.

units.la: De quo iterum inculco & repeto hæc testimonia, Matth. 20. verf.28. Filius hominis nō venit, ut pateretur sibi ministrari, sed ut ministraret, daretque animam suam in redemtionis pretiū pro multis. Ecce causa adventus Filii Dei in mundū, est ut nobis ministraret non tantum annuntiando nobis viam salutis, sed præcipuè etiam offerendo seipsum ꝑ nobis in cruce ad expiandū nostra peccata. 1. Tim.2. v.6. Qui sese ipse dedit redemtionis pretium pro o-mnibus. En pretium redemtionis dicitur Christus Mediator, quatenus pro nobis in cruce oblatus est, & sanguis eius effusus cum sensu irae Dei.
units.tr: On this I again insist and repeat these testimonies: Matt. 20 verse 28: The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many. Behold the reason for the coming of the Son of God into the world: it was that he might minister to us, not only by announcing to us the way of salvation, but chiefly also by offering himself for us on the cross, to expiate our sins. 1 Tim. 2 v. 6: Who gave himself a ransom for all. Behold, Christ the Mediator is called the price of redemption, inasmuch as he was offered for us on the cross, and his blood was poured out with the sense of the wrath of God.

units.la: Coloss. 1. v. 13. & 14. Pater eripuit nos ex potestate tenebrarum ac transtulit nos in Regnum Filii sui dilecti. In quo habemus redemptionem eius per sanguinem ipsius, hoc est, remissionem peccatorum. En hic sanguis Christi est λύτρον illud, quo redemti sumus, seu quo parta nobis est remissio peccatorum in Christum tanquam Sponsorem cojectorum: ut ita satisfactum intelligatur justitiae Dei.
units.tr: Col. 1 v. 13 and 14: The Father delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son. In whom we have redemption through his blood, that is, the forgiveness of sins. Behold, this blood of Christ is that ransom by which we have been redeemed, or by which forgiveness of sins has been obtained for us, Christ being our surety for those who were held guilty; so that satisfaction is understood to have been made to the justice of God.

units.la: Hebr. 9. v. 12. Christus Pontifex per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in Sacrarium, aeternam redemptionem nactus. Vide hic sanguinem Christi vim habere expiandi peccata, siquidem ipse se per spiritum aeternum obtulit inculpatum Deo, & purgat conscientiam nostram a mortuis operibus. Haec autem vis sanguinis pendet a duabus causis praecipue ab excellentia Divinae naturae, & sanctitate humanae naturae Christi.
units.tr: Heb. 9 v. 12: Christ the High Priest, by his own blood, entered once into the Sanctuary, having obtained eternal redemption. See here that the blood of Christ has the power of expiating sins, since he offered himself without blemish to God through the eternal Spirit, and cleanses our conscience from dead works. This power of the blood depends chiefly on two causes: on the excellence of the divine nature, and on the holiness of the human nature of Christ.

units.la: Illa notatur hoc ipso, quod dicitur ipse obtulisse per Spiritum aeternum: haec vero, cum dicitur semel inculpatum obtulisse. Idem signisignificaturà Pet. 1. Epist. c. 1. cum inquit, nos esse redemtos pretioso sanguine Christi, tanquam Agni inculpati & incontaminati.
units.tr: The former is noted by this very fact, that it is said he offered himself through the eternal Spirit; the latter, when it is said he offered himself once, without blemish. The same thing is signified by 1 Pet. 1, chapter 1, where he says that we were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.

units.la: Actor. 20. v. 28. Deus Ecclesiam proprio illo sanguine acquisivit. Quia sanguis, quâ Ecclesia est acquisita, est pretiosissim*. Est enim sanguis Dei, seu Filii Dei. Nō igitur dubito illo sanguine pro nostris peccatis esse plenissimè Deo satisfactū.
units.tr: Acts 20 v. 28: God acquired the Church with his own blood. Because the blood by which the Church has been acquired is most precious. For it is the blood of God, or of the Son of God. I therefore do not doubt that by that blood full satisfaction has been made to God for our sins.

units.la: Apocal. 5. v. 9. Dignus es, qui accipias li-brum & aperias ejus sigilla; quoniam mactatus es & redemisti nos Deo per sanguinem tuum, En redemtionem nostri factā per sanguinem Mactati agni Dei, qui ideò tollit peccata mundi.
units.tr: Rev. 5 v. 9: You are worthy to take the book and open its seals; for you were slain and have redeemed us to God by your blood. Behold the redemption of us made by the blood of the slain Lamb of God, who therefore takes away the sins of the world.

units.la: 1. Corinth. 6. v. 19. Neq; vos estis vestri ipsorum: quia emti estis pretio, scilicet per Christum, qui nos emit, hoc est, redemit, pretio scilicet magno, quod est sanguis Christi effusus. Et cap. 7. v. 23. Pretio emti estis; ne igitur estote servi hominum, pretio, scilicet sanguine Christi, pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum effuso, qui est, pre-tiosissimus, cum sit sanguis Agni illi-us immaculati, & sit sanguis Filii Dei: adeoq; ipsius Dei.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 6 v. 19: Nor are you your own, for you were bought with a price, namely through Christ, who bought us, that is, redeemed us, with a price, namely a great price, which is the blood of Christ shed. And chapter 7 v. 23: You were bought with a price; do not therefore become servants of men, with a price, namely the blood of Christ, shed for us for the forgiveness of sins, which is most precious, since it is the blood of that spotless Lamb, and is the blood of the Son of God, and so of God himself.

units.la: 1. Pet. 1. v. 18. Vt quisciatis vos non cadu-cis rebus, argento vel auro fuisse redemtos &c. Sed pretioso sanguine, utpote Agni illius immaculati & incontaminati, Christi.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1 v. 18: Knowing that you were redeemed not with corruptible things, silver or gold, etc. But with the precious blood, as of that spotless and undefiled Lamb, Christ.

units.la: Jam hoc ipsum λύτρον[?] nec Diabolo, nec peccato, nec morti (quæ hac ratione abolevit Christus Servator noster) sed justo Deo, execranti omnes legis suæ transgressores, persolutum est. Unde fit, ut per sanguinem hunc Christi di-camur ab illa ventura ira liberati. Hebræor. 2. vers. 14. & 15. Ipse quoq; consimiliter particeps factus est carnis & sanguinis, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis imperium habet, hoc est, Diabolum. Et liberos redderet, quotquot metu mortis per omnem vitam obnoxii erant servi-tuti. 1. Johan. 3. vers. 8. Adhuc patefactus est Filius Dei, ut dissolvat opera Diaboli. Galat. 3. vers. 13. Christus nos redemit ab execratione le-gis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio. Rom. 5. v. 9. Multo magis justificati nunc sanguine ejus, servabimur per illam ab ira illa.
units.tr: Now this very ransom was paid not to the Devil, nor to sin, nor to death (which Christ our Saviour has in this way abolished), but to the just God, who curses all transgressors of his law. Hence it comes about that through this blood of Christ we are said to be delivered from that coming wrath. Heb. 2 vv. 14 and 15: He also likewise partook of flesh and blood, that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil. And might deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to bondage all their life. 1 John 3 v. 8: For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the Devil. Gal. 3 v. 13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, since he became a curse for us. Rom. 5 v. 9: Much more, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved by him from that wrath.

units.la: Adhuc itaque manet Christus Redemtor meus, quatenus verum pretium redemtionis meæ[?] Deo persol-vendo à me satisfecit.
units.tr: Christ therefore remains my Redeemer still, inasmuch as he has made satisfaction on my behalf by paying to God the true price of my redemption.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: ASSERTIO ET DEMONSTRATIO Meriti & satisfactionis Christi, ex eo, quòd Christus tulerit iniquitates nostras; pro nobis fit passus & mortuus; sanguine & morte ejus expiemur & purgemur à peccatis.
units.tr: ASSERTION AND DEMONSTRATION of the merit and satisfaction of Christ, from the fact that Christ bore our iniquities; that he suffered and died for us; and that we are atoned for and cleansed from sins by his blood and death.

units.la: MEDIATOREM, Reconciliatorem & Redemtorem nostrum Jesum Christum esse Sponsorem nostrum, qui sacrificio suo propitiatorio nobis Deum placaverit, pro nobis satisfecerit, & salutem æternam acquisierit, fidem mihi faciunt oracula illa divina, quæ me docent. 1. Christum Jesum iniquitates nostras portasse seu tulisse. 2. Christum pro nobis esse vulneratum afflictum, passum & mortuum. 3. Sanguine & morte Christi peccata nostra expiari, nos ab iis purgari, ab- lui, emundari. Unde jam sigillatim argumentabimur.
units.tr: That Jesus Christ, our Mediator, Reconciler and Redeemer, is our Surety, who by his propitiatory sacrifice has appeased God for us, made satisfaction for us, and obtained eternal salvation, is attested to me by those divine oracles which teach me: (1) that Christ Jesus bore or carried our iniquities; (2) that Christ was wounded, afflicted, suffered and died for us; (3) that our sins are expiated by the blood and death of Christ, and that we are purged, washed and cleansed from them. Therefore we shall now argue each of these point by point.

units.la: CAPITIS V. SECTIO I.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. SECTION I.

units.la: Ut peccata nostra sustulit in corpore suo super lignum, ita ut Deus ipse ei illi tanquam Sponsori nostro imposuerit, ut eorum poenas sustineret, & nos livore eius sanaremur, atque ille peccata nostra auferret: is certè ut Sponsor noster sustinuit personam nostram, & in ea poenas nobis debitas pertulit, ideoq; à nobis persolvit.
units.tr: He bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that God himself laid them upon him as our Surety, that he might undergo their punishments and that we might be healed by his bruises, and he might take our sins away. Certainly he, as our Surety, bore our person, and in it suffered the punishments due to us, and so paid them on our behalf.

units.la: Atqui Christus Iesus, Mediator, Reconciliator & Redemtor noster peccata nostra sustulit in corpore suo super lignum. 1. Pet. 2. ver. 24.
units.tr: But Christ Jesus, our Mediator, Reconciler and Redeemer, bore our sins in his body upon the tree. 1 Pet. 2.24.

units.la: Qui peccata nostra ipsemet sustulit seu sursum tulit in corpore suo super lignum, ut peccatis mortui, justitiae viveremus, cujus vibicib. sanati estis. Nam eratis velut oves errantes, sed conversi nunc estis ad pastorem illum & curatorem animarum vestrarum.
units.tr: He himself bore our sins, that is, carried them up, in his body upon the tree, so that we, being dead to sins, might live to righteousness, by whose stripes you were healed. For you were like sheep going astray, but now you have turned to the shepherd and guardian of your souls.

units.la: Hic explicanda & observanda quaedam sunt. Explicandae sunt primum voces quaedam. 1. ἀνήνεγκεν[?], quidam vertunt pertulit, quod est sustinere & pati, ut intelligatur Christus in corpore suo in cruce poenas peccatis debitas exsolvisse. Quidam vero ἄνωθεν ἤνεγκεν sursum tulit. Er hat vnsere Sünde hinauff getragen auffs [illegible, ~4 letters]/ ut intelligatur, eum respicere verba Jesaiae: Morbos nostros ipse portavit, & dolores nostros bajulavit. Alii vertunt, sustulit, sive abstulit, sicut ad Hebr. 9. v. 28. & Joh. 1. v. 29. dicitur: tollere peccata.
units.tr: Some things here need explaining and noting. First, certain words must be explained. 1. ἀνήνεγκεν [?]: some render it "bore", that is "endured and suffered", so that Christ is understood to have paid in his body on the cross the penalties owed for sins. Others render ἄνωθεν ἤνεγκεν, "carried up". "He has carried our sin up onto the [illegible, about four letters]", so that it is understood he had in mind the words of Isaiah: "He bore our diseases and carried our sorrows." Others render it "took away, or removed", as in Heb. 9.28 and John 1.29, where it is said "to take away sins."

units.la: 2. Deinde dicunt praepositionem IN ex Hebraei sermonis proprietate, hoc in loco significare PER, ut vertendum sit; Qui peccata nostra ipse per corpus suum super lignum sustulit seu abstulit. Sed hic Modus tollendi disceptatur.
units.tr: 2. Then they say that the preposition IN, by the idiom of the Hebrew language, here means THROUGH, so that it must be translated: "who through his body upon the tree took away, or removed, our sins." But the manner of taking away is disputed here.

units.la: Adversarii volunt, Christum corpus suum crucis morti tradendo, suo modo peccata nostra abstulisse, ut negent, Christū sustinuisse peccata nostra, seu poena peccatorum nostro-rū, in suo corpore cruci affixo. Dicunt autem, quod ex eo, quod Christus poenas nostro-rū delictorum exolverit, non sequatur (quae tamen est sententia Petri) eum velle, nos peccato mori, & justitiae vi-vere. Sunt enim haec duo, inquiunt, admodum separata; sicut ex eo, quod quis alicujus debita solverit, non sequi-tur, eum velle, nullum aes alienum jam ab ipso in posterum contrahi. At hoc falsum esse, cuivis sententiam nostram probè examinanti liquet. Retineatur igitur verbum tollere sive auferre, at non illico modus ille, sed hic sequitur: Christus cum convitiis afficeretur, nulla regessit maledicta, cum iniquè ac crudeliter affligeretur, nullam vindictam est minatus, sed eam omnem justè judicanti commisit.
units.tr: Our opponents want Christ, by giving up his body to death on the cross, to have taken away our sins in his own way; they deny that Christ bore our sins, or the punishment of our sins, in his body fixed to the cross. They say that from the fact that Christ paid the penalties of our offences it does not follow (though this is Peter's view) that he wills us to die to sin and live to righteousness. For these two things, they say, are quite separate: just as, from the fact that someone has paid another's debts, it does not follow that he wills that no further debt be contracted by that person in future. But that this is false is clear to anyone who examines our view carefully. Let the word "take away" or "remove" stand, but the manner does not follow at once; rather, the following is what follows: when Christ was reviled, he returned no insults; when he was unjustly and cruelly afflicted, he threatened no vengeance, but committed all to him who judges justly.

units.la: Non sustinuit igitur poenam hanc suis peccatis debitam, quippe qui nulla propria habuit, sed propter nostra peccata perpessus est illa omnia. Etenim peccata nostra per corpus suum ligno crucis affixum sustulit, ut videlicet nos peccatis mortui, justitiae deinceps vivamus, atque ita perfectam sa-lutem obtineamus. Hujus itaq; vibi-cibus & livore, vos quoque Judæi, jam ad fidem conversi, veram animi con-secuti estis sanitatem. Quod si qua ratione istud factum sit, scire vultis, ita habete: Eratis antea velut oves errantes, quam diu in ignorantia & impietate versati estis: sed nunc per sanguinem CHRISTI, pro vobis in cruce effusum, revocati estis ab erroribus illis, ad Pastorem & curatorem illum bonum animarum vestrarum, nempe Iesum Christum, qui vitam suam pro nobis omnibus idcirco profudit, ut nos ab aeterna morte liberatos, aeterna vita donaret.
units.tr: He therefore did not bear this punishment due to his own sins, since he had none of his own, but he suffered all those things on account of our sins. Indeed he took away our sins by his body fixed to the cross of the tree, that is, so that we, being dead to sins, might thereafter live to righteousness, and so obtain perfect salvation. By his bruises and his wound, therefore, you too, Jews, now converted to the faith, have obtained true soundness of soul. If you wish to know in what way this has come about, understand this: "You were formerly like sheep going astray, as long as you lived in ignorance and impiety; but now, through the blood of CHRIST shed for you on the cross, you have been called back from those errors to the shepherd and good guardian of your souls, namely Jesus Christ, who for this reason poured out his life for us all, so that, freed from eternal death, he might grant us eternal life."

units.la: Hic sensus est.
units.tr: This is the sense.

units.la: Hinc observamus Mortis & passionis Christi duplicem finem. 1. Ut per eam peccatis moriamur & justitiae vivamus. 2. Ut reatus peccatorum a nobis auferatur, atque ita nos veram animae sanitatem ac salutem consequamur. Ubi & hoc notandum, sub vocibus, Passionis, Mortis, Sanguinis, Livoris, Crucis, totam Christi humiliationem, sanquam Meritum intelligi debere.
units.tr: Here we observe a twofold end of the death and passion of Christ. 1. That through it we may die to sins and live to righteousness. 2. That the guilt of sins may be taken away from us, and so we may obtain true soundness and salvation of the soul. It must also be noted here that under the words passion, death, blood, bruises, and cross, the whole humiliation of Christ is to be understood, as his merit.

units.la: II. CHRISTUS deinde sucтulit iniquitates nostras, in corpore suo, super lignum, quia Deus peccata nostra CHRISTO, tanquam Sponsori nostro, imposuit, ut eorum illae poenas sustineret, & nos livore ejus sanaremur. Iesaiae 53. v. 6. Omnes nos sicut oves (pecus) erravimus, quisque in viam suam
units.tr: II. CHRIST then bore our iniquities in his body upon the tree, because God laid our sins upon Christ, as our Surety, so that he might undergo their punishments and we might be healed by his bruise. Isaiah 53.6: "We all like sheep (flock) have gone astray, each to his own way."

units.la: NB. dictum am nos convertimus; Jehova autem conjecit in illum iniquitatem seu poenam omnium nostrum.
units.tr: NB. The saying: but we have turned; Jehovah, however, laid upon him the iniquity or punishment of us all.

units.la: 1. Hic aiunt, Verbum Hiphgias non po-nere aut conjicere, sed vel occurrere vel occurrere facere, significare. Ut sit versio, vel: Et Jehova occurrit per eum; seu potius, cum eo, iniquitati omnium nostrum. Vel: Et Jehova occurrere fecit ei, iniquitatem omnium nostrum.
units.tr: 1. Here they say that the Hebrew verb Hiphgias does not mean "to lay upon" or "to cast", but either "to meet" or "to cause to meet". So the translation would be either: And Jehovah met with him, or rather, with him, the iniquity of us all. Or: And Jehovah caused the iniquity of us all to meet him.

units.la: Priore modo, volunt hunc sensum esse: Deum per Christum omnes iniquitates, seu iniquitatum poenas, à nobis, illis quodammodo per ipsum, vel cum ipso, occurrendo depulisse. Posteriore autem modo, sensum hunc: Deum effecisse, ut omnium nostrum iniquitates Christo obviam fierent, & ipsum quodammodo aggrederentur, cum nostrarum iniquitatum causa eum mori voluerit.
units.tr: On the former reading they want this sense: that God, through Christ, removed all iniquities, or the penalties of iniquities, from us, by meeting them in some manner through him or with him. On the latter reading, the sense is this: that God brought it about that the iniquities of us all should meet Christ and in some way attack him, since he willed him to die on account of our iniquities.

units.la: Fatemur, si verbum ex verbo reddatur, dicendum esse: fecit currere in eum: sed haec phrasis aequipollet his: Trajecit, conjecit, traduxit, vel transtulit in eum poenam omnium nostrum. Verbum enim Pahgah, id est, occurrit vel incurrit in Hiphil significat, Fecit incurrere, vel fecit ut incurrat. Qua Phrasi potius incomprehensibilis Dei bonitas extollitur, quâ poenam nostris peccatis debitam in Christum traduxit, ne nos sub peccatorum onere contabesceremus, Deinde vox Hebræa Havon tam pa-nam, quàm culpam significat. Reatus & poena peccatorum in Christum translata & conjecta fuit, eam nostro nomine ipse, ut Sponsor noster, pertulit, & suo sanguine delevit. Inquit Propheta, Veruntamen infirmitates nostras tulit & dolores nostros portavit: nos aute aftimavimus eum plagis afflictum, percussum Dei & afflictum. Sed ipse vulneratus est propter pravaricationes nostras: attritus est propter iniquitates nostras. Castigatio pacis nostra super eum est, & propter livorem ejus sanitas facta est nobis.
units.tr: We grant that, if the word is rendered word for word, it must be said "he made it run upon him"; but this phrase amounts to the same as these: he transferred, cast, carried over, or transferred upon him the punishment of us all. For the Hebrew verb Pahgah, that is "to meet" or "to run upon", in the Hiphil means to cause to run, or to make it run upon. By this phrase rather the incomprehensible goodness of God is extolled, by which he transferred the punishment due to our sins onto Christ, lest we should waste away under the burden of sins. Next, the Hebrew word Havon means both punishment and guilt. The guilt and punishment of sins were transferred and laid upon Christ; he, as our Surety, bore them on our behalf and blotted them out with his blood. The prophet says: Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten of God and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities. The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed.

units.la: 1. Hic dubitatio oritur, quomodo dicat Matthæus Cap.8,17[?]. hanc prophetiam esse impletam, cum Jesus sanaret ægrotos, cum tamen Propheta loquatur non de morbis, qui hærent in corporibus, sed de doloribus & cruciatibus, quos Christus in corpore & anima suâ sensurus erat. Sunt, qui ita interpretentur, quasi illis verbis utrumq; significetur, nempe Christû, cùm morbos & infirmitates humanas, tum earum causas gratiosè ex hominibus ex-mturum[?], videlicet dum propter illorum peccata dolores fit passurus. Aliis videvidetur hoc loco, Metonymice usurpari verbum Impleretur, pro eo, quod est, ut significaretur, per hunc IESVM impletum iri id quod dictum est per Prophetam, &c.
units.tr: 1. Here a doubt arises: how Matthew (ch. 8:17) says that this prophecy was fulfilled when Jesus healed the sick, since the prophet speaks not of diseases which cling to bodies, but of the sorrows and torments which Christ was to feel in body and soul. Some interpret it as if both things were meant by those words: that Christ, having graciously taken away human diseases and infirmities, and their causes from men, namely by suffering sorrows on account of their sins. To others it seems that in this place the verb "was fulfilled" is used metonymically, so that it signifies that "what was said through the prophet would be fulfilled through this Jesus", and so on.

units.la: 2. Deinde in testimonio Iesaiæ verbum Hebræũ Nasa, licet vertatur sustulit, vel abstulit, ut sit sensus: Christum à nobis omnes dolores & languores nostros abstulisse (fatetur autem hic significari reatum & poenam delictorum nostrorum) non tamen negatur statim nostra sententia: Christum portasse nostra peccata & in se suscepisse, & à nobis auferendo, & in se transferendo. Hæc duo enim se invicem non necessario tollunt.
units.tr: 2. Further, in the testimony of Isaiah, the Hebrew word Nasa, although it is rendered "took away" or "removed", so that the sense is that Christ removed from us all our sorrows and languors (but it is admitted that the guilt and penalty of our offences is meant here), nevertheless our view is not at once refuted: that Christ bore our sins and took them upon himself, both by removing them from us and by transferring them to himself. For these two do not necessarily exclude each other.

units.la: Ajunt Hebræi: Verbum Nasa, quando cum nomine Peccatum, vel simili construitur, esse venia & misericordia verbum, & peculiari phrasi significare, onus peccati ab aliquo auferre, & cum sublevare. Sic igitur Christus nostras infirmitates à nobis auferre & in se etiam suscipere dicitur, & eas suâ passione & morte sustulit & abolevit, sic, ut ne unquam amplius appareant.
units.tr: The Hebrews say: The verb Nasa, when it is construed with the word sin or a similar one, is a word of pardon and mercy, and by a peculiar idiom signifies to take the burden of sin away from someone and to relieve him. Thus Christ is said to take our infirmities away from us and also to take them upon himself, and by his passion and death he has taken them away and abolished them, so that they may never appear again.

units.la: Dicimus etiam, Christum dicit[?] peccatum & Mundi tollere, hoc est, ea remittere & condonare, sed id propter mortis suæ preupretium aç[?] meritum. Sic etiam verbū Hebraeū Sabal, Portare, significat, & qui-dem hic onus aliquod ab aliquo tolle-re & assumere, sibiq; imponere, illúd-que portare, & patiendo abolere.
units.tr: We also say that Christ takes away sin and the sins of the world, that is, forgives and pardons them, but he does so on account of the price and merit of his death. In the same way the Hebrew word sabal, "to bear," means to take up some burden from someone, to assume it and lay it on oneself, and to carry it, and by suffering to remove it.

units.la: 3. Castigatio pacis nostrae SUPER EUM, illis significat, Christum flagella & afflictiones subiisse, quae nobis pacem, id est, felicitatem & quietem pepere-runt: Ita autem, ut castigationis vox Afflictionem & Percussionem, non autem Punitionem significet. Atqui Deus sece-rat in ipsum incurrere omnium nostrum poenam, & propter iniquitates nostras, nempe expiandas, ipse attritus hic dicitur. Christus itaq;, ut nos cum Deo pacem haberemus, castigatus est, in se a nobis suscepta omnium nostrum poena pro peccatis nostris,
units.tr: 3. The chastisement of our peace upon him signifies that Christ underwent the scourges and afflictions which brought us peace, that is, happiness and quiet. The word for chastisement, however, means affliction and striking, not punishment. Yet God had determined that the punishment of all of us should fall upon him, and he is said to have been crushed for our iniquities, that is, to make atonement for them. Christ therefore was chastised so that we might have peace with God, the punishment of all of us having been taken up by him, in himself, for our sins.

units.la: 4. In livore ejus, sanitas nobis, legunt illi ad verbum, scilicet, quia livor & mors CHRISTI nos ad Christum convertit, atq; ab errore & perditione nostra in viam salutis revocavit. Bene non nego) Alii legunt: Propter livorem ejus sa-nitas nobis facta est, Sed livorem & mortem Christi tantum esse causam nostræ ad Christum conversionis, & simul Meritoriam sanationis nostræ, nec credere posse um, nec pondera verborum in hoc capite permittunt.
units.tr: 4. "By his stripes we are healed," they read literally, namely, because the bruise and death of Christ turned us to Christ and recalled us from error and ruin to the way of salvation. I do not deny that this is good. Others read: "By his stripes we have been made whole." But the words of this chapter do not allow us to believe that the bruise and death of Christ is only the cause of our conversion to Christ, and at the same time the meritorious ground of our healing.

units.la: III. Sic igitur Christus instar illius Emissarii Capri, de quo Levit. 16. super quem Aaron, jussu Dei, omnia populi delicta confitebatur, & ejus capiti imponebat, quæ ille deinde emissus, in desertum secum asportabat, peccata nostra abstulit. Auferre autem peccata, non solum à peccatorum pœnis liberare, sed etiam ab ipsa peccati servitute, in hac vita, vindicare, significare, non nego, modo liberatio illa Meritum, quo à Christo acquisita est, nō excludat.
units.tr: III. So Christ, like that scapegoat of which we read in Leviticus 16, upon which Aaron, at God's command, confessed all the transgressions of the people and laid them on its head, and which was then sent away and carried them with it into the wilderness, has taken away our sins. I do not deny that to take away sins signifies not only to free from the punishments of sins, but also to deliver from the very bondage of sin in this life, provided that this deliverance, by which it has been obtained from Christ, is merit and is not excluded.

units.la: Dicitur insuper de Christo Psal. 69.5. Reddidit, quæ non rapuit. Et Jes. 53. Inter iniquos reputatus est, ut sciamus, eum suscepisse nostram personam, & in eâ pœnas nobis debitas pertulisse.
units.tr: Moreover, it is said of Christ in Psalm 69:5, "He restored what he did not take away." And in Isaiah 53, "He was reckoned among the wicked," so that we may know that he took upon himself our person and in it bore the punishments due to us.

units.la: Manet itaq; Christus Sponsor meus, qui portando & tollendo mea peccata, ac potius peccatorum pœnas, à me persolvit & satisfecit.
units.tr: Christ therefore remains my Surety, who, by bearing and taking away my sins, or rather the punishments of sins, has paid and satisfied them for me.

units.la: CAPI.
units.tr: CAPI.

units.la: CAPITIS V. SECTIO II.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. SECTION II.

units.la: SI Christus pro nobis, pro peccatis nostris, propter peccata nostra, est vulneratus, attritus, passus, & deniq; mortuus, ita, ut prapositi-ones illa, PRO & PROPTER, indicent, & causam finalem, & efficientem impulsivam, ita nimirum, ut in finali causa intelligamus satisfactionem, in efficiente impulsiva Imputationem: Utiq; Christus patiendo & moriendo pro nobis judicio Dei satisfecit, & poenas peccatis nostris debitas exsolvit.
units.tr: If Christ was wounded, crushed, suffered, and at last died for us, for our sins, on account of our sins, so that those prepositions, FOR and ON ACCOUNT OF, indicate both a final cause and an efficient impulsive cause, namely that in the final cause we understand satisfaction, and in the efficient impulsive cause imputation: then clearly Christ, by suffering and dying for us, satisfied the judgment of God and paid the penalties owed for our sins.

units.la: Atqui Christus pro nobis, pro peccatis nostris, propter peccata nostra, in S. literis dicitur vulneratus, attritus, passus & deniq; mortuus. Sed parumper subsistamus, & audiamus alios, qui fatentur, &, ut dicunt, in Deo suo gloriantur, Jesum Christum, Dei Filium, propter iniquitates nostras, & pro peccatis nostris, ut universa sacra Scriptura testatur, mortuum esse: sed inde tamen consequi constanter negant, Christum Dei judicio pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, sive illi id solvisse, quod nos propter peccata nostra solvere debuissemus. Mori enim propter peccata, inquiunt illi, seu pro peccatis alicujus, nihil aliud est, quàm causa sive Occasione Peccatorum illius mori.
units.tr: But Christ for us, for our sins, on account of our sins is said in the Holy Scriptures to have been wounded, crushed, to have suffered and at last to have died. But let us pause a little and hear others, who confess, and, as they say, glory in their God, that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, died for our iniquities and for our sins, as all of holy Scripture testifies; yet they firmly deny that it follows from this that Christ satisfied for our sins by God's judgment, or paid to him what we ought to have paid on account of our sins. For to die on account of sins, they say, or for someone's sins, is nothing other than to die because of, or on the occasion of, someone's sins.

units.la: Causa autem sive Occasione peccatorum alicujus is certè moritur, qui ideò moritur, ut quis à peccatis suis retrahatur, utque illi fides fiat, peccata sibi, si ab illis se retraxerit, condonatum iri, ac praeterea, ut is fructum ejusmodi condonationis, & ita ipsam condonationem reipsa sentiat & consequatur. Atque ut nobis omnia haec evenirent, mortuus est Christus.
units.tr: But he surely dies because of, or on the occasion of, someone's sins who dies so that someone may be drawn back from his sins, and so that faith may be made in him that, if he withdraws from them, his sins will be forgiven; and besides, so that he may feel and obtain in fact the fruit of such forgiveness, and thus forgiveness itself. And Christ died so that all these things might happen to us.

units.la: Docent etiam, posse aliquem puniri, propter sua vel aliena peccata, nec tamen pro ipsis satisfacere. Item: Præpositionem PROPTER, non solùm finalem, sed etiam efficientem causam significare posse, sed PRO, semper finalem notare. Jam ad probationem nostram accedamus.
units.tr: They also teach that someone can be punished on account of his own or others' sins, and yet not satisfy for them. Likewise: the preposition PROPTER can signify not only a final but also an efficient cause, but PRO always denotes a final cause. Now let us come to our proof.

units.la: I. CHRISTUM, Jes. 53. legimus Vulneratum esse, propter praevaricationes nostras, & attritum esse, propter iniquitates nostras. Hic ajunt, dictione Hebraeam, quae reddita est PROPTER, esse MIN, quae non causam finalem, sed efficientem notat. Hinc ita nonnulli ververtunt: Ipse dolore afficitur à defectionibus nostris, atteritur ab iniquitatibus nostris.
units.tr: I. We read in Isaiah 53 that Christ was wounded on account of our transgressions, and crushed on account of our iniquities. Here they say the Hebrew word translated PROPTER is MIN, which denotes not a final but an efficient cause. Hence some translate thus: He is afflicted with grief by our defections, he is crushed by our iniquities.

units.la: Certè verum est, hîc caussam reddi, cur Christus tanta passus sit, nimirum nostra peccata. Sed particulam MIN hîc vim habere præpositionis Propter, alii observant, ut vertendum sit: vulneratus est propter prævaricationes nostras.
units.tr: Certainly it is true that a cause is given here why Christ suffered so much, namely our sins. But others observe that the particle MIN here has the force of the preposition propter, so that it must be rendered: he was wounded on account of our transgressions.

units.la: Ut ita utrumque constet, & nostra peccata esse caussam efficientem passionis Christi, & expiationem peccatorum nostrorum esse finem illius.
units.tr: So that both may stand: that our sins are the efficient cause of Christ's passion, and that the expiation of our sins is its end.

units.la: Heb. 2. v. 9. Sed Iesum illum cernimus{1} gloria & honore coronatum; qui paulo fuit inferior Angelis factus, propter mortis perpessionem ut beneficio DEI [?] pro omnibus Mortem gustaret. Objectio est: At nunc nondum videmus ei omnia esse subjecta.
units.tr: Heb. 2:9. "But we see that Jesus, crowned with glory and honour, who was made a little lower than the angels, because of the suffering of death, by the grace of God, might taste death for all." Objection: "But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him."

units.la: Responsio est: Etsi ipsis credentibus adhuc in terra militant, nondum sunt omnia subjecta: tamen omnia subjecta sunt ipsorum Principi & Capiti Christo, quippe qui jam in cœlis gloria & honore coronatus est. Ec cùm Christus per mortem in gloriam suam sit ingressus, hac occasione de morte Christi disserit, & ait, Christum factum esse hominem, ut mortem perpeti posset, et subdit, Deum ex gratuita Misericordia Christum nobis ordinasse in Sacerdotem, qui sacrificio sua mortis expiaret omnium nostrum peccata, gustando pro illis mortem, ac iram Dei adversus peccata nostra, qua ipse ut Sponsor in se receperat.
units.tr: Answer: Even though the believers still fight on earth and not all things are yet subjected to them, nevertheless all things are subjected to their Prince and Head, Christ, who is already crowned with glory and honour in heaven. And since Christ entered into his glory through death, on this occasion he discourses about the death of Christ, and says that Christ was made man so that he could suffer death; and he adds that God, from free mercy, appointed Christ for us as Priest, who by the sacrifice of his death would expiate the sins of all of us, tasting death for them, and the wrath of God against our sins, which he as Surety had taken upon himself.

units.la: His ita stantibus, nō eo inficias, nos benignitate Dei maximum beneficium consecutos esse ex morte Christi, cum propter ipsam mortem Christus gloria & honore coronatus fuerit, ideo nos quoq; gloria & honore coronabi-mur suo tempore: Sed simul intelligo, eum ꝓ[?] peccatis nostris expiandis gu-stasse mortem.
units.tr: Given these things, I do not deny that by God's kindness we have obtained the greatest benefit from the death of Christ, since Christ was crowned with glory and honour because of that death, so that we too will be crowned with glory and honour in due time. But at the same time I understand that he tasted death for the expiation of our sins.

units.la: Johan. 10. 15. Ego animam meam, id est, vitam depono pro ovibus. Et Johan. 17. 19. Pro eis ego sanctifico me ipsum, ut sint & ipsi sanctificati per veritatem. Pro eis, scilicet, ut eis promerear apud te remissionem peccatorum, & vitam æternam. Uti Christus ipse, in institutione sacræ cœnæ, exponit præpositionem ἀντί, positam ꝓ ὑπὲρ[?], cum ait: Hoc est sanguis meus novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in re-missimissionem peccatorum. Sanctifico meipsum, id est, offero me tibi in sanctam victi-mam.
units.tr: John 10:15. "I lay down my soul, that is, my life, for the sheep." And John 17:19. "For them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified through the truth." For them, namely, that I may merit for them forgiveness of sins and eternal life from you. As Christ himself explains in the institution of the Lord's Supper, the preposition anti [ἀντί], used for hyper [ὑπέρ], when he says: "This is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins." "I sanctify myself," that is, I offer myself to you as a holy victim.

units.la: Johan. 6. 51. Panis autem, quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam dabo, scilicet crucifigendam pro mundi vita, id est, ad ꝑmeren-dam vitam aeternam mundo. Caro autem Christi crucifixa, est cibus nobis vivificus, quia est personaliter unita Filio Dei, fuit aequivalens pretium ad satisfaciendum pro nostris peccatis, quę ipsi fuerant a Deo imposita, & fide manducatur ad salutem.
units.tr: John 6:51. "The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give," namely to be crucified for the life of the world, that is, to obtain eternal life for the world. Now the crucified flesh of Christ is life-giving food for us, because it is personally united to the Son of God; it was an equivalent price to satisfy for our sins, which had been imposed on him by God, and it is eaten by faith unto salvation.

units.la: Hoc certe non tantum significat ge-neraliter, propter nostram salutem, vel nostri caussa, eum esse mortuum, quo modo & nos animam pro fratribus ponere jubemur, 1. Joh. 3. 16. & dum omnia sustinemus propter electos, ut est 2. Tim. 2. 10, & Col.1. 24. Sed significat, propter peccata nostra, ipsi imputata, traditum esse in mortem. Sic enim legimus Rom. 4. 25. Christus traditus est propter lapsus nostros, Christus à Deo Patre traditus est in mortem, ad expiandum nostra peccata.
units.tr: This certainly does not mean only in general that he died for our salvation, or for our sake, in the way that we too are commanded to lay down our lives for the brethren (1 John 3:16), and "while we endure all things for the elect" (2 Tim. 2:10; Col. 1:24). But it signifies that he was delivered to death on account of our sins, imputed to him. For so we read in Rom. 4:25: "Christ was delivered on account of our offences; Christ was delivered by God the Father to death, to expiate our sins."

units.la: I. Corinth. 15[?]. 3. Tradidi enim vobis in-primis, quod & accepi, Christum videlicet mortuum esse pro peccatis nostris, secundum scripturas. Pro peccatis nostris, id est, peccatorum causa, ut expiaret ea.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15:3. "For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures." "For our sins," that is, on account of sins, to expiate them.

units.la: 1. Pet. 3. v. 18: Nam & Christus semel pro peccatis (id est, propter peccata nostra) justus pro injustis, ut nos ad Deum adduceret, id est, ut nos, purgatos a peccatis, ad beatam D e i communionem addu-ceret.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 3:18. "For Christ also suffered once for sins" (that is, on account of our sins), "the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God," that is, that he might bring us, cleansed from sins, into the blessed communion of God.

units.la: III. Et quidem sic mortuus est, ut quia unus ille mortuus est, omnes mortui esse censeamur. Ut videre est, 2. Corinth. 5, v. 12. Caritas enim illa Christi constringit nos, ut qui hoc statuerimus, si unus pro omnibus mortuus fuit (hoc simpliciter accipio de satisfactione pro peccatis nostris; Unus nempe Christus) nempe hos omnes fuisse mortuos (id est, perinde esse, ac si illi omnes essent mortui, & moriendo pro suis peccatis satisfecissent) & illum pro omnibus mortuum esse, ut qui vivunt, posthac non sibi vivant, sed ei, qui pro ipsis mortuus est et resurrexit. (Ut ita mors & resurrectio CHRISTI tendant ad nostri tùm justificationem, tùm regenerationem). Sic equidem non est pro nobis crucifixus. 1. Cor. 1. v. 13[?].
units.tr: III. And indeed he died in such a way that, because that one died, we are reckoned to have all died. As can be seen in 2 Cor. 5:14: "For the love of Christ constrains us, since we judge this: if one died for all" (I take this simply of satisfaction for our sins; that one, namely Christ), "then all died" (that is, it is the same as if they had all died and by dying had satisfied for their own sins), "and he died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them." (So that the death and resurrection of Christ tend to our justification and also to our regeneration.) Thus indeed he was not crucified for us (1 Cor. 1:13).

units.la: Quid? quòd dicatur CHRISTUS pro nobis factus Maledictio, ut nos à maledictione legis eximeremur. Gal. 3. v. 13. Ubi dicitur, quòd Christus ab illa legis execratione nos asseruerit[?], factus pro nobis execratio, quatenus exsecrabilem crucis mortem nostrâ caussâ adierit.
units.tr: What of the fact that Christ is said to have been made a curse for us, so that he might free us from the curse of the law? Gal. 3:13. Where it is said that Christ rescued us from that execration of the law, having been made an execration for us, inasmuch as he underwent the accursed death of the cross on our account.

units.la: Ecce dilectus Dei Filius, quatenus exsecrabilem crucis mortem pro nobis reconciliandis obiit, non immerito.
units.tr: Behold the beloved Son of God, inasmuch as he underwent the accursed death of the cross to reconcile us, not undeservedly.

units.la: Execratio pro nobis factus dicitur: nempe ut sua temporali morte, æternam, quæ nobis imminebat, aboleret.
units.tr: He is said to be made "an execration for us": namely, that by his temporal death he might abolish the eternal death which hung over us.

units.la: Ergo patere jam arbitror, praepositi-ones illas, in his dictis, PRO & PRO-PTER, indicare & finalem causam, & efficientem impulsivam, ita nimirum, ut in finali causa intelligamus satisfa-ctionem, in efficiente impulsiva Impu-tationem: quia nisi per mortem Chri-sti nec potuerunt nobis peccata remit-ti, nec in nobis aboleri. Heb. 9. 22. 23. Absque sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Itaque necesse fuit exemplaria quidem eorum, quae sunt in coelis, hisce rebus purificari; ipsa vero coelestia, potioribus, quam ha sint, victimis, &c.
units.tr: Therefore I think it is now plain that those prepositions, PRO and PROPTER, in these sayings, indicate both a final cause and an efficient impulsive cause, namely that in the final cause we understand satisfaction, and in the efficient impulsive cause imputation: because unless through the death of Christ sins could neither be remitted to us nor abolished in us. Heb. 9:22-23: "Without shedding of blood there is no remission. Therefore it was necessary that the copies of the things in the heavens should be purified with these things; but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these," etc.

units.la: CAPITIS V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: SECTIO III.
units.tr: SECTION III.

units.la: Qui peccata nostra suo sanguine expiavit, nos a peccatis purgat, non tantum quo ad effectum, & cognitionem ejus expiationis in nobis, sed etiam re ipsa, effundendo nimirum sanguinem suum in remissionem peccatorum nostrorum, & se ipsum immaculatum pro nobis offerendo Deo Patri, ita ut tollat peccatum, adeoque id, quod nos a Deo separavit, & sic Deo reconciliet; & sic expiat peccata reipsa, quoad impetrationem expiationis apud Deum: is profecto jure optimo iram Dei placasse, judicio Dei pro nobis satisfecisse, & pacem ac vitam aeternam nobis promeruisse dici potest.
units.tr: He who has atoned for our sins by his own blood cleanses us from our sins, not only as regards the effect and our knowledge of that atonement, but also in very deed, namely by pouring out his blood for the forgiveness of our sins and by offering himself, a spotless offering, to God the Father for us. In this way he takes away sin, and so that which separated us from God, and thus reconciles us to God. And so he really atones for sins, as regards the obtaining of atonement before God. Such a one may rightly be said to have appeased the wrath of God, to have made satisfaction for us to the judgement of God, and to have merited peace and eternal life for us.

units.la: At vero Iesus Christus suo sanguine peccata nostra expiavit, non tantum, quoad effectum et cognitionem expiationis.
units.tr: But Jesus Christ atoned for our sins by his own blood, not merely as regards the effect and the knowledge of the atonement.

units.la: Adversarii enim Primum docent, expiare peccata, non esse pro ipsis justitiae divinae satisfacere, sed eorum reatum auferre, & ea purgare. Nam verbum Hebraeum Caphar idem significare, quod tegere & operire, ita ut intelligas, peccata non alia ratione expiari, & auferri, nisi quia teguntur & absconduntur, nimirum a DEo, sive DEi gratia & benignitate. Verbum vero CHRISTUS significare idem, quod nobis Mun-dare & purgare: purgari autem nulla alia ratione peccata, quàm clementia & pu-râ ipsius DEi benignitate, dum scilicet ea nobis liberaliter condonat.
units.tr: For our opponents first teach that to atone for sins is not to satisfy the justice of God for them, but to remove their guilt and cleanse them. For the Hebrew word Caphar means the same as "to cover and conceal," so that you might understand that sins are atoned for and taken away in no other way than because they are covered and hidden, namely by God, that is, by the grace and kindness of God. Moreover, the word CHRISTUS means for us the same as "to cleanse and purge." Sins are purged in no other way than by the mercy and pure kindness of God himself, when he freely pardons them for us.

units.la: Interim concedunt, hominem sua quoque expiare peccata posse, quatenus ea facit, quae DEus fieri vult, ut hanc supremam ejus liberalitatem in condo-nando experiamur & cōsequamur, scilicet si obedientiam praestet.
units.tr: Meanwhile they concede that a man can also atone for his own sins, insofar as he does what God wills to be done, so that we may experience and obtain this supreme liberality of his in pardoning, namely if he renders obedience.

units.la: 2. Secundò tradunt, veram oblationem expiatoriam corporis Christi, quā auctor ad Hebręos legalibus sacrificiis opponit, non esse ipsius Christi mortem, & per mortem ingressum in cœlū, ubi nunc pro nobis coram Deo apparet.
units.tr: 2. Secondly, they teach that the true expiatory offering of Christ's body, which the author of Hebrews sets against the legal sacrifices, is not Christ's death itself, nor through death his entry into heaven, where he now appears before God for us.

units.la: I. Conferunt autem ipsius Christi mortem cum sacrificiis legalibus expi-oriis, primùm in expiationis effecto, inde in ejus cognitione, similiter, & pariter,
units.tr: I. They compare Christ's death with the legal expiatory sacrifices, first in the effect of expiation, then in its knowledge, in a similar and parallel way.

units.la: 1. In effecto sic: Ut sacrificia illa legalia non ideo peccata expiare dicta fuerint, quod in ipsis aliquid esset, quod vel Deum ad condonanda peccata movere posset, vel ejus, pro quo offerebantur, culpam compensaret; Sed quia ipsis peractis, expiatio, quae ex pura Dei benignitate pendebat, statim consequebatur, hoc est, ille a poena suis peccatis debita penitus eximebatur: Ita etiam (inquiunt illi) Christi mors peccata nostra expiasse dicitur, non quia vel Deum ad peccata nobis condonanda moverit, vel delictorum nostrorum culpam compesaverit (hic plane dissentimus) sed quia peccatorum nostrorum expiatio, quae ex sola Dei clementia tota pendebat, Christi supplicio peracto, statim consecuta est.
units.tr: 1. As to the effect, it goes like this: those legal sacrifices were not called atoning because there was anything in them that could move God to forgive sins, or that could compensate for the guilt of the one for whom they were offered. Rather, when they had been performed, the atonement, which depended entirely on the pure kindness of God, followed at once; that is, the one was wholly freed from the punishment owed for his sins. So too (they say) the death of Christ is said to have atoned for our sins, not because it moved God to forgive us our sins, or because it compensated for the guilt of our offences (here we plainly disagree), but because the atonement of our sins, which depended wholly on the mercy of God alone, followed at once upon the completed punishment of Christ.

units.la: Simul enim atq; Christus crucis mortem passus fuit, id ex Dei decreto adeptus est, ut non solum ipse immortali & sempiterna vita donatus fuerit, sed nos quoq;, qui illi fidem habemus, & ipsius sumus, eadem donandi potestatem habuerit. Sic igitur expiatio pec-catoeatorum nihil aliud est, quàm à morte, peccati poenâ, plena & perpetua libe-ratio.
units.tr: For as soon as Christ suffered death on the cross, he obtained by the decree of God that not only he himself was given immortal and everlasting life, but that he also had the power to give the same to us, who believe in him and belong to him. Thus the atonement of sins is nothing other than a full and lasting deliverance from death, the punishment of sin.

units.la: 2. In cognitione sic fit collatio: Sic-ut sacrificiis illis peractis, is, pro quo victima offerebatur, iam de divina erga se benignitate & placatione amplius dubitare non poterat, & sibi delictum suum condonatum, pro certo habe-bat: Sic morte ([illegible, ~7 letters])Christi, seu supplicio ejus peracto, nemo est, qui, Deum nos supremâ caritate complexum fuisse, non agnoscat, eumque erga nos placatissimum non videat, qui dile-ctissimum Filium suum, ut nobis ad aeternam salutem, eâ viâ, quam ipse ad potentiam & gloriam suam patefaci-endam sapientissimè elegit, Dux & Præcursor esset, tantis malis objecerit; & jam sibi universa delicta, ipsius summâ liberalitate, condonata esse (iis tamen conditionibus acceptis, quas ipse æquissimas in condonatione adscripsit) pro certo non habeat.
units.tr: 2. As to knowledge, the comparison goes like this: just as, when those sacrifices had been performed, the one for whom the victim was offered could no longer doubt the divine kindness and appeasement towards him, and held for certain that his offence was forgiven him; so, by the death of [illegible] Christ, or by his completed punishment, there is no one who does not acknowledge that God has embraced us with supreme love, and does not see that he is most appeased towards us, who exposed his most beloved Son to such great evils, so that he might be leader and forerunner to our eternal salvation by that way which he most wisely chose for displaying his power and glory; and no one can hold for certain that all his offences have been forgiven him by the supreme liberality of God (on those conditions, however, which he himself laid down as most just in forgiving).

units.la: II. Imparitèr verò conferunt Christi mortem, cum victimis legalibus, cùm docent, duplici de causa ipsam Christi mortem multo plus efficere in expiandis peccatis: Unam dicunt, quod sacrificia illa à peccatorum quidè poenâ liberabant, verùm à peccatis populum cessare non faciebant: Sed Christi mors non solùm à peccatorum poenâ nos subtrahit, sed etiam, ut à peccâdo desistamus, efficit.
units.tr: II. They compare Christ's death unequally with the legal victims, since they teach that for two reasons the death of Christ itself accomplishes far more in expiating sins. The first reason they give is that those sacrifices indeed freed the people from the punishment of sins, but did not make the people cease from sinning. But the death of Christ not only delivers us from the punishment of sins, but also brings it about that we give up sinning.

units.la: Alteram dicunt, quod sacrificia illa ab antecedentium anni illius tantum, delictorum reatu populum liberū reddebant: Christi autem mors, & à praecedentium omnium delictorum, & à futurorum reatu, nos liberos reddit, nosque in perpetuum sanctificat, & coram Deo inculpatos in sempiternum efficit.
units.tr: The second reason they give is that those sacrifices freed the people only from the guilt of the offences of that year which had gone before; but the death of Christ frees us from the guilt both of all offences past and of those to come, and sanctifies us for ever, and makes us blameless before God for eternity.

units.la: Haec de sententiâ Adversariorum praemittere volui. Jam ad assumti mei confirmationem.
units.tr: I wanted to set these things out first, from the opinion of our opponents. Now to the confirmation of my assertion.

units.la: I. Sicut secundum legem Mosis omnia sanguine victimarum mundabatur. Heb. 9. 22. Omniaferè secundum legem sanguine purificantur: & absq; sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Etsi peccata non reipsâ isto sanguine expiarentur: Heb.10. ab initio. Ibi probat auctor sacrificia legalia non sanctificasse cultores, seu non abstulisse aut expiasse eorum peccata, tribus argumentis.
units.tr: I. Just as, according to the law of Moses, all things were cleansed by the blood of victims (Heb. 9.22): "Almost all things are cleansed by blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness." Even though sins were not really atoned for by that blood itself. Heb. 10, from the beginning: there the author proves, by three arguments, that the legal sacrifices did not sanctify the worshippers, that is, did not take away or atone for their sins.

units.la: 1. Quia non desierunt offerri (nempe durante politia Mosaica) sed quotannis iterum fuerunt oblata, 2. Quia fuit opus, quotanis apud sacrificia illa, ex praescripto legis, Levit. 16. repetero peccatorum confessionem, 3. Quia sanguis taurorum & hircorum non potest auferre peccata, nempe propter naturalem vilitatem. Ita sanguis Christi Jesu Filii Dei verè & re ipsa (non tantum effectu [?] & cognitione) expiat omnia nostra peccata. Hoc probant sequentia testimonia. 1. Johan. 1, v. 7. Quod si in luce incedimus, sicut ipse est in luce; communionem habemus cum eo mutuam, & sanguis Jesu Christi Filii Dei purgat nos ab omni peccato.
units.tr: (1) Because they did not cease to be offered (namely while the Mosaic polity lasted), but were offered again every year; (2) because, in those sacrifices, according to the prescription of the law (Lev. 16), there had to be each year a repeated confession of sins; (3) because the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins, on account of its natural worthlessness. So the blood of Christ Jesus, the Son of God, truly and in very deed (not merely in effect and knowledge) atones for all our sins. The following testimonies prove this. 1 John 1.7: "But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin."

units.la: Purgatio peccatorum, est remissio seu condonatio peccatorum, per quam fit, ut poenas propter peccata non luamus, verum loco earum praemium vitae aeternae reportemus, Psalm. 32. 1. 2. Alio tamen sensu peccata purgari dicuntur, cum ab eorum servitute eximimur, sive cum à peccatis ad serviendum Deo vivo convertimur, Heb. 9. 14. Utraq; hæc purgatio in nobis est necessario conjuncta, 1.Corint. 6. 10.11. Sed non tollit purgationem per sanguinem.
units.tr: The purging of sins is the remission or pardon of sins, by which it comes about that we do not pay penalties on account of sins, but instead obtain the reward of eternal life (Ps. 32.1, 2). Yet in another sense sins are said to be "purged" when we are freed from their servitude, or when we are turned from sins to serve the living God (Heb. 9.14). Both of these purgings are necessarily joined in us (1 Cor. 6.10, 11). But this does not remove the purging through blood.

units.la: Causæ hujus purgationis, de quâ hic, tres observari possunt. Prima exprimitur v. 9. nempe liberalis Dei benignitas, quâ ipse nullis nostris meritis provocatus, veniam omnium peccatorum ultrò nobis offert, si modò in Christum credamus ac respiscamus. Hic ipse se debitorem quodammodo nobis constituit, ac proinde pro sua æquitate ac fidelitate promissum præstat: Fidelis est ac justus Deus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & purget nos ab omni iniquitate.
units.tr: Of the cause of this purging, of which we speak here, three things can be noted. The first is expressed in verse 9, namely the free kindness of God, by which he, moved by none of our merits, offers pardon of all sins to us of his own accord, if only we believe in Christ and repent. Here he makes himself in some sense a debtor to us, and accordingly, by his justice and faithfulness, he performs what he has promised: "God is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

units.la: 2. Altera causa exprimitur v. 7. nempe Sanguis Christi Filii Dei, qui tamen hic ꝑ[?] tota Christi oblatione, per quâ peccata expiantur, accipi debet. Mentio-ne interim Sanguinis & Mortis Christi, in purgationis hujus doctrinâ, velut cō-pendio quodam, nobis ob oculos ponitur Immensa Dei & Christi erga nos Caritas, per quā à peccatis eximimur. Rom. 5. 1. & Cap. 8. v. 23. Ephes. 1. 6. 7. Joh. 10. 11. &c. Purgantur autem sic nostra peccata, quatenus ipse, utpote Mediator ac Sponsor novi fœderis, ea dixit, fecit, passus & adeptus est, per quæ peccatorum remissionis, à Deo decretæ, non modo cognitionem, verum etiam effectum reipsa in nobis producit.
units.tr: The second cause is expressed in verse 7, namely "the blood of Christ the Son of God," which, however, here must be taken to mean the whole offering of Christ, by which sins are atoned for. By the mention of the blood and death of Christ, in this doctrine of purging, as in a kind of summary, the immense love of God and Christ towards us, by which we are freed from sins, is set before our eyes (Rom. 5.1; ch. 8.23; Eph. 1.6, 7; John 10.11, etc.).
