Our sins are purged in this way inasmuch as he, as Mediator and Surety of the new covenant, has said, done, suffered and obtained those things by which he produces in us, in very deed, not only the knowledge but also the effect of the remission of sins decreed by God.

units.la: 3. Tertia causa, vel potius conditio, est Lux & in luce ambulatio. Fides scilicet viva, cum quā necessariò vera cohæret ad Deum conversio. Requiritur enim hic conditio ambulandi in luce, ab iis, qui peccata sua reipsā purgari volunt. Etv. 9. Confessio peccatorum, seu pœnitentia similiter ante purgationem peccatorum exigitur. Hinc pœnitentia passim cum remissione peccatorum conjungitur. Actor. 3. 19. & 8. 22.
units.tr: 3. The third cause, or rather condition, is light and walking in the light. That is, living faith, with which a true conversion to God necessarily goes together. For here the condition is that those who want their sins actually purged must walk in the light. Etv. 9. Confession of sins, or repentance, is likewise required before the purging of sins. Hence repentance is everywhere joined with the remission of sins. Acts 3:19 and 8:22.

units.la: Hinc etiam est, quòd nos ipsi in S. literis peccata nostra purgare, sive nos ab eis mundari & lavari dicimur, quatenus sc. conditionem fidei & pœnitentiæ, per Dei gratiam, præstamus, atq; ita veniā peccatorū reipsā consequimur. Jef. 1. 16. Ier. 4. 14. 2. Cor. 7. 1. 2. Tim. 2. 22. 1. Pet. 1. 22.
units.tr: Hence too it is that in the Holy Scriptures we are said to purge our own sins, or to be cleansed and washed from them, inasmuch as we, by God's grace, perform the condition of faith and repentance, and so actually obtain forgiveness of sins. Isa. 1:16. Jer. 4:14. 2 Cor. 7:1. 2 Tim. 2:22. 1 Pet. 1:22.

units.la: Caussa ... tia quae et-iam effectu, effi potest.
units.tr: Cause ... which can also be effective by its effect.

units.la: 1. Iohan. 3. 4. Si ita vero interpreteris, ut ex ambulatione in luce, confirmemur in fide remissionis peccatorum, nolo repugnare.
units.tr: 1 John 3:4. If, however, you so interpret it that, by walking in the light, we are strengthened in faith in the forgiveness of sins, I am not willing to object.

units.la: Porro, 1. Iohan. 2. 2. Iesus Christus iustus, ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: nec pro nostris solum, sed etiam pro totius mundi. 1. Iohan. 3. 10. In hoc est caritas, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & miserit Filium suum, ut esset propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Apoc. 1. 5. Iesus Christus, fidus ille testis, primogenitus ille ex mortuis, ac Princeps Regum terrae, dilexit nos, & lavit nos a peccatis per sanguinem suum.
units.tr: Further, 1 John 2:2: Jesus Christ the righteous is himself the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. 1 John 4:10: Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Rev. 1:5: Jesus Christ, that faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead and the prince of the kings of the earth, loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood.

units.la: Hic autem sciendum est, Christum dici, Propitiationem seu propitiatorem peccatorum nostrorum, quia seipsum Deo Patri obtulit victimam propitiatoriam, sive expiatricem pro peccatis nostris. Atque ita effecit, ut quotquot in ipsum credimus, non modo cognitionem, verum etiam ipsum factum remissionis peccatorum consequamur: partim, cum vi illius sacrificii sui nos a peccatis nostris abstrahit; partim, cum reatum istum nostrum coram Deo abolet, nosque ab aeterna morte liberatos ad vitam sempiternam traducit, atqș ita à se verè nobis impetratam & promeritam vitam nobiscum communicat.
units.tr: Here, however, it must be noted that Christ is called the propitiation or propitiator of our sins, because he offered himself to God the Father as a propitiatory, or expiatory, victim for our sins. And so he brought it about that all of us who believe in him obtain not only the knowledge but the actual fact of the forgiveness of sins: partly, in that by the power of his sacrifice he draws us away from our sins; partly, in that he abolishes our guilt before God and, having freed us from eternal death, brings us to everlasting life, and so shares with us the life which he has truly obtained and merited for us.

units.la: II. Expiat ergò Sanguis hic Filii Dei peccata nostra, quia in remissione pec-catorum nostrorū,ut Filii Dei sanguis, est effusus. Matth.26.28. Hoc est sanguis meum Novi Testamenti: qui pro multis effun-ditur in remissionem peccatorum. Lucas ait: Hoc poculum est Novum illud Testamentum in sanguine meo, qui pro vobis effunditur. Vel quia Christus se ipsum immaculatum obtulit, ut victimam Deo Patri. Heb. 9.14. Quantò magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus, ad serviendum Deo vivo. Gal. 2. 20. Vitam, quam nunc vivo in carne, vivo per fidem Filii Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me.
units.tr: II. This blood of the Son of God therefore expiates our sins, because it was poured out for the remission of our sins, as the blood of the Son of God. Matthew 26:28: "This is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins." Luke says: "This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Or because Christ offered himself without blemish to God the Father as a victim. Heb. 9:14: "How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God." Gal. 2:20: "The life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me."

units.la: III. Atqș ita Agnus ille Dei sustu-lit peccata mundi. Johan. 1. 29. Agnus ille Dei, scilicet persona illa, à Deo ordi-nata in victimam, ut scilicet instar Agni mactetur & offeratur, ad expiandum peccata nostra: sustulit, id est, abstulit à nobis, quatenus nimirum pro nobis mactamactatus & sacrificatus est in cruce, vel portavit, scilicet expiandi gratia, sed, ut Jesaias dixit, Morbos nostros ipse portavit, & dolores nostros bajulavit.
units.tr: III. And so that Lamb of God took away the sins of the world. John 1:29. That Lamb of God, that is, that person appointed by God as a victim, so that he should be slain and offered in the manner of a lamb to expiate our sins; took away, that is, removed from us, inasmuch as he was indeed slain and sacrificed for us on the cross; or bore, namely for the sake of expiation, but, as Isaiah said, "He hath borne our sicknesses, and carried our sorrows."

units.la: Atque simul ita nos Deo reconciliavit, tollens id, quod Deum a nobis separavit, scilicet peccatum nostrum, Jes. 59. v. 2. Reconciliavit nos per mortem su-am[?]. Rom. 5. 10.
units.tr: And at the same time he thus reconciled us to God, removing that which separated us from God, namely our sin. Isa. 59:2. He reconciled us by his death. Rom. 5:10.

units.la: IV. Unde jam manifestum evadit, cum dicimus peccata nostra sanguine Christi expiari, non modo significari effectu & cognitionem illius expiationis in nobis: sed etiam veram illius impetrationem apud Deum: quia Deus, nisi interveniente morte CHRISTI (quâ phrasi etiam Adversarii libenter utuntur) nec peccata nobis remittit, nec gratiam nobis largitur ad ipsa peccata in nobis ipsis exstinguendum.
units.tr: IV. From this it now plainly appears that when we say that our sins are expiated by the blood of Christ, we mean not only the effect and the knowledge of that expiation within us, but also its true obtaining before God; because God, unless the death of Christ intervenes (a phrase which our opponents also gladly use), neither remits our sins nor bestows grace on us to extinguish those very sins in ourselves.

units.la: Quod ipsum etiam declarant nobis victimae expiatoriae in Veteri Testamento factae, quae adumbrabant Sacrificium Jesu Christi, Heb. 10.1, nempe ad significandum peccatorum purgationem coram Deo. Lev. 16. 14. 15. ubi illu-
units.tr: This the expiatory victims made in the Old Testament also show us, since they foreshadowed the sacrifice of Jesus Christ, Heb. 10:1, namely to signify the purging of sins before God. Lev. 16:14, 15, where that remarkable foreshadowing was made

units.la: illustris fuit adumbratio illa, per aquâ lustralem, factam ex cinerib' rufæ vaccæ. Num. 19. 9.
units.tr: by the lustral water made from the ashes of the red heifer. Num. 19:9.

units.la: Huc etiam referri potest ipsius Christi concio de carne suâ pro nobis datâ, quâ tanquam cibo vitæ fideles aluntur, dum sacrificio corporis Christi peccata sua expiata, gratiam & favorem Dei sibi conciliatum esse, persuasi, recreantur: Vide Cap. 6. Iohan. 27. 32. 33. 49. 50. 51. &c. Idem de sanguine ipsius pro nobis effuso judiçandum est, quo conscientiæ piorum per fidem asperguntur. 1. Pet. 1. v. 2.
units.tr: To this can also be referred Christ's own discourse about the flesh given for us, by which the faithful are nourished as with the food of life, while, persuaded that their sins are expiated by the sacrifice of Christ's body and that God's grace and favour have been won for them, they are refreshed. See chapter 6: John 27, 32, 33, 49, 50, 51, etc. The same judgment must be made about his blood poured out for us, by which the consciences of the godly are sprinkled through faith. 1 Pet. 1:2.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: ASSERTIO ET DEMONSTRATIO Meriti & satisfactionis Iesu Christi; ex eo, quòd Christus sit summus noster Sacerdos, ex fine mortis Christi principe; ex virtute mortis ejus amplissimâ.
units.tr: ASSERTION AND DEMONSTRATION of the merit and satisfaction of Jesus Christ: from the fact that Christ is our chief Priest; from the principal end of Christ's death; from the most ample power of his death.

units.la: MEDIATOREM, Reconciliatorem & Redemtorè nostrum IESUM CHRISTUM, esse SPONSOREM nostrum, qui sacrificio suo expiaexpiatorio nobis Deum placaverit, pro nobis Dei judicio satisfecerit, & æter-nam redemtionem pepererit, persua-dent mihi ea sanctæ Scripturæ effata, quæ docent: 1. Jesum hunc Servatorem meum, esse summum Sacerdotem nostrum, qui semetipsum pro nobis obtulerit, & pro nobis interpellet. 2. Christum esse mortuum, ut partâ remissione peccatorum, justitiâ, quâ coram Deo consistendum, nobis repararetur. 3. Mortis Christi virtutem fuisse efficacem in eis, qui ante ipsius adventum in carnem, fuerunt in Veteri Testamento.
units.tr: That Jesus Christ, our Mediator, Reconciler and Redeemer, is our Surety, who by his expiatory sacrifice has appeased God for us, has made satisfaction for us to the judgment of God, and has obtained eternal redemption, is persuaded to me by those sayings of Holy Scripture which teach: 1. That this Jesus, my Saviour, is our chief Priest, who offered himself for us and intercedes for us. 2. That Christ died so that, the remission of sins having been obtained, the righteousness by which we may stand before God might be restored to us. 3. That the power of Christ's death was effective in those who were in the Old Testament before his coming in the flesh.

units.la: CAPITIS VI. SECTIO I.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. SECTION I.

units.la: QUt summus est noster Sacerdos, à legali olim Pontifice, qui typicè populum à peccatis expiabat, & pro eo orabat, adumbratus; ita ut ipse & semet Deo victimâ peccatorum expiatricem obtulerit, & pro nobis intercesserit, & adhuc suo modo intercedat: hoc certè pro nobis oblato & deprecante, Deum nobis placari, & gratiam ejus nobis verè cōciliari, non tantum placatum & propitium nobis Deum declarari, manifestum est.
units.tr: As our high priest is the one foreshadowed in the legal high priest of old, who typically atoned for the people's sins and prayed for them, so that he himself offered himself to God as a victim that expiates sins, and interceded for us, and still intercedes in his own way: it is certainly clear that, with him offering and interceding for us, God is appeased toward us and his grace is truly reconciled to us, and not merely that God is declared to be appeased and propitious toward us.

units.la: Nota. Dico, non tantum ostendi & declarari. Quia adversarii in collatione legalis Pontificis, cum Sacerdote nostro Jesu Christo, 1. Docent: Sicut cō-stat, victimas legales nullam divinæ justitiæ satisfaciendi vim habuisse: sic nec Pontificis personam, præsertim cum sacrificiorum vis in victima potius, quàm in Sacerdote residere videatur: immò ad ipsam satisfactionem peragendam, Sacerdotis personam nihil ꝑ[?]sus momenti afferre posse.
units.tr: Note. I say not merely shown and declared. For the adversaries, in comparing the legal high priest with our priest Jesus Christ, (1) teach: as is agreed, the legal sacrifices had no power to satisfy divine justice; so neither does the person of the high priest, especially since the power of the sacrifices seems to reside in the victim rather than in the priest. Indeed, the priest's person can add nothing of its own weight to the satisfaction itself.

units.la: 2. Cùm dicitur in Levitico: Et expiabit eum Sacerdos à peccato, & remittetur ei, docent, hoc nihil aliud esse, quàm peracto sacrificio illo, Sacerdotem liberaturum esse illum à noxâ, non quidem Deo satisfaciendo, aut propter dignitate, vel suam, vel ipsius Sacrificii, Deum ad liberationem ejusmodi concedendam inducendo: sed in peragedo, quod pro illo peragi voluit Deus, ut is delicti sui veniam consequeretur: & propter Dei spontaneam & puram benignitatem, qui eo sacrificio peracto, illum coram se mundum ab eo peccato fore decreverat, Et sic Expiare & Mundare significare ajunt, Expiatum & Mundatum tum declarare, seu pronuntiare. Uti & illud Johannis etiam: Sanguis Jesu Christi emundat nos ab omni peccato, explicant, nos Mundes esse fidem facit.
units.tr: (2) When it is said in Leviticus, And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him, they teach that this means nothing other than that, once that sacrifice has been completed, the priest will free him from guilt. This is not by satisfying God, nor by moving God, through the dignity of either himself or the sacrifice, to grant such deliverance; rather, it is by carrying out what God willed to be done on his behalf, so that he might obtain pardon for his offence, and on account of God's spontaneous and pure kindness, who had decreed that once that sacrifice was completed he would count him clean of that sin before himself. And so they say that to expiate and to cleanse signify to declare expiated and cleansed, or to pronounce so. Likewise they explain that saying of John too, The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin, as makes us know that we are clean.

units.la: 3. Sic quoq; Christum Sacerdotem nostrum peccata nostra expiasse dicunt, non quia ex persona vel victima sua divinae justitiae pro eis ulla ex parte satisfecerit, vel Deum nobis placaverit: sed quia ea peregerit, quibus peractis, veniam delictorum nostrorum, jam à Deo nobis sponte decretam & promissam consecuti simus, vel etiam eam veniam nos consecutos esse, declaratum sit. His praemissis jam ad Assumtionem perveniamus.
units.tr: (3) So too they say that Christ our priest expiated our sins, not because by his person or his victim he satisfied divine justice for them in any way, or appeased God toward us, but because he performed those things by which, once they were done, we obtained the pardon of our offences, already freely decreed and promised to us by God, or it is declared that we have obtained that pardon. With these premises laid down, we now come to the assumption.

units.la: Atqui Jesus Christus à Deo Mediator inter partes dissidentes, se & homines, constitutus, est (ummus[?] ille noster, à legali Pontifice olim adumbratus Sacerdos, qui semetipsum hostiam & victimam Deo pro peccatis nostris obtulit, & pro nobis intercessit, & suo modo adhuc intercedit.
units.tr: But Jesus Christ, constituted by God as Mediator between the parties at variance, himself and men, is that high priest of ours, once foreshadowed by the legal high priest, who offered himself as both sacrifice and victim to God for our sins, and interceded for us, and in his own way still intercedes.

units.la: 1. Ipse enim Agnus ille Dei (Jesa. 53. v. 7. Johan. 1. v. 29. 1. Pet. 1. v. 19. Apocal. 5. 6. 12. 13. ut supra) unico sacrificio sui corporis (Hebraor. 10. v. 5. & seqq. Matth. 26. verf. 28.) in cruce λύτρον (Galat. 3. verf. 13. 1.Pet.2.ver.24.) seu pœnas sufficientes, tempore quidem finitas, valore tamen & vigore, tum propter dignitatem seu prœstantiam PERSONÆ (Actor. 20. 28. Rom. 8.3. 1.Joh. 1.7.) tum ob gravitatem cruciatuum, (Psal. 22. Jes. 53. v. 5. 10. 11. Matth. 26. & 27. Actor. 2.24. Heb. 5..7.) & ignominiæ (Jes. 53.12. Matth. 26. &c.) infinitas, pœnisq; æternis æquivalen-tes pro nobis persolvit, atque ita nobis Justitiam & Remissionem peccatorū, viramq; æternam ꝓmeruit. (Dan. 9. 24. 26. Rom. 3.24. & 4.6. Gal. 3.4. 5. Heb. 10.19.)
units.tr: (1) For that Lamb of God (Isa. 53. v. 7. John 1. v. 29. 1 Pet. 1. v. 19. Rev. 5. 6. 12. 13. as above), by the single sacrifice of his body (Heb. 10. v. 5ff. Matt. 26. v. 28) on the cross, paid as a ransom [λύτρον] (Gal. 3. v. 13; 1 Pet. 2. v. 24), that is, sufficient penalties, limited indeed in time but infinite in worth and power, both on account of the dignity or excellence of his PERSON (Acts 20. 28; Rom. 8. 3; 1 John 1. 7) and on account of the severity of his torments (Ps. 22; Isa. 53. v. 5, 10, 11; Matt. 26 and 27; Acts 2. 24; Heb. 5. 7) and of his shame (Isa. 53. 12; Matt. 26, etc.), and he paid them on our behalf, equivalent to eternal punishments; and so he obtained for us righteousness and the remission of sins and eternal life (Dan. 9. 24, 26; Rom. 3. 24 and 4. 6; Gal. 3. 4, 5; Heb. 10. 19).

units.la: CHRISTUS ergo per supplicium crucis sentiens in illo iram Dei (Matth. 27.46.) adversus peccata, ꝑsolvit pœnas illis debitas, (Rom. 3.24.25. Eph. 1.7.) seu satisfecit ꝓ peccatis nostris, Col. 2.13.14, seu deniq; illa expiavit, (1.Joh. 2.1. Jes. 53.10. 2.Cor. 5.21, Rom. 3.25.) nosq; à ma-ledictione legis, & ab omni potestate Diaboli redemit. (Gal. 3.13. Heb. 9.12. Rō. 1.14.) Atq; hinc patet, cur Christus tā-topere ab illo supplicio abhorruerit, tamque ardenti querulatione illud de-preçatus sit, (Matth. 26.38.) cum tamen MartyMartyres plerique alacriter supplicia sustinuerint, &jugulum carnificib. ul-tro praebuerint, nonnulli etiam in me-diis flammis hymnos laeti cecinerint: quia scilicet omnes tempestates & flu-ctus irae Dei in se effusum iri praesentie-bat. Psal. 22. Jes. 53. Matth. 27.
units.tr: Christ therefore, through the punishment of the cross, feeling in it the wrath of God against sin (Matt. 27. 46), paid the penalties owed by them (Rom. 3. 24, 25; Eph. 1. 7), or satisfied for our sins (Col. 2. 13, 14), or finally expiated them (1 John 2. 1; Isa. 53. 10; 2 Cor. 5. 21; Rom. 3. 25), and redeemed us from the curse of the law and from all the power of the devil (Gal. 3. 13; Heb. 9. 12; Rom. 1. 14). And from this it is plain why Christ so greatly shrank from that punishment and prayed about it with such fervent lamentation (Matt. 26. 38), whereas many martyrs bore their punishments cheerfully, offered their throats to the executioners of their own accord, and some even sang hymns joyfully in the midst of the flames. The reason, namely, is that he foresaw that all the storms and waves of God's wrath would be poured out upon himself (Ps. 22; Isa. 53; Matt. 27).

units.la: II. Ipse deinde summus Sacerdos, partim paulo ante oblationem pro nobis oravit (Johan. 17.) Patrem, ut scilicet satisfactionem illam suam credentibus imputaret: Partim vero, posteaquam ex mortuis excitatus, in coelum ascendit, atque ita in SANCTUARIUM illud non manufactum ingressus est, victimamque semel in terris oblatam in illum intulit, continenter coram facie Patris pro nobis apparet, (Heb. 9. 24.) & se, ac victimam illi ostendens, vigore illius semel oblati, perpetuo pro nobis interpellat. Rom. 8. 34.
units.tr: II. Then the high priest himself, partly shortly before the offering, prayed to the Father for us (John 17), that is, that he would impute that satisfaction of his to believers; and partly afterwards, when he had been raised from the dead and ascended into heaven, and so entered that sanctuary not made with hands and carried the victim once offered on earth into it, he continually appears before the face of the Father for us (Heb. 9. 24), and, showing himself and his victim to him, by the power of that once-offered sacrifice he intercedes for us perpetually (Rom. 8. 34).

units.la: Quamobrem, sicut Pontifex legalis populum suum typice expiabat, & pro eo orabat: Lev. 4. &5.[?] & 6. & 9. & 16. &c. Sic Christus summus noster Pontifex, purgatione peccatorum nostrorum per se ipsum facta, intercedit pro nobis in coelo. Heb. 1. 3. (sed hoc dictum sic illi exponunt) Christum purgationem peccatorum nostrorum per se ipsum fecisse, quatenus Dei erga nos voluntatem omnem in ipso expressam vidimus, declaratum nobis apertissime est, remissa & deleta esse peccata nostra. Vidimus autem, (inquiunt) expressam in Christo divinam voluntatem, non modo, quia is eam nobis patefecit, sed etiam, quia jam in ipsa re impletum scimus, quod nobis Deus per ipsum est pollicitus, & certissimum pignum divina voluntatis nobis patefa-sta habemus.
units.tr: Wherefore, just as the legal high priest typically atoned for his people and prayed for them (Lev. 4, 5, 6, 9, 16, etc.), so Christ our high priest, having made the purification of our sins by himself, intercedes for us in heaven (Heb. 1. 3). (But they explain this saying thus:) Christ made the purification of our sins by himself, inasmuch as, seeing God's will toward us fully expressed in him, it has been most plainly declared to us that our sins are remitted and blotted out. We see, they say, the divine will expressed in Christ, not only because he has revealed it to us, but also because we know that what God promised us through him has already been fulfilled in fact, and we have a most certain pledge of the divine will made manifest to us.

units.la: Sic ajunt: Christum nos sanctificasse per pro-prium sanguinem, quatenus per Christi sanguinem ad veritatis agnitionem, hoc est, ad divinam voluntatis et bonitatis, peccatorum scilicet remis-sionis, id est, aeternae vitae, poenitentibus oblata ac parta, notitiam pervenimus, & ita a profano ho-minum vulgo separamur. Quorsum ista contorta explicatio? Et ut Christi Dei-tas, & ut Christi Meritum, & realis pec-catorum expiatio negetur. Sed nos verbum Dei audiamus, glossas mittamus.
units.tr: Thus they say: Christ sanctified us through his own blood, inasmuch as through Christ's blood we come to the knowledge of the truth, that is, of the divine will and goodness, namely the remission of sins, that is, eternal life, offered and secured for the repentant; and so we are separated from the profane common run of men. Why this twisted explanation? It is so that both Christ's divinity and Christ's merit, and the real expiation of sins, may be denied. But let us hear the Word of God, and set aside the glosses.

units.la: Rom. 8. v. 34. Quis est, qui condemnet? Christus is est, qui mortuus est, imo vero, qui etiam excitatus est, qui etiam est ad dexteram Dei, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. En qui aude-at cleat electos Dei condemnare? Siquidem ipse Christus, qui judex omnium a Deo constitutus est, mortem pro illis obiit, nec tantum ipsorum causâ mortuus est, verum etiam a mortuis excitatus, in cœlum ascendit, ibique ad dextram Dei evectus, summam potestatem in cœlo & terra obtinuit; denique quod fidum & misericordem Pontificem decet, continenter apud Deum pro nobis intercedit, nosque suo favore & præsidio perpetuo protegit.
units.tr: Rom. 8. v. 34. Who is he who condemns? Christ is he who died, yes rather, who was also raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us. Behold, who would dare to condemn God's elect? Since Christ himself, whom God has appointed judge of all, died for them, and died not only on their account but was also raised from the dead, ascended into heaven, and, exalted to the right hand of God, obtained supreme power in heaven and on earth; and finally, as befits a faithful and merciful high priest, he continually intercedes for us with God and protects us perpetually by his favour and help.

units.la: Observa & hoc, causam, quæ Deum Judicem movet, ut nos justificet, est Mors Christi, quatenus per illâ satisfactū est justitiæ ipsius pro nobis. Quod autem per mortem divinæ justitiæ plenè satisfactum sit, & peccata nostra perfectè expiata, demonstrant hic, tum Resurrectio Christi ex morte, tum Ascensio ejusdem in cœlum, & Sessio ad dexteram Dei Patris. Neq; enim ex morte ad vitam illam cœlestem ac gloriosam resurgere potuisset, nisi ꝑ peccatis nostris, quæ ut Sponsor in se susceperat, plenè satisfecisset. Unde 1,
units.tr: Observe this too: the cause that moves God the Judge to justify us is the death of Christ, inasmuch as through it his justice has been satisfied on our behalf. That by his death divine justice has been fully satisfied and our sins perfectly expiated is shown here both by the resurrection of Christ from death, and by his ascension into heaven, and by his sitting at the right hand of God the Father. For he could not have risen from death to that heavenly and glorious life unless he had fully satisfied for our sins, which as our Surety he had taken upon himself. Hence (see) 1 Cor. 15, If Christ has not been raised, you are still in your sins.

units.la: Cor. 15. Si Christus non est excitatus, adhuc vos in peccatis vestris.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15. If Christ is not raised, you are still in your sins.

units.la: Heb. 2. 17. Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri, ut Misericors esset & fidelis Pontifex, in iis quae apud Deum agenda forent, ad expiandum peccata populi. Ecce, Pontifex noster pro nobis agit apud Deum, & cum Deo, ut nostra peccata expientur.
units.tr: Heb. 2. 17. "Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every way, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in the things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people." Behold, our High Priest acts for us before God, and with God, that our sins may be expiated.

units.la: Cap. 4. 16. Accedamus igitur ad thronum gratiae cum fiducia, ut consequamur misericordiam, & gratiam inveniamus ad opportunum auxilium.
units.tr: Heb. 4. 16. "Let us therefore draw near to the throne of grace with confidence, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help."

units.la: Quare? Quia habemus Pontificem magnum, qui penetravit coelos, Jesum Filium Dei: teneamus hanc professionem. Non enim habemus Pontificem, qui non potest affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tentatum in omnibus similiter nobis, absque tamen peccato. Nota hic Apostolum Operculum illud arcae foederis vocare thronum gratiae: illud enim ceu propitiatorium, fuit typus Christi, ut qui sacrificio sui corporis DEUM nobis propitium reddidit, gratiamq; ejus nobis conciliavit.
units.tr: Why? "Because we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God; let us hold fast to our confession. For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin." Note here that the Apostle calls the cover of the ark of the covenant the throne of grace; for that cover, as the mercy seat, was a type of Christ, who by the sacrifice of his body made God propitious to us and reconciled his grace to us.

units.la: Et Cap. 7. 24. 25. At ipse (Christus) propterea quod in aeternum manet, perpetuum habet Sacerdotium. Unde & servare perfecte potest[?] eos, qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum, semper viuens, vt interpellet pro eis.
units.tr: And Heb. 7. 24, 25. "But he, because he remains forever, has an unchangeable priesthood. Therefore he is able also to save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them."

units.la: Hic Pontifex noster non habuit o-pus pro se ipso offerre. Hebr. 7. 26. & 27. Talis enim nos decebat Pontifex, Sanctus, Innocens, Impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, & sublimior coelis factus: cui non fit quotidie necesse, quemadmodum illis pontificibus, primùm pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre, deinde pro peccatis populi: id enim fecit semel, cùm semetipsum obtulit. Lex enim homines constituit Pontifices infirmitate laborantes: at sermo iurisiurandi post legem conceptus, Filium constituit, qui in aeternum est sanctificatus.
units.tr: Our High Priest had no need to offer for himself. Heb. 7. 26, 27. "For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; who does not need daily, as those high priests did, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for the sins of the people; for this he did once for all when he offered himself. For the law appoints men as high priests who have weakness; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son, who has been made perfect forever."

units.la: Adversarii docent, Christum non quidem pro suis peccatis obtulisse, sed quia non minus, quàm nos, dum hîc ageret, infirmitate carnis, hoc est, mortalitate & patibilitate, vt ita dicam,cir-cumdatus fuit, à quâ, vt liberaretur, nō minus quàm nobis, illi opus erat, (ajunt illi) & à quâ nisi ipse liberatus fuisset, nec nos unquam liberati fuissemus. Nos loquimur hîc de oblatione sacrifi-cii, & deprecatione pro nobis. Chri-stum quoq; pro se preçatū esse, hîc non disceptatur. Non opus fuit Christo pro propriis peccatis & infirmitatibus victimas offerre, pro seipso obtulisse, licitur nusquam.
units.tr: The adversaries teach that Christ offered not indeed for his own sins, but because, while he lived here, he was no less than we encumbered by the weakness of the flesh, that is, by mortality and passibility, as I may say, surrounded; from which, that he might be freed, he had no less need than we did (so they say); and unless he himself had been freed from it, we would never have been freed. We speak here of the offering of sacrifice and of intercession for us. That Christ also prayed for himself is not disputed here. There was no need for Christ to offer victims for his own sins and infirmities; that he offered for himself is nowhere stated.

units.la: Ipse sese[?] pro nobis obtulit, pro quibus etiam se-ipsum sanctificavit. Johan. 17. 19. Et pro eis ego sanctifico meipsum, ut sint & ipsi sanctificati per veritatem. Pro nobis Christus Patri sei-ipsum in sanctam victimam ad expiandā omnia nostra peccata obtulit, per quam oblationem nos quoq; sanctificati sumus. Heb. 10. 10. & 14.
units.tr: "He offered himself for us, for whom he also sanctified himself." John 17. 19. "And for them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified through the truth." Christ offered himself to the Father for us as a holy victim, to expiate all our sins, and through this offering we also have been sanctified. Heb. 10. 10, 14.

units.la: Nota, hic sanctificationem & oblationem Christi pertinere ad meritū, quo Christus est Servator noster; sanctifi-cationem vero nostri per veritatē, pertinere ad efficaciam Christi, quā etiam est noster Servator. Christus enim nos sanctificat & servat, partim suo me-rito, partim sua efficacia.
units.tr: Note here that the sanctification and offering of Christ pertain to the merit by which Christ is our Saviour; but the sanctification of us through the truth pertains to the efficacy of Christ, by which he is also our Saviour. For Christ sanctifies and saves us partly by his merit, partly by his efficacy.

units.la: Merito, quatenus sanctificans sei-ipsum pro nobis, in victimam, oblatio-ne sui corporis expiavit nostra pec-cata, & ita illorum remissionem est promeritus.
units.tr: By merit, insofar as, sanctifying himself for us as a victim, he expiated our sins by the offering of his body, and so merited their remission.

units.la: Efficacia vero, quatenus curat nobis annuntiari veritatem illam cœlestem, & per illius annuntiationem in nobis efficit fidem, virtute sui Spiritus, quâ fide purgantur corda nostra, quatenus per illam sanguine Christi in cruce effuso asperguntur.
units.tr: By efficacy, indeed, insofar as he causes that heavenly truth to be announced to us, and through that announcement effects faith in us by the power of his Spirit, by which faith our hearts are purified, insofar as through it they are sprinkled with the blood of Christ poured out on the cross.

units.la: Ephef. 5. 2. Christus dilexit nos, & tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem, & victimam Deo in odorem bonae fragrantiae. Unde etiam ἱλασμὸς sive ἱλαστήριον nostrum appellatur, Rom. 3.25. & 1. Joh. 2.2. Ut intelligamus, cum oblatione corporis sui Deum nobis ob peccata vere offensum placasse.
units.tr: Eph. 5. 2. "Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God as a fragrant aroma." Hence he is also called our propitiation or propitiatory [ἱλασμός, ἱλαστήριον], Rom. 3. 25 and 1 John 2. 2, so that we may understand that by the offering of his body he truly appeased God, who was truly offended by our sins.

units.la: Concludo igitur, Iesum Christum summum Pontificem nostrum semetipsum pro nobis victimam Deo offerendo, & pro nobis intercedendo, iram Dei vere nobis placasse, favorem ejus reconciliasse, non vero tantum nos placatos declarasse.
units.tr: I conclude, therefore, that Jesus Christ, our High Priest, by offering himself to God as a victim for us and by interceding for us, has truly appeased the wrath of God toward us and reconciled his favour, not merely declared us to be reconciled.

units.la: CAPITIS VI. SECTIO II.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI, SECTION II.

units.la: Qui ideo semetipsum obtulit Deo in mortem, non modo ut annuntiatae salutis viam ostenderet[?], confirmaret, & significaret, sed principaliter, ut peccata propter eum nobis remitti possent: atq; ita justitia, quae coram Deo nobis est consistendum, instauraretur, is professio[?] ideo mortuum dici potest, ut morte sua pro peccapeccatis nostris satisfaciens, Deo nos reconciliaret.
units.tr: For this reason he offered himself to God in death, not only to show, confirm and signify the way of announced salvation, but chiefly so that sins might be remitted to us on account of him, and thus the righteousness by which we must stand before God might be restored. He may therefore be said to have died so that, by his death, satisfying for our sins, he might reconcile us to God.

units.la: Verum Christus Iesus Servator Mundi id- eo semetipsum obtulit Deo in mortem, non qui-dem tantum, ut scribunt nonnulli, ut patefa-[?]ctam annuntiata salutis viam nobis ostenderet, morte confirmaret, sanguine obsignaret: Sed ideo principaliter, ut peccata nobis nostra propter eum remitti possent, & ita iustitia, qua nobis coram Deo consistendum est, repararetur.
units.tr: Indeed Christ Jesus, the Saviour of the world, offered himself to God in death for this reason: not merely, as some write, so that he might show us the way of salvation that had been announced, confirm it by his death and seal it with his blood. Rather, he did so chiefly so that our sins might be remitted to us on account of him, and so that the righteousness by which we must stand before God might be restored.

units.la: Quod jam probandum.
units.tr: This is now to be proved.

units.la: Galat. 2, 21. Quod si per legem esset iustitia, frustra, & sine causa, Christus esset mortuus. Hic finis mortis Christi indicatur, qui fuit, ut nobis mereretur remissionem peccatorum, atq; adeo, ut nos per iustitiam morte ipsius partam, nobisq; im-putatam, iustificaremur, quem finem certe, ille adeptus non est, si iustitia no-stra per legem est.
units.tr: Gal. 2. 21. "If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died in vain and without cause." Here the purpose of Christ's death is indicated, which was that he might merit for us the remission of sins, and so that we might be justified through the righteousness obtained by his death and imputed to us. Certainly, that purpose would not have been achieved if our righteousness were through the law.

units.la: Alii finem sic exprimunt: Si per legis observationem iustitia contingeret, utique Christus frustra mortuus esset, quippe cuius morte non illa legalis, & in meritis nostris fundata, sed alia plane gratuita iustitia, qua Evangelii propria censetur, nobis comparata est.
units.tr: Others express the purpose thus: If righteousness were attained through the observance of the law, Christ would certainly have died in vain, since by his death not that legal righteousness founded on our merits, but another wholly gratuitous righteousness, which is considered proper to the Gospel, has been obtained for us.

units.la: Adversarii locum ita exponunt: Si per Legem iustitiam consequi aut debemus, aut et- iam iam possumus, quid attinebat, CHRISTUM nobis DEI nomine peccatorum remissionem annuntiare, & aliam justitiam consequenda ratione tradere, proq; ea afferenda morti, ut inde ad resurrectione pervenire posset? Viam autem consequendi justitiam, quam nobis Christus attulit, à via legis diversam, sic docent: justitia, quae est secundum Legem, requirit, ut ipsam Legem absolutè servemus: justitia verò, quam per Christum consequimur, vitae emendatione & peccatorum remissione continetur. Atqui vitam emendare, & peccata remitti, pugnant cum absoluta legis observatione. Ergo, si à lege justitia petenda est, frustra & sine causa mortuus est Christus. Sic illi.
units.tr: Our opponents explain the passage thus: If we ought to obtain righteousness through the Law, or even now can do so, what was the point of Christ announcing to us, in the name of God, the remission of sins, and of delivering to us another way of obtaining righteousness, and of giving himself to death for it, so that from there he might come to the resurrection? They teach that the way of obtaining the righteousness which Christ brought us differs from the way of the law, as follows: The righteousness which is according to the Law requires that we keep the Law itself perfectly; but the righteousness which we obtain through Christ consists in the amendment of life and the remission of sins. But to amend one's life and to have sins remitted are incompatible with perfect observance of the law. Therefore, if righteousness is to be sought from the law, Christ died in vain and without cause. Thus they.

units.la: At simpliciter verbis inhaerendo sic nos dicimus: Si per legem est justitia, quid attinebat, Christum pro nobis mori. Ideo enim mortuus est, ut nobis justitiam, morte sua partâ, donaret, cum nos justitia propria, quae est ex lege, videret destitui: Annuntiatio salutis & remissionis peccatorum, ejusq; assertio & confirmatio, non debent annihilare meritoriam ejus causam, quâ ipsa nobis est impetrata.
units.tr: But we, adhering simply to the words, say this: If there is righteousness through the law, what was the point of Christ dying for us? He died so that he might give us, by his death, the righteousness he had obtained, since he saw us deprived of our own righteousness, which is from the law. The announcement and assertion and confirmation of salvation and of the remission of sins do not annul the meritorious cause by which they have been obtained for us.

units.la: Necesse fuit peccatum in nostra carne da-mnari, mnari, ut justitia legis in nobis impleretur. Rō.
units.tr: It was necessary for sin to be condemned in our flesh, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us. Rom.

units.la: 8. 3. Nam quod erat impossibile legi, quatenus infirmabatur per carnem, id Deus fecit, suo ipsius Filio misso in for-ma consimili carni peccato obnoxiæ, & (sacrificio) pro peccato condemna-vit peccatum in illa carne; ut justifica-tio legis impleretur in nobis, qui non secundum carnem incedimus, sed secundum spiritum.
units.tr: 8. 3. For what was impossible for the law, insofar as it was weakened by the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and (as a sacrifice) for sin he condemned sin in that flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

units.la: Aliter exponunt hoc: Quod legi Mo-saica impossibile erat præstare, quatenus scilicet per ipsam carnis nostræ fragilitatem infirmabatur, id Deus hac ratione effecit: Misit in hunc mundum Filium suum unigenitum, mortali carne, non minus quam nos, circundatum, eumque tanquam peccatorem morti crucis subjecit: atque ut peccatum plane aboleret, in ipsius Filii sui carne id exstinguere aggressus est. Idque hoc consilio fecit, ut nos perfecte justi coram ipso efficeremur, non secus atque illi habiti fuissent, qui omnia divina legis præcepta servassent, nos, inquam, qui non carni, sed Spiritui obtemperamus.
units.tr: Others explain this otherwise: What was impossible for the Mosaic law to accomplish, insofar as it was weakened by the frailty of our own flesh, God brought about in this way: he sent into this world his only-begotten Son, clothed in mortal flesh no less than we are, and subjected him as a sinner to the death of the cross. And in order to abolish sin completely, he undertook to extinguish it in the flesh of his own Son. He did this with this purpose: that we might be made perfectly righteous before him, just as those would have been regarded who had kept all the precepts of the divine law, namely we, I say, who obey not the flesh but the Spirit.

units.la: Alii sic: Deus in carne Filii sui condemnavit peccatum peccati, hoc est, propterea quod ipsum in Christum peccavit, afferens illi mortem, cum tamen esset innocens: ac proinde Deus ademit posthac peccato suum jus erga credentes, ut non possit eis[?] nocere. Simplicior est sententia quæ statuit, Deum in carne filii innocente condemnasse, hoc est, abolevisse nostrum peccatum, illius carni impositum, quatenus ille carnem suam obtulit Deo, in victimam pro peccato.
units.tr: Others thus: God in the flesh of his Son condemned the sin of sin, that is, because it sinned against Christ, bringing death upon him although he was innocent; and so God henceforth took away from sin its right over believers, so that it could not harm them. The simpler view holds that God in the flesh of his innocent Son condemned, that is, abolished, our sin, which was laid upon his flesh, insofar as he offered his flesh to God as a victim for sin.

units.la: Mortuus est Christus, ut nos legi subjectos redimeret. Gal. 4. 4. Postquam venit plenū tempus, emisit Deus filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum legi subjectum[?], ut eos, qui legi erant subjecti, redimeret, ut adoptionem acciperemus.
units.tr: Christ died so that he might redeem those under the law. Gal. 4. 4. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made subject to the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive adoption.

units.la: Ecce idcirco Filius Dei homo factus est, ut legi subjectā[?] eam perfectè præstaret, adeoq; maledictione ipsius incurreret, atq; ita eos, qui maledictioni, itemq; efficaci pædagogiæ subjecti erant, in veram libertatem assereret, id est, ex servis & pueris perfectos Dei Filios efficeret.
units.tr: Therefore the Son of God became man so that he might perfectly fulfil the law to which he was subject, and thus incur its curse, and so set free in true liberty those who were subject to the curse and also to its effective tutelage; that is, he might make them perfect sons of God instead of servants and children.

units.la: Sumus autem redemti à lege per Christum, partim à Maledictione ejus, partim à Ceremoniis, per mortem CHRISTI, quatenus ipse pro nobis factus est Maledictio in cruce. Vide Cap. 3. ad Galat. v. 13.
units.tr: We are redeemed from the law through Christ, partly from its curse, and partly from the ceremonies, through the death of Christ, insofar as he himself was made a curse for us on the cross. See Cap. 3 on Galat. v. 13.

units.la: Mortuus est ut deleret Chirographum, quod erat nobis contrarium, illud cruci affigens, Col. 2. 14. Deleto & adversum nos erat Chirographo, in ritibus posito, quod erat nobis occultum contrarium: ipse vero cruci affixum e medio sustulit. Ritus legales & maxime sacrificia erant instar Chirographi, quo confitebantur reatum suum. Christo itaque exhibito, & reatu per sacrificium ejus expiato, debitoque persoluto, ac deniq; rebus praefiguratis ipso facto praestitis, consequenter ceremoniae legales sunt abolitae.
units.tr: He died in order to blot out the handwriting that was against us, nailing it to the cross. Col. 2. 14. Blotting out the handwriting which was against us, which was set in ordinances and was hidden from us as an adversary; he himself took it away, nailing it to the cross. The legal rites, and especially the sacrifices, were in the place of a handwriting by which they confessed their guilt. Therefore, when Christ had been presented, and the guilt had been expiated by his sacrifice, and the debt had been paid, and finally the things foreshadowed had been accomplished by the fact itself, the legal ceremonies were consequently abolished.

units.la: Ergo etiam propter nomen Christi peccata nobis remittuntur. 1. Joh. 2. 12. Ut intelligamus praecipue hac de causa Christum mortuum, ut pro nostris peccatis sua morte satisfaciens, Deo nos reconciliaret. Equidem ad ostendendam tantum, & obsignandam, & confirmandam salutis viam, nihil opus erat tantis cruciatibus, & tam diræ Morti Christum exponi: proinde res ipsa clamat, morte Christi abolita esse morte æternam, nobis ob peccata debita, 1. Cor. 15. 55. & 56. &c. Per Christum absorpta est Mors ad victoriam. Heb. 2. v. 14. Christus per mortem suam abolevit eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, Diabolum.
units.tr: Therefore also sins are forgiven us on account of the name of Christ. 1 John 2. 12. Let us understand that Christ died chiefly for this reason: that by his death, satisfying for our sins, he might reconcile us to God. Indeed, to show and seal and confirm only the way of salvation, there was no need for Christ to be exposed to such torments and such a dreadful death. The thing itself therefore cries out that by the death of Christ the eternal death owed to us on account of sins has been abolished. 1 Cor. 15. 55 and 56, etc. Death is swallowed up in victory through Christ. Heb. 2. 14. Christ by his death destroyed him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil.

units.la: CAPITIS VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: SECTIO III.
units.tr: SECTION III.

units.la: SI fructus sacrificii & mortis Iesu Christi pertinuit quoq;,& pervenit ad eos, qui ante Christi incarnationem fuerunt in Veteri Testamento, & ad eos, qui Christum ipsum necauerunt, nec resurgentem viderunt, nec alios audivisse, aut vidisse acceperunt: Certè non quia illis Christi sacrificium divinas promissiones, & ipsius Christi doctrinam confirmaverit, vel futuræ immortalitatis spem fecerit, sed quia Mors & Sacrificium illud peccata expiandi, & ita divinæ justitiæ pro ipsis satisfaciendi, facultatem habuerit, id contigisse omninò dicendum videtur. Confirmatio enim fidei, quâ doctrinæ creditur, ex visâ vel auditâ morte Christi, non potuit ad eos redundare, qui ante Christum in carne manifestatum vixerunt.
units.tr: If the fruit of the sacrifice and death of Jesus Christ also extended to, and reached, those who lived before the incarnation of Christ in the Old Testament, and to those who put Christ himself to death and neither saw him rise nor heard or saw that others had, then it seems entirely right to say that this happened, though not because that sacrifice confirmed for them the divine promises and the doctrine of Christ himself, or gave them hope of future immortality, but because that death and sacrifice had the power to expiate sins and so make satisfaction to divine justice on their behalf. For the confirmation of faith, by which doctrine is believed, from a death seen or heard of, could not extend to those who lived before Christ was manifested in the flesh.

units.la: At quæ antecedunt, sunt vera. Heb. 13. 8. Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem est & in saecula. Apocal. 13. 8. Est Agnus ille ab ori-
units.tr: But what goes before is true. Heb. 13.8: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever. Rev. 13.8: He is that Lamb who from the origin

units.la: gine mundi mactatus[?]: hujus diem expectarunt & fidei oculis viderunt, imo hujus gratia veteres servati sunt. Johan. 8. 56. Abraham Pater ge-stivit, ut videret diem meum: & vidit, & gavisus est. (Unde non immerito colligitur, sanctos Patres in Veteri Testamento non aliter servatos esse, quam nos, nempe per fidem Jesu Christi pro nobis mortui) Actor. 15. v. 11. Nunc ergo quid tentatis Deum, imponendo jugum cervici discipulorum, quod neque Patres nostri, neque nos portare valuimus? Imo per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi credimus nos servatum ut, quemadmodum & illi, scilicet Patres servati fuerunt, nempe per gratiam Dei, partim morte Christi. Illi, inquam, Patres in Veteri Testamento servati sic sunt, qui expectiverunt redemtionem Israelis. Luc. 2. 25. Ubi Simeon dicitur exspectasse consolationem Israelis. v. 38. Loquebatur de eo omnibus, qui expectabant redemtionem Hierosolymis.
units.tr: of the world slain[?]. They looked for his day and saw it with the eyes of faith; indeed the ancients were preserved for the sake of it. John 8.56: Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and was glad. (Whence it is not without reason concluded that the holy Fathers in the Old Testament were not saved in any other way than we are, namely through faith in Jesus Christ who died for us.) Acts 15.11: Now therefore why do you tempt God, placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples, which neither our Fathers nor we were able to bear? Nay, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they also were saved, namely through the grace of God, partly by the death of Christ. Those Fathers, I say, were saved in the Old Testament in this way, those who waited for the redemption of Israel. Luke 2.25, where Simeon is said to have waited for the consolation of Israel. v. 38: He spoke of him to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem.

units.la: Imo hujus Christi crucifixa carne & e fuso sanguine, qui non reficitur, non habet vitam aeternam, jurante sic Christo, Joh. 6. 53. Amen, Amen dico vobis, nisi ederitis carnem Filii hominis, & biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Ergo omnes S. Patres, qui vitam habuerunt in se, ederunt carnem & biberunt sanguinem CHRISTI, crediderùntque carne Christi crucifixum iri, & sanguinem ejus effusum iri in remissione peccatorum suorum. 1.Cor.10.3, Scitis omnes (Patres) eandem escam spiritualem edisse, et omnes eundem potum spiritualem bibisse. Bibebant autem ex sequenti spirituali petra: petra vero illa erat Christus. 1.Ioh.f.11.12. Est autem hoc testimonium, nempe quod vitam aeternam dedit nobis Deus: & haec vita in filio ejus est: Qui habet filium, habet vitam: qui non habet filium Dei, vitam non habet.
units.tr: Nay, one who does not feed on the crucified flesh of this Christ and on his shed blood, which is not renewed, does not have eternal life, Christ himself swearing so, John 6.53: Amen, amen I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. Therefore all the holy Fathers who had life in them ate the flesh and drank the blood of CHRIST, and believed that Christ would be crucified in the flesh and that his blood would be shed for the remission of their sins. 1 Cor. 10.3: You all know that (the Fathers) ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them: and that rock was Christ. 1 John 5.11, 12: Now this is the testimony, namely that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son: he who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life.

units.la: Sensus est, haec est summa eorum, quae Deus de filio suo testatus est, videlicet ipsum esse nostrum Servatorem, si modo in ipsum credamus. Nam Deus ex pura sua misericordia Filium suum nobis constituit aeternae vitae auctorem, quippe quam omnibus in Filium credentibus dare decrevit, & quidem per ipsum filium. Qui igitur habet filium Dei per fidem, scilicet per quam in nobis habitat, is habet vitam aeternam: hic quidem certa spe, & fide, olim habiturus re ipsa plena possessione. Contrā, qui non habet Filium Dei, alienus est à vitæ æternæ spe: cum nullus sit alius salutis, nisi hic unicus nobis à Deo constitutus auctor; ac proinde frustra salus extra hunc Servatorem speratur. Ergò & Patres Veteris Testamenti, qui vitam habent æternam, eam per CHRISTUM Filium DEI habent. Unde tandem vel maximè elucet orthodoxæ sententiæ veritas, quæ præcipuum fructum mortis Christi, non in confirmatione doctrinæ salutis, sed in merito & satisfactione constituit.
units.tr: The meaning is this: this is the sum of what God has testified concerning his Son, namely that he is our Saviour, if only we believe in him. For God, out of his pure mercy, has appointed his Son to be for us the author of eternal life, which he has decided to give to all who believe in the Son, and indeed through the Son himself. Therefore he who has the Son of God through faith, that is, through whom he dwells in us, has eternal life; he has it with a certain hope and faith, to possess it in full reality one day. On the contrary, he who does not have the Son of God is a stranger to the hope of eternal life, since there is no other author of salvation, but this one alone has been appointed by God for us; and therefore salvation is hoped for in vain apart from this Saviour. Therefore the Fathers of the Old Testament also, who have eternal life, have it through CHRIST the Son of GOD. Hence at last the truth of the orthodox opinion shines out most clearly, which places the chief fruit of the death of Christ not in the confirmation of the doctrine of salvation, but in merit and satisfaction.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: ASSERTIO ET DEMONSTRATIO Meriti et satisfactionis Jesu Christi, ex eo, quod Christi obedientia nobis imputatur ad justitiam; quòd seviro Dei judicio fuerit satisfaciendum; quòd Christus non peccator sit mortuus.
units.tr: ASSERTION AND DEMONSTRATION of the merit and satisfaction of Jesus Christ, from the fact that Christ's obedience is imputed to us for righteousness; that a satisfaction had to be made to the severe judgment of God; and that Christ died not as a sinner.

units.la: {M}MEDIATOREM, Reconcili-atorem & Redemtorem nostrum JESUM CHRISTUM esse Servatorem nostrum, Merito & satisfactione pro pecpeccatis nostris pstita[?] demum mihi persuadet obedientia ejus, qua nos constituimur justi, quatenus illa nobis per fidem ad justitiam imputatur: deinde summa Dei justitia, & severum ejus peccatores exsecrantis judicium, cui satisfaciendum, ut liberemur: denique mors, quae peccatis debetur, & Christus a propriis peccatis plane purus nihilominus moriens. Unde ad fidei confirmationem ita argumentor.
units.tr: That Mediator, reconciler and redeemer of us, Jesus Christ, is our Saviour, is finally persuaded in me by his obedience, through which we are made righteous, insofar as that obedience is imputed to us for righteousness through faith; then by the supreme justice of God and his severe judgment against sinners who curse, to which satisfaction must be made so that we may be freed; and finally by the death that is owed to sins, and by Christ, who, though dying, was entirely free of his own sins. Whence I argue thus for the confirmation of faith.

units.la: CAPITIS VII. SECTIO I.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. SECTION I.

units.la: QUia Deo factum est pro nobis peccatum, seu hostia pro peccato, quique ab eodem factus est nobis justitia, ita ut ejus obedientia nos credentes constituamur justi, quatenus illa nobis per fidem ad justitiam imputatur, & ipsa fides in hunc Christum, talem nobis a Deo factum, pro justitia imputatur: certe is quandam pro nobis Deo praestitit satisfactionem, qua poenas nobis debitas exsolvit.
units.tr: Because God made sin for us, that is, a victim for sin, and the one who was made by him to be justice for us, so that we who believe are constituted just by his obedience, inasmuch as that obedience is imputed to us for righteousness through faith, and faith itself in this Christ, so made by God for us, is imputed for righteousness: assuredly he rendered to God on our behalf a certain satisfaction, by which he paid the penalties owed by us.

units.la: Atqui Jesus Christus Servator noster, ab ipso Deo factus est pro nobis peccatum, seu sacrificium pro peccato, ut supra aliquoties est demonstratum, ita ut ipsius Christi obedientia constituamur jufti,quatenus illa nobis per fidem ad justitiam imputatur, ac si eam ipsi praestitissemus. Rom. 5. 19. Deus enim neminem justificat, (cum judicium ejus sit secundum veritatem, Rom. 2. 2. nisi justum illum fecerit justitia imputativa, quae sola fide apprehendi potest. Justitia imputata jam praeditum hominem pronuntiat Deus justum. Roman. 5. 16. Judicium quidem ex uno in condemnationem: gratia autem ex multis delictis in justificationem. Et v. 18. Sicut per unius lapsum in omnes homines peccatum introit ad condemnationem: Sic etiam per unius δικαίωμα[?], juste factum sen justum opus, justitia introivit in omnes homines ad justificationem vitae. Cap. 8. 33. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat, quis est, qui condemnet?
units.tr: But Jesus Christ our Saviour was made sin for us by God himself, that is, a sacrifice for sin, as has been shown several times above, so that we are constituted just by the very obedience of Christ, inasmuch as it is imputed to us for righteousness through faith, as if we ourselves had rendered it. Rom. 5. 19. For God justifies no one (since his judgment is according to truth, Rom. 2. 2) unless he has made that person just by imputed righteousness, which can be laid hold of by faith alone. God pronounces a man who is already endowed with imputed righteousness to be just. Rom. 5. 16: The judgment indeed was of one unto condemnation, but the free gift is of many offences unto justification. And v. 18: As by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life [δικαίωμα, a righteous act; here, a righteous deed]. Rom. 8. 33: Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth.

units.la: Deinde homo a Deo pro justo habetur & pronuntiatur, cum Deus illi remittit peccata propter satisfactionem Christi. Rom. 4. 5. Et, qui non operatur, sed credit in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad justitiam: sicut etiam David dicit: beatificationem hominis esse, cui Deus imputat justitiam absque operibus, dicens: Beati, quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, & quorum obteste sunt peccata: Beatus vir, cui non imputa-rit Dominus peccatum. Roman. 3. 25.[?] Quem Christum proposuit Deus placamentum, per fidem, in sanguine ipsius, &c. ut sit ipse justus & justificans eum, qui est ex fide Jesu Christi. Cap. 4. v. 24. Futurum est, ut nobis imputetur (scilicet fides ad justitiam) qui credimus in eum, qui excitavit Jesum Dominum nostrum a mortuis; qui traditus est propter lapsus nostros; & excitatus est propter justificationem nostri. Cap. 5. v. 9. Justificati per sanguinem ejus. Cap. 10. v. 6. 7. Quae ex fide est justitia, ita dicit: Ne dixeris in corde tuo: Quis ascendet in coelum, hoc est Christum ex alto deducere: aut, Quis descendet in abyssum, hoc est Christum ex mortuis reducere. Galat. 2. ver. 20. 21. Vivo per fidem filii Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit seipsum pro me. Non abrogo gratiam Dei. Nam si per legem est justitia, igitur Christus frustra mortuus est. Ephes. 1. v. 6. 7. Deum per suam gratiam effecit nos gratiosos in illo dilecto, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum. (Nota, hic idem fere esse; aliquem justificari per sanguinem Christi: Et alicui peccata remitti propter (sanguinem Christi) Actor. 13. 38. Per hunc annuntiatur nobis remissio peccatorum: & ab omnibus, a quib. non potuistis per legem Mosis justificari, per hunc omnis, qui credit, justificatur. Porrò homo iustificatur fide, quatenus fide apprehendit sibique applicat obedientiam & satisfactionem Christi. Rom. 3. 24. Iustificantur per redemtionem factam in Christo, quem proposuit Deus placamentum, per fidem, in sanguine ipsius, Cap. 4. v. 24. Futurum est, ut imputetur nobis, qui credimus in eum, &c. Homo autem dicitur iustificari sola fide, hoc est, propter solam satisfactionem sola fide apprehensam, Rom. 3. 28. Concludimus igitur; fide iustificari hominem absq; operib. legis. Gal. 2. 16. Scientes non iustificari hominem ex operibus legis, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi, etiam nos in Iesum Christum credidimus, ut iustificaremur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis. Ephes. 2. 8. Gratiâ estis servati per fidem, non ex operibus. Phil. 3. 9. Ut inveniar in eo, non habens meam iustitiam, quae est ex lege, sed eam, quae per fidem est Christi.
units.tr: Then a man is held and pronounced just by God when God remits his sins on account of the satisfaction of Christ. Rom. 4. 5: But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. As David also says, that blessedness is of the man to whom God imputes righteousness without works, saying: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Rom. 3. 25: whom God set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, etc., that he might be just and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ. Ch. 4. v. 24: it shall be imputed to us (namely faith for righteousness) who believe on him who raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. Ch. 5. v. 9: Being now justified by his blood. Ch. 10. v. 6, 7: The righteousness which is of faith speaks thus: Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven, that is, to bring Christ down from above; or, Who shall descend into the deep, that is, to bring Christ up again from the dead. Gal. 2. v. 20, 21: I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. I do not set aside the grace of God. For if righteousness is by the law, then Christ died in vain. Eph. 1. v. 6, 7: God made us accepted in the Beloved through his grace, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. (Note that here it is nearly the same thing to say that someone is justified by the blood of Christ and that sins are forgiven someone on account of the blood of Christ.) Acts 13. 38: Through this man is preached to you the forgiveness of sins; and by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses. Moreover, a man is justified by faith, inasmuch as by faith he lays hold of the obedience and satisfaction of Christ and applies it to himself. Rom. 3. 24: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood. Ch. 4. v. 24: It shall be imputed to us, if we believe on him, etc. But a man is said to be justified by faith alone, that is, on account of the satisfaction laid hold of by faith alone. Rom. 3. 28: We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. Gal. 2. 16: Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law. Eph. 2. 8: By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves. Phil. 3. 9: And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ.

units.la: Praeterea homo iustificari dicitur ex Gratia seu gratuita Dei dilectione, quatenus DEUS ex gratia homini CHRISTUM ordinavit in Mediatorem, qui fit satisfactor noster. Actor. 15. v. 11. Per gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi credimus nos servatum iri, quemadmodum & illos. Rom. 3. 24. Iustificamur gratis ejus gratia per redemtionem factam[?] factam in Jesu Christo. Rom. 5.[?] 15. Si illius unius lapsu multi mortui sunt: multò magis gratia Dei, & donum per gratiam, quæ est unius hominis Jesu Christi, in multos redundavit.
units.tr: Furthermore, a man is said to be justified by grace, that is, by the free love of God, inasmuch as God of his grace appointed Christ as Mediator, who becomes our satisfier. Acts 15. 11: But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they. Rom. 3. 24: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Rom. 5. 15: If through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many.

units.la: Deniq; homo etiam dicitur justificari ex Dei justitia, quâ is satisfactionem CHRISTI acceptat pro nobis. Rom. 3. 25. Quem proposuit Deus placamentum[?] per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam justitiam suam per remissionem præcedentium peccatorum, ex Dei tolerantia; ad declarandam justitiam suam præsenti tempore, ut sit ipse justus, & justificans eum, qui est ex fide Jesu Christi.
units.tr: Finally, a man is also said to be justified by the righteousness of God, by which he accepts the satisfaction of Christ on our behalf. Rom. 3. 25: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; to declare, I say, his righteousness at this time: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.

units.la: En Deus declarat justitiam suam, quatenus remittit peccata nobis, pro quibus Christus satisfecit. Justisiæ[?] n. est contentum esse, si pro debito per Sponsorem satisfactum sit, non autem ab ipso debitore satisfactionem exigere. Jam si imputatur nobis à Deo justitia, seu nos pro justis à Deo habemur, propter mortem Christi, quâ scilicet pro nostris peccatis judicio ipsius satisfecit, adeoq; satisfactio Christi nobis credentib° à Deo ad justitiam imputatur: Certè omninò credenda est aliqua satisfactio Christi, quâ pœnas nobis debilebitas exsolvit, maximè verò, quia Deus Christum pro nobis fecit peccatum, ut nos credentes consequamur iustitiam coram Deo consistere valentem.
units.tr: Behold, God declares his righteousness, inasmuch as he remits sins to us, for which Christ has satisfied. For it is a matter of justice to be content if the debt has been paid by a surety, and not to demand satisfaction from the debtor himself. Now if righteousness is imputed to us by God, or we are held by God as just, on account of the death of Christ, by which he satisfied his judgment for our sins, and so the satisfaction of Christ is imputed by God to us who believe for righteousness, then assuredly some satisfaction of Christ must be believed, by which he paid the penalties owed by us; and this especially because God made Christ sin for us, so that we, believing, might obtain righteousness that can stand before God.

units.la: CAPITIS VII. SECTIO II.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. SECTION II.

units.la: Si Deus non modo est summè misericors, sed etiam summè iustus, ita ut secundum sententiam à se latam exsecretur peccatores & transgressores legùs sua; nos vero in peccatis concepti & filii iræ nati, perpetuo peccemus ac maledictioni simus obnoxii, à qua ut liberaremur, Deus misericordia dives Servatorem Christum nobis dedit, ut is sua morte pro nobis satisfaciens à severo Dei judicio nos eximeret, & sic populum suum à peccatis ipsorum liberaret, ac denique hæredes æterna felicitatis efficeret: Certè credendum est, Jesum Christum poenas nobis debitas luendo pro nobis severo Dei judicio satisfecisse.
units.tr: If God is not only supremely merciful but also supremely just, so that, according to the sentence he has pronounced, he curses sinners and transgressors of his law; and if we, conceived in sin and born children of wrath, sin continually and lie under the curse, from which God, rich in mercy, gave us Christ our Saviour to set us free, so that by his death, making satisfaction for us, he might deliver us from the severe judgment of God, free his people from their sins, and finally make them heirs of eternal blessedness: then we must certainly believe that Jesus Christ, by bearing the punishments owed by us, has satisfied the severe judgment of God on our behalf.

units.la: At quæ antecedunt vera esse ostendit veritas divinorum oraculorum. Exod. 20. v. 5. 6. Ego sum Jehova Deus tuus & Zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum super filios, in tertiam & quartam (generationem) odio habentes me: & faciens misericordiam in multibus diligentibus me & custodientibus præcepta mea. Exod. 34. v. 67. Transiens, Jehova ante eum, clamavit: Jehova, Jehova, Deus misericors & clemens, tardus ad iram, & multum mi-sericordiâ & veritate, servans misericordiam millibus, auferens iniquitatem & transgressio-nem & peccatum, & innocentem non faciens, visitans iniquitatem Patrum super filios, & su-per filios filiorum in tertios & in quartos. (Visitare est hic, ob peccata inquirere, in iisdem deprehendere homines, ut Deus eos puniat) Numer. 14. v. 18. Jehova est longanimus, & multus benignitate, condonans iniquitatem & defectionem, qui prorsus non absolvit, (fontem) visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in nepotes & abnepotes.
units.tr: That the foregoing is true is shown by the truth of the divine oracles. Exod. 20. vv. 5, 6: "I am the LORD your God, a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments." Exod. 34. vv. 6, 7: "The LORD passed before him and proclaimed: The LORD, the LORD God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in mercy and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and by no means leaving the guilty unpunished, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and upon the children's children, to the third and the fourth generation." (Here "to visit" means to search out sins and find people in them, so that God may punish them.) Num. 14. v. 18: "The LORD is slow to anger and abundant in kindness, forgiving iniquity and rebellion, but by no means clearing the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation."

units.la: Est igitur in Deo summa benignitas, Clementia, & Misericordia : & summa rectitudo, æquitas & justitia tum remunerans, tum vindicans. Psal. 145. v. 17. Justus Jehova in omnibus viis suis, & benignus in omnibus operibus suis.
units.tr: There is therefore in God the highest kindness, clemency and mercy, and also the highest uprightness, equity and justice, both in rewarding and in punishing. Psal. 145. v. 17: "The LORD is righteous in all his ways, and kind in all his works."

units.la: 2. Ergo secundum sententiam à se latam odit & exsecratur omnes peccatores, & legis suæ transgressores. Psal. 5. vers. 5. &c. Nam non es Deus fortis, qui delectetur improbitate, non est commoraturum apud te malum (vel malum non commorabitur) non consistent insani, (gloriabundi) e regione oculorum tuorum (inconspectu tuo) odisti omnes, qui operam dant iniquitati, perdes loquentes mendacium. Virum sanguinarium & dolosum abominatur Iehova. Deut. 27. v. 26. Maledictus, qui non praestiterit verba legis huius faciendo ea, & dicet totus populus: Amen.
units.tr: 2. Therefore, according to the sentence he has pronounced, he hates and curses all sinners and transgressors of his law. Psal. 5. v. 5, etc.: "For you are not a God who delights in wickedness; evil shall not dwell with you. The boastful shall not stand before your eyes; you hate all who do iniquity. You will destroy those who speak lies; the LORD abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man." Deut. 27. v. 26: "Cursed is he who does not establish the words of this law by doing them. And all the people shall say: Amen."

units.la: 3. Nos igitur in peccatis concepti, cum Davide Psalm. 51. v. 7. fateri habemus: Ecce in iniquitate conceptus sum, & in peccato calefecit me mater mea; & nati sumus Filii irae. Ephes. 2. v. 3. Inter quos & nos omnes conversati sumus olim in cupiditatibus carnis nostrae, facientes, quae carni & cogitationibus libebant: eramusque Natura Filii irae, ut etiam reliqui.
units.tr: 3. Therefore we, conceived in sin, must confess with David, Psalm 51. v. 7: "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me; and we were born children of wrath." Eph. 2. v. 3: "Among whom we also all once conducted ourselves in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest."

units.la: Unde apparet hominem corrupta Natura esse mancipium Diaboli, cui servit perpetrando peccata; ac proinde est reus irae Dei atq; aeternae damnationis.
units.tr: From this it appears that man, by his corrupt nature, is a slave of the Devil, whom he serves by committing sins; and consequently he is liable to the wrath of God and to eternal damnation.

units.la: Sed Deus cum dives sit Misericordia, propter multam caritatem suam, qua dilexit nos, nos cum per lapsus mor-cui[?] essemus, una vivificavit cum Christo, Ephes. 2. Et sic nos dilexit, ut Unigenitum Filium suum dederit, ut in sua obedientia & morte pro nobis satisfaciens, a severo Dei judicio nos eximeret. imeret. Gal. 3.13. Christus nos redemit ab exe-cratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio: Scriptum est enim: Execrabilis est quisquis pendet in ligno. Execratio dicitur Christus pro nobis factus, quatenus ex-secrabilem crucis mortem p[?] exsecrabilibus nostris peccatis expiandis obi-it, ut ita sua temporali morte, aeternam, quae nobis iminebat[?], aboleret. Heb.2.4[?].
units.tr: But God, being rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ. Eph. 2: "And so he loved us that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that by his obedience and death, making satisfaction for us, he might deliver us from the severe judgment of God." Gal. 3. v. 13: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us; for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." Christ is said to have become a curse for us insofar as he underwent the accursed death of the cross to expiate our accursed sins, so that by his temporal death he might abolish the eternal death which threatened us. Heb. 2. v. 4 [?].

units.la: 4. Christus itaque veniens in mun-dum salvos facere peccatores, Sponsor noster factus, in quem Deus fecit incurrere omnium nostrum iniquitates, factus pro nobis peccatum, & maledictum, a nobis solvit, ut populum suum a peccatis ipsorum liberaret. Matth. 1.21. Vocabis nomen ejus JESUM, ipse enim salvabit populum suum a peccatis ipsius. Servat autem tum Merito, tum Efficacia. Merito: quia morte sua & obedientia meritus est nobis apud Deum remissionem peccatorum, ac donationem Spiritus S. & vitae aeternae. Efficacia vero, quia per Evangelium & Spiritum S. efficit in nobis fidem in Servatorem Christi, & ex fide studium serviendi Deo secundum sancta ipsius mandata. Hic adversarii fatentur Deum Justum & Misericordem, sed non hac ratione; Fatentur, non primos tantum parentes, sed universum etiam humanum genus morti, & quidem æternæ obnoxium esse. Verum id non ex aliqua Dei justitia, sed ex libera ejus voluntate fluxisse, qua etiam potuisset homines licet peccantes, morti æternæ non mancipare, ajunt.
units.tr: 4. Christ, therefore, coming into the world to save sinners, was made our Surety, on whom God caused the iniquities of us all to fall; made sin and a curse for us, he has freed us, so that he might deliver his people from their sins. Matth. 1. v. 21: "You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." Now he saves both by merit and by efficacy. By merit, because by his death and obedience he has merited for us with God the forgiveness of sins, the gift of the Holy Spirit and eternal life. By efficacy, because through the Gospel and the Holy Spirit he works in us faith in Christ the Saviour, and from faith a zeal for serving God according to his holy commandments. Here our adversaries confess that God is just and merciful, but not in this way. They confess that not only our first parents but the whole human race is liable to death, and indeed to eternal death. But they say that this did not flow from any justice of God, but from his free will, by which he could also have spared men, though sinners, from eternal death.

units.la: Falsum quoque dicunt, justitiam Dei peccatores æterna morte plectendos censere. Deum iniquitatem impunitam non relinquere, tum verum esse, si obstinatam hominis malitiam, ejusq; perseverantiam & perpetuam delectationem in malis perpetrandis intelligamus: alioquin falsum esse.
units.tr: They also say falsely that "the justice of God judges sinners to be punished with eternal death." That God does not leave iniquity unpunished is true only if we understand an obstinate malice in man, and his perseverance and continual delight in committing evils; otherwise it is false.

units.la: Proinde justitiam Dei, quoad hanc disputationem, qua misericordiæ ejus opponi potest, distinguunt ita: Justitia Dei alia est, qua iniquos & impios, hoc est, illos, qui in malitia perseverat, & qui suorum scelerum pœnitentia non ducuntur, neq; ad ipsum Deum, ejusq; opem atq; misericordiam confugiunt, giunt, punit & perdit. Hac Deus perpetuò utitur. Alia, quâ peccatores nonnunquam, neq; contumaces, neq; omnino desperatos, eorum pœniten-tia non exspectata ex sua lege punit; vel etiamsi velit, quanquam resipiscentes, promissione misericordiæ suæ, qua se volens quodammodo nobis devinxit, exclusa, punire potest.
units.tr: Accordingly, they distinguish the justice of God, as far as this dispute is concerned, from which his mercy can be opposed, as follows: there is one justice of God, by which he punishes and destroys the wicked and the ungodly, that is, those who persist in malice, who are not led to repentance of their crimes, and who do not flee to God himself and his help and mercy. God always uses this justice. There is another, by which he may, according to his law, punish sinners who are sometimes neither obstinate nor wholly despairing, without waiting for their repentance; or even, if he wishes, punish those who repent, though he has bound himself to them in some measure by the promise of his mercy, which he has excluded.

units.la: Hinc una Misericordia Dei illis dicitur, quâ resipiscentibus, ut ipsius promissa ferunt, omnia scelera condonat, & salutem vitamque largitur. Altera, quâ planè homines prævenit, & peccatis adhuc immersos, ad se vocat & allicit, gratuitóque ne cogitantibus nobis delictorum veniam & salutem offert. Illa perpetuò utitur, hacverò tum demum, cum liber.
