Cæterum cum tradunt ad infirmandum argumentum nostrum, nullam esse in Deo talem justitiam, quæ punitionem ob peccata requirat, modò peccator resipiscat, expresse pugnant cum absoluta Dei sententia, adversus peccatores lata,
units.tr: Hence one mercy of God is said to be that by which, to those who repent, as his promises declare, he forgives all crimes and grants salvation and life. Another is that by which he plainly anticipates men, still immersed in sins, calls and entices them to himself, and offers them pardon and salvation freely, even when we are not thinking of it. He always uses the first, but the second only when he pleases. But when they teach, in order to weaken our argument, that there is no such justice in God as requires punishment for sins, provided only that the sinner repents, they plainly contradict the absolute sentence of God pronounced against sinners,

units.la: Etenim Genes. 2. verf. 17. Quæcunque die comederis ex eo, morte morieris: Quàm primùm transgressus fueris homo, mandatum meum, non acquiescens iis, qua tibi sunt exposita, morte morieris, Symmachus reddit, mortalis eris, subiectus eris morti et legibus illius morti corporis & animae, temporali & aeterna. Hinc Apostolus Roman. 5. veri. 12. &c. Sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum intrauit, ac per peccatum Mors; & ita in omnes homines Mors pervasit, eo quod omnes peccaverunt. Item: Regnavit Mors ab Adam usque ad Moysen, in eos etiam qui peccaverunt ad similitudinem: transgressionis Adam. Item, per inobedientiam illius unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi.
units.tr: For Gen. 2. v. 17: "In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." Symmachus renders it: "You shall be mortal, you shall be subject to death and to its laws, bodily and spiritual, temporal and eternal." Hence the Apostle, Rom. 5. vv. 12 ff.: "As sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin; so death spread to all men, because all have sinned." Likewise: "Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of the transgression of Adam." Likewise, "through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners."

units.la: Hîc audis Legislatoris Dei justitiam postulantem obedientiam, audis & poenam, propter inobedientiam homini inflictam. Sententia Dei est, Deuter. 27. v. 26. Maledictus seu execrabilis omnis, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in libro legis, ut faciat ea.
units.tr: Here you hear that the justice of God as Lawgiver demands obedience; you hear also the punishment inflicted on man for disobedience. The sentence of God is, Deut. 27. v. 26: "Cursed, that is, accursed, is everyone who does not persist in all that is written in the book of the law, to do them."

units.la: Deinde peccatum cum sit ἀνομία & privatio justitiae à lege justâ justi Dei requisitae, producit immediatum effectum; nempe reatum hominis peccantis, h. e. obligationem ejus ad luendam poenâ à Deo constitutâ. Unde postea pœnæ ipsæ consequuntur, nisi fiat remissio propter Christum. Peccata vestra, inquit Jes. Cap. 59. 2. diviserunt inter Deum & vos. Job. 9. 28. Verebar omnia opera mea, sciens quod non parcis omni delinquenti, Galat. 3. Exsecrabilis omnis, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis, ut faciat ea. Ezech. 18. 4. Anima, quæ peccaverit, moritur. Rom. 6, v. ult. Stipendium peccati mors est. Jacob. 1. 25. Peccatum cum fuerit consummatum, parit mortem.
units.tr: Then, since sin is ἀνομία (lawlessness) and a privation of the justice required by the just law of the just God, it produces an immediate effect, namely the guilt of the sinning man, that is, his obligation to pay the penalty appointed by God. From this the punishments themselves follow afterwards, unless remission is granted on account of Christ. "Your sins," says Isaiah 59:2, "have divided between God and you." Job 9:28: "I feared all my works, knowing that you will not spare any offender." Galatians 3:10: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things which are written in the book of the Law, to do them." Ezekiel 18:4: "The soul that sins, it shall die." Romans 6, last verse: "The wages of sin is death." James 1:15: "Sin, when it is completed, brings forth death."

units.la: Ergo suâ naturâ omne peccatum perpetratum, etiam minimum, mortem meretur: & quidem mortem non solum temporalem, sed & æternam. Interim fateor, è-contra veniam adipisci omnes, qui resipiscunt, & in Christum credunt, etiamsi gravissima peccata admiserint.
units.tr: Therefore by its own nature every sin committed, even the smallest, deserves death: and indeed not only temporal death but also eternal death. Meanwhile I admit that, on the contrary, all who repent and believe in Christ obtain pardon, even if they have committed the gravest sins.

units.la: Sed Tertiò observandum, hominem non posse resipiscere, nisi fide in Christo fit donatus, & utrumque esse Dei gratiam, quam Deus inimicis suis, quamdiu tales sunt, largiri non solet. 2. Tim. 2. 25. Servum Domini oportet cum lenitate erudire eos, qui contrario animo sunt affecti, expe[?]turus, an forte daturus sit eis Deus refipiscentiam, per cognitionem veritatis; & ipsi ad sobrietatem redituri sint, ex Diaboli laqueo, à quo captiu-nentur[?], entur, ad prastandam illius voluntatem.
units.tr: But thirdly, it must be observed that a man cannot repent unless he is given faith in Christ, and that both are the grace of God, which God is not accustomed to bestow on his enemies as long as they are such. 2 Timothy 2:25–26: "The servant of the Lord must teach with gentleness those who are opposed to him, if perhaps God may give them repentance, leading to the knowledge of the truth; and that they may come to their senses out of the snare of the Devil, by whom they have been taken captive to do his will."

units.la: Vide hic miserum naturalis hominis statu, Mens ejus ignoratione voluntatis [illegible, ~6 letters] est: voluntas a Diabolo captiva tenetur. Vide etiam Dei esse, dare resipiscentiam hominibus, adeoq; nō vulgare, sed singulare esse Dei donum. Efficit autem illam Deus per agnitionem veritatis, nempe coelestis, patefactæ verbo Dei, tum de cultu Dei, tum de salute nostra.
units.tr: See here the wretched state of natural man: his mind is in ignorance of the will of God; his will is held captive by the Devil. See also that it is God's to give repentance to men, and therefore it is not a common but a singular gift of God. God effects it, however, through the knowledge of the truth, namely the heavenly truth revealed by the Word of God, both concerning the worship of God and concerning our salvation.

units.la: Qui enim ex verbo legis cognovit, Deum æternis suppliciis punire velle omnes in impietate perfistētes, ac tum ex verbo Evangelii, Deum in gratiam recipere velle omnes resipiscentes, & in Christum credentes, fieri nequit, quin per gratiam Dei resipiscat, & gratiam Dei fide apprehendens posthac pietati serio studeat. Dei interim est, per spiritum & verbum suum illuminare & convertere corda nostra.
units.tr: For it cannot but happen that one who has learned from the word of the Law that God wishes to punish with eternal torments all who persist in impiety, and then from the word of the Gospel that God wishes to receive into favour all who repent and believe in Christ, should, by the grace of God, repent, and, grasping the grace of God by faith, afterwards earnestly apply himself to piety. Meanwhile it belongs to God to illuminate and convert our hearts through his Spirit and Word.

units.la: Ergo si quæritur, quifiat, ut mortè æter-nam meriti peccatis nostris, nihilominus ab eâ liberati, ad vitam æternâ perveniamus? Christianum responsum est: quia supplici-um mortis æternæ, cujus judicio eam peccatis nostris meriti eramus, nobis pro ineffabili ipfiusMifericordiâ & bonitate propter Jesu Christi Sponsoris & pacificatoris nostri satisfactionem & meritum, quo ipse à nobis persolvens pro nobis satisfecit Deo, condonatum fuit, atq; ejus loco datum vitæ æternæ præmium : modò credamus in Chri- ftum Jesum propitiatorem nostrum, resipiscamus, & abnegatâ omni impietate, vitæ innocentiæ & sanctimoniæ studendo, fidei veræ vitam & fructus Deo & homini comprobemus.
units.tr: Therefore if it is asked, how is it that we, who have deserved eternal death by our sins, are nevertheless freed from it and attain to eternal life? the Christian answer is this: because the punishment of eternal death, by whose judgment we had deserved it for our sins, has been forgiven us, by the unspeakable mercy and goodness of God, on account of the satisfaction and merit of Jesus Christ, our Surety and Reconciler, who, paying the price in our place, has satisfied God on our behalf; and in its place the reward of eternal life has been given; provided only that we believe in Jesus Christ our propitiator, repent, and, renouncing all impiety and striving after a life of innocence and holiness, show forth the life and fruits of true faith to God and to men.

units.la: Quòd fi quâ ratione nobis innotuerit, quæratur, cùm neque Deum videamus unquam, nec audiamus loquentem, quisve nobis tanta divina gratia & liberalitatis non dubiam fidem fecerit ? Responsum est: ipsum Dei Filium dilectum, quem Pater de cœlo jussit audire, quiq; in sinu patris est, nobis id enarraffe, & multis modis confirmaffe, quin seipsum nobis salutem & vitam æternam, quam nobis suo merito acquisivit, daturum promisisse & probasse, ut sit Servator noster doctrinâ, Merito & Efficacia (li[?]eet doctrina sub efficacia alioqui con-tineri possit.)
units.tr: But if it is asked, by what means it has become known to us, since we never see God nor hear him speaking, and who has given us an assured faith in such great divine grace and generosity? The answer is: that the beloved Son of God himself, whom the Father commanded from heaven to be heard, and who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared this to us and confirmed it in many ways; moreover, that he himself promised and proved that he would give us salvation and eternal life, which he has acquired for us by his own merit, so that he is our Saviour by his teaching, his merit and his efficacy (although teaching may otherwise be included under efficacy).

units.la: CAPITIS VII. SECTIO III.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. SECTION III.

units.la: Quicunque moritur, hunc vel necesse est esse peccatorem, vel aliena peccata inse solvenda recepisse.
units.tr: Whoever dies must either be a sinner himself, or have taken upon himself to pay the debts of others.

units.la: Mors enim stipendium peccati à iustitiā Dei constitutū est. Rom. Ut pietati amplissima merces promissa est, beata immortalitas seu vita æterna: Ita Mors proprium peccati stipendium à Deo constitutum est. Ubi nomine mortis potissimum æternam mortem intelligi docet antithesis vitæ æternæ: præter illam tamen etiam aliæ peccati pœnæ ita comparatæ sunt, ut ad illam mortem, tanquam ultimum scopum, tendant.
units.tr: For death has been appointed by the justice of God as the wages of sin (Rom.). Just as a most ample reward is promised to piety, namely blessed immortality or eternal life, so death has been appointed by God as the proper wage of sin. Here the antithesis to eternal life teaches that by death is chiefly meant eternal death; yet besides that, other punishments of sin are so arranged that they tend toward that death as their final goal.

units.la: Deinde certum est, mortem intrasse in mundum, vi illius sententiæ, à DEO latæ. Genes. Cap. 2. vers. 17. Quocunq; die, de eo comederis, morte morieris. Unde Roman, 5. vers. 12[?] Paulus dicit: Sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, ac per peccatum mors: Et ita in omnes homines mors pervasit, eo quod omnes peccaverunt, hoc est: Quemadmodum per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, ac per peccatum necessaria ac perpetua mors, atque ita mors s-sta[?] in omnes homines ab Adamo prognatos pervasit, quatenus quidem omnes peccarunt: Sic etiam per unum hominem justitia in mundum ingressa est, & per justitiam coelestis ac perpetua vita, atque ita aeterna vita participes facti sunt, quicunque à Christo secundum Spiritum propagantur, quatenus quidem justi sunt. Quapropter quicunq; moritur, vel hunc necesse est esse peccatorem, vel aliena peccata in se solvenda recepisse.
units.tr: Next, it is certain that death entered the world by virtue of that sentence pronounced by God: Genesis 2:17, On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death. Hence Paul says in Romans 5:12: As through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, so death spread to all men, because all have sinned. That is to say: just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin a necessary and perpetual death, and so death spread to all men born of Adam, inasmuch as indeed all have sinned; so also through one man righteousness entered the world, and through righteousness a heavenly and perpetual life, and so all who are spiritually begotten of Christ have been made partakers of eternal life, inasmuch as indeed they are righteous. Therefore whoever dies must either be a sinner himself, or have taken upon himself to pay the debts of others.

units.la: At Christus mortuus, quâ de re nulla est dubitatio.
units.tr: But Christ died, about which thing there is no doubt.

units.la: Ergo Christus, aut fuit peccator, aut aliena, scilicet nostra, peccata in se solvenda recepit.
units.tr: Therefore Christ either was a sinner, or took upon himself to pay the sins of others, namely ours.

units.la: Atqui Christus peccator non fuit, Heb. 4. Tentatus fuit in omnibus similiter nobis, sed absq; peccato. Paulus inquit, Eum non novisse peccatum. Petrus ait: Christum peccatum non fecisse, nec in eius ore dolum inventum esse. Unde & ipse Judaeis dicit Joh.8. Quis ex vobis me arguet peccati ullius?
units.tr: But Christ was not a sinner: Hebrews 4:15, He was tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin. Paul says that he knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21). Peter says that Christ did not commit sin, nor was guile found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22). Hence he himself also says to the Jews in John 8:46: Which of you convicts me of any sin?

units.la: Ergo Christus aliena peccata expianda in se recepit. Ipse igitur purus & non peccator, pro nostris peccatis Moriendo satisfecit, sicut & sanctitas & expiatio peccatorum conjungi solent. 1. Pet. 1.19. Redeti estis pretioso sanguine, utpote agni immaculati, et incontaminati, nempe Christi. 1.Pet.2.22. Qui Christus peccatū non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ipsius; & statim: Qui peccata nostra ipse met sustulit in corpore suo super lignum, ut peccatis mortui, iustitiæ viveremus; cuius vulneribus sanati estis. Cap. 3.18. Christus semel pro peccatis passus fuit, iustus pro iniustis, ut nos ad Deum adduceret. Heb. 7. v.28, Talis enim nos decebat Pontifex sanctus, innocens, impollutus, segregatus a peccatoribus, sublimior cœlis factus. Et post: pro peccatis populi obtulit victimam semel, cum seipsum obtulit. Heb. 9. ad finem: Ad abolendum peccatum per immolationem sui ipsius patefactus est. Et sicut illud statutum est hominibus, ut semel moriantur, postea vero iudicium: Ita & Christus semel oblatus est, ut multorum peccata tolleret: secundo absq; peccato conspicietur iis, qui ipsum exspectant ad salutem.
units.tr: Therefore Christ took upon himself the sins of others to be expiated. He, then, being pure and not a sinner, made satisfaction for our sins by dying, just as holiness and the expiation of sins are customarily joined together. 1 Pet. 1:19, You were redeemed with precious blood, as of a lamb unblemished and undefiled, namely Christ. 1 Pet. 2:22, Christ, who committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth; and immediately after: who himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness; by whose wounds you were healed. 1 Pet. 3:18, Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God. Heb. 7:26–27, For such a high priest became us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, made higher than the heavens. And afterwards: He offered up a sacrifice for the sins of the people once, when he offered himself. Heb. 9:26 (end): He was made manifest to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. And just as it is appointed to men once to die, and after that the judgment, so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and to those who await him for salvation he will appear a second time, apart from sin.

units.la: Nota, Absq; peccato, quia in primo suo adventu conspectus fuit cum peccato Mundi sibi imputato, Tes. 53.6. 2. Corinth. 5.21. At nō fuit conspectus cum peccapeccato proprio. Sanctè enim conceptus est, & sanctè semper vixit.
units.tr: Note: "apart from sin," because at his first coming he was seen with the sin of the world imputed to him (Isa. 53:6; 2 Cor. 5:21). But he was not seen with his own sin. For he was conceived in holiness and always lived in holiness.

units.la: Sed Adversarii propositionem pugnare contra omnem scripturâ, contra omne jus, & omnem rationem. Aut enim primò, inquiunt, verbum Moritur, in propositione significat mortem perpetuam, aut temporariam. At neque perpetuam, neq; temporariam.
units.tr: But our opponents say that the proposition fights against all Scripture, all law and all reason. For, they say, first, the word dies in the proposition signifies either perpetual death or temporary death. But it signifies neither perpetual nor temporary death.

units.la: Non perpetuam, ut sensus sit. Qui moritur æternam mortem, aut ipse peccator est, aut aliena peccata in se expianda suscepit. Cur verò? Quia, inquiunt, omnes homines, post primos parentes, etiam sine ullis propriis peccatis, eam mortem subire coguntur: & nemo est, qui pro alienis peccatis mortem æternam subeat. Ajunt verò, omnes ab Adamo prognatos morti perpetuæ esse obnoxios, non ideo, quòd ipsis Adami delictum imputetur, sed quia ab eo sunt progeniti. Sed aliud est, omnes esse obnoxios, aliud jam subire cogi mortem æternam: illi liberari possunt, hi non. Aliud jus, aliud factum: Intervenire potest Dei Patris benignitas ac Miseri-
units.tr: Not perpetual death, so that the sense would be: Whoever dies the eternal death is either himself a sinner, or has taken upon himself to expiate the sins of others. Why not? Because, they say, all men after the first parents are compelled to undergo that death even without any sins of their own, and no one undergoes eternal death for the sins of others. They say, moreover, that all born of Adam are liable to perpetual death, not because Adam's offence is imputed to them, but because they have been begotten of him. But it is one thing to be liable, another thing to be compelled actually to undergo eternal death: the former can be freed, the latter cannot. One thing is right, another thing is fact. The kindness and mercy of God the Father may intervene,

units.la: cordia,
units.tr: mercy,

units.la: *. Objectio. Responsio. cordia, Christi JEsu satisfactio & intercessio. Obnoxiorum resipiscentia & fides.
units.tr: *. Objection. Response. mercy, the satisfaction and intercession of Jesus Christ, and the repentance and faith of those who are liable.

units.la: Deinde negant, Christum perpetuam mortem subiisse. Respondetur: Etiamsi Christus ad tempus tantum cruciatus damnatorum passus sit: quippe execratio pro nobis factus est, adeo, ut se derelictum putaret a DEo. tamen istud aequipollet morti aeternae, propter dignitatem personae, quae est Deus aeternus.
units.tr: Next, they deny that Christ underwent perpetual death. The answer is: even though Christ suffered the torments of the damned only for a time (for he was made a curse for us, so much so that he thought himself forsaken by God), nevertheless this is equivalent to eternal death, on account of the dignity of the person, who is the eternal God.

units.la: Non etiam temporariam significat Mortem, inquiunt: Quia significaret aut violentam aut naturalem.
units.tr: They say that temporary death also is not meant, because it would signify either violent or natural death.

units.la: At neque violentam. Quia nemo est, qui jure propter aliena peccata occidatur: At jure occidi potest, si sponte alienum debitum in se exsolvendum recepit. Deinde, inquiunt, quia innumerabiles reperiuntur, qui quamvis nec propter sua, nec propter aliena peccata, tamen interficiuntur, ut sunt Martyres Dei & Christi.
units.tr: But neither violent: for no one is rightly put to death on account of the sins of others; yet a man may rightly be put to death if he has voluntarily taken upon himself a debt of another to be paid. Next, they say, there are countless people who, though neither on account of their own nor of others' sins, are nevertheless killed, such as the martyrs of God and of Christ.

units.la: Sed propositio sit: Qui moritur violenta morte, is aut peccator est, aut aliena peccata in se recepit, expianda. At Martyres passi sunt violentam mortem. Ergo aut peccatores fuerunt, aut aliena peccata tulerunt. Sed non hoc. Ergo illud. Quis enim neget illos esse vel fuisse peccatores, licet non propter peccata sua tollenda, ut quae ipsis condonata sunt ex gratia propter Christum, perpessi sint illam mortem?
units.tr: But let the proposition be: Whoever dies a violent death is either a sinner, or has taken upon himself the sins of others to be expiated. But the martyrs suffered a violent death. Therefore they were either sinners, or bore the sins of others. But not this. Therefore that. For who would deny that they were, or had been, sinners, although they did not undergo that death in order to bear away their own sins, which were forgiven them by grace on account of Christ?

units.la: Sed ad Christum redeamus. Affirmo Christum quidem non Naturalem, sed violentam mortem, & quidem necessario obiisse, idque his testimoniis, quibus ipsa experientia accedit, fretus.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ. I affirm that Christ died not a natural but a violent death, and indeed of necessity; and I rely for this on those testimonies, to which experience itself adds its witness.

units.la: Luc. 9. v. 22. Jesus dixit: Oportet Filium hominis multa pati, & reprobari a senioribus et principibus Sacerdotum, & scribis, & trucidari, & tertio die excitari. Matth. 16. 21. Ex eo tem-pore capit Jesus indicare discipulis suis. Oportere se abire Hierosolymam, & multa pati a senioribus, & primariis Sacerdotibus, & scribis & occidi & tertio die suscitari. Idem[?] dicitur Marci 8. 31. Et coepit eos docere, quod oporteret filium hominis multa pati & reprobari a Senioribus, Principibusque Sacerdotum ac Scribis, & trucidari, & tribus post diebus resurgere. Luc. 18. 32. Ecce, inquit Jesus, ascendimus Hierosolymam & per & perficientur de filio hominis omnia, quae scripta sunt per Prophetas. Tradetur n. gentibus & illudetur, et contumeliis afficietur, et conspuetur, et postquam eum flagellaverint, trucidabunt eum.
units.tr: Luke 9:22: Jesus said, The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and on the third day be raised up. Matthew 16:21: From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. The same is said in Mark 8:31: And he began to teach them that the Son of man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and after three days rise again. Luke 18:31–32: Behold, said Jesus, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things that are written by the prophets concerning the Son of man will be accomplished. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, and will be mocked and insulted and spat upon, and after they have scourged him they will kill him.

units.la: Luc. 24.7. dicut Angeli ex ore Christi: Oportet filium hominis tradi in manus hominum peccatorum, & crucifigi, & die tertio resurgere.
units.tr: Luke 24:7, the angels say, in the words of Christ: The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.

units.la: Hic necessitas cum violentia moriendi conjuncta spectatur.
units.tr: Here the necessity of dying is considered together with the violence of the death.

units.la: Docent vero illi; Christum etiam naturali morti subjectum fuisse, non quidem propter peccata vel sua vel aliena, sed quia homo natus erat.
units.tr: But they teach that Christ was also subject to natural death, not indeed on account of his own sins or those of others, but because he had been born a man.

units.la: Docent deinde, Christum mortuum esse propter peccata nostra, (suo modo) non quatenus illi alioqui, postquam homo natus fuerat, naturaliter moriendum erat; sed quatenus violentam mortem subiit volens. Adde: Voluit autem, quia nostra peccata ac debita in se receperat exsolvenda.
units.tr: Next they teach that Christ died for our sins (in a certain manner), not in so far as he otherwise had to die naturally after being born a man, but in so far as he willingly underwent a violent death. Add that: he willed it because he had taken on himself our sins and debts, to be paid off.

units.la: Concedunt item divino & incommutabili, decreto statutum esse, ut Christus moreretur. Atqui istam necessitatem moriendi non esse eam, quae dicto isto: Stipendium peccati mors est, continetur, peccati enim stipendium est moriendi necessitas & mors aeterna. Quid tum? Christus enim non habuit peccata propria, sed Sponsor & Mediator noster factus, nostra sursum tulit, in corpore suo, super lignum crucis. Satis igitur est, si ex immutabili DEI decreto mortem illam sibi destinatam necessario pro nobis & nostris pœnis luendis perpessus sit.
units.tr: They also concede that it was decreed by the divine and unchangeable decree that Christ should die. But that necessity of dying is not the one contained in the saying, "The wages of sin is death"; for the necessity of dying and eternal death are the wages of sin. What follows? Christ did not have sins of his own, but, made our Surety and Mediator, he bore ours upward, in his body, upon the wood of the cross. It is enough, therefore, if, by the unchangeable decree of God, he suffered that death destined for him, necessarily, for us and to pay our penalties.

units.la: II. Rursus autem sic sophisticantur ad jugulandum hoc argumentum nostrum. Cum dicis: Qui moritur, aut est peccator, aut aliena peccata in se solvenda receperit, aut verbum moritur, ita intelligis, ut id, quod fit, spectetur, aut id quod fieri debeat, aut id, quod fieri potest.
units.tr: II. Again they quibble in this way to strangle our argument. "When you say: whoever dies is either a sinner, or has received the sins of others to be paid in himself, or you understand 'dies' in one of three ways: either as what is done is viewed, or as what ought to be done, or as what can be done."

units.la: 1. Si id, quod fit, spectas, idem est, ac si dicas: Quicunq; mortuus est unquam, ille aut est seu fuit peccator, aut aliena in se peccata tollenda recepit. Esto: detur aliquis, qui mortuus est, vel qui jam moriatur, qui non peccator, aut peccatorum Sponsor. Si Christum afferunt, principium petunt. Hunc sponsorem & reconciliatorem nostrum defendimus. Nec est quod dicitur, Multa fieri jure, quæ nunquam vel ante vel post facta fuerunt. Nam & hoc, quod CHRISTUS suâ morte pro nobis satisfecit, jure divino factum actum est, licet nunquam id ante factum, vel post futurum sit.
units.tr: 1. If you look at what is done, it amounts to the same as if you said: "Whoever has ever died, he either is or was a sinner, or has received other people's sins to be removed in himself." Grant it: let someone be given who has died, or who is now dying, who is not a sinner or a Surety for sins. If they bring up Christ, they beg the question. We defend this Surety and Reconciler of ours. Nor is there force in their saying, "Many things are done by right which were never done either before or after." For this too, that Christ by his death satisfied for us, was done and carried out by divine right, although it never happened before, nor will it happen afterwards.

units.la: 2. Si id, quod fieri debet, spectas, erinde est, ac si dicas: Quisquis tenetur mori, aut tenetur mori quia peccator est, aut quia peccatorum salvandorum Sponsor est.
units.tr: 2. If you look at what ought to be done, it is just as if you said: "Whoever is bound to die is bound to die either because he is a sinner, or because he is the Surety for the sins to be saved."

units.la: Esto: Detur aliquis, qui mori non tenetur alterutro modo. Datur <bl>CHRISTUS</bl> ab istis, qui ideo mortuus sit, non quia mori teneretur, sed quia ita & Deo & ipsi visum est. Imò CHRISTUM mori oportuit, & sic eum mori visum est DEO, non quia ipse peccator, sed quia peccatorum Sponsor & pacificator esse voluit.
units.tr: Grant it: let someone be given who is not bound to die in either way. Christ is given by them, who for this reason died, not because he was bound to die, but because it seemed good both to God and to himself that it be so. Indeed, Christ had to die, and it seemed good to God that he die thus, not because he was himself a sinner, but because he willed to be the Surety and Peacemaker for sinners.

units.la: 3. Si ad id, quod fieri potest respiceis, aut jus aut ipsum factum spectas. Si de facto loqueris, hic sensus erit: Fieri non potest, (scilicet, ita juste decernente Deo) ut quis moriatur, nisi aut sit ipse peccator in se, aut alienà peccata solvenda in se susceperit.
units.tr: 3. If you look to what can be done, you regard either the right or the deed itself. If you speak of the deed, the sense will be: "It cannot happen (namely, with God decreeing so justly) that anyone die, unless either he himself is a sinner in himself, or he has taken on himself to pay another's sins."

units.la: Falsum hoc esse proclamatur, sed non demonstratur. Detur ista possibilitas
units.tr: They proclaim that this is false, but do not demonstrate it. Let that possibility be granted.

units.la: Respons. litas ex decreto voluntatis divinæ in hoc nostro statu. Affertur Mortalitas, seu Mors naturalis, quam aiunt esse humanæ naturæ sequelam annexam in ipsa creatione, ita ut etiam homo in statu integritatis permanens mortalis fucerit[?], & absq; peccato mortuus fuisset. Sed hoc nunc disceptatur. Maneat itaq; propositio in statu lapsum subseeuta.
units.tr: Answer: [it is possible] from the decree of the divine will in this our state. There is brought forward "mortality," or natural death, which they say is a consequence attached to human nature in creation itself, so that man, remaining in the state of integrity, would have been mortal and would have died even without sin. But this is now under dispute. Let the proposition therefore remain: "in the fallen state."

units.la: Si de jure, inquiunt, loqueris, ut loqui videris, sensus erit; injustum & iniquum esse, ut quis moriatur; q non aut sit ipse peccator, aut alienorum peccatorum pœnas exsolvedas in se receperit: Quia mors peccati pœna fit, & nemo morte teneatur, nisi quis vel ipse peccaverit, vel alius quispiam, pro quo ipse pœnas luat. Esto autem hic sensus.
units.tr: "If you speak of right," they say, "as you seem to do, the sense will be: it is unjust and iniquitous that anyone die who either is not himself a sinner or has not received on himself the penalties of others' sins to be paid. For death is the penalty of sin, and no one is bound to death unless either he himself has sinned, or some other person for whom he pays the penalties." Let this be granted as the sense.

units.la: At vero, inquiunt, an nō potest quis volens id perpeti, quod perpeti alioqui non tenetur: nec tamen propterea ulla ex parte justitiam ladere?
units.tr: But, they say, "can someone not, willingly, undergo that which otherwise he is not bound to undergo, and yet not in any way injure justice on that account?"

units.la: Quæro & Ego: An nō potuit Filius Dei volens in se, ut Mediator & Sponsor noster debita nostra dissolvenda recipere, & id propter eā perpeti, nempe morte nobis debitam, quam perpeti alioqui (extra casum huius Mediationis & Sponsionis) non tenebatur, nec tamen propterea ulla ex parte justitiam ladere; imo potius justitia debitum nostrum exigenti satisfacere? Imò a-junt: quid magis laudabile & admiratione dignum[?] esse potest, quàm cum quis id facere nullo modo teneatur, multa tamen mala experiri velle, ut aliis bene sit. Imo & ego ajo, quid magis laude & admiratione dignum esse potest, quàm si filius ipse Dei propter nos & salutem nostram, duram mortem, ut Servator noster, voluerit subire, quam ipse sustinere alioqui non tenebatur, nisi ipse Sponsor noster fuit, ultrò passus sit omnium nostrum iniquitates in se conjici? Sed satis: infra de hac re fusius.
units.tr: I too ask: could not the Son of God, willingly taking on himself, as our Mediator and Surety, the receiving of our debts to be paid, and on account of this undergoing that which otherwise (apart from the case of this Mediation and Suretyship) he was not bound to undergo, namely death owed to us, and yet not in any way injure justice; indeed rather satisfy justice demanding our debt? Indeed they say: "What can be more praiseworthy and worthy of admiration than when someone, who is not at all bound to do this, is willing to undergo many evils so that it may go well for others?" Indeed I too say: what can be more praiseworthy and worthy of admiration than if the Son of God himself, for us and for our salvation, as our Saviour, was willing to undergo a harsh death, which he otherwise was not bound to bear, unless he was our Surety, and of his own accord suffered the iniquities of all of us to be laid upon him? But enough: more fully on this matter below.

units.la: CONCLUSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Neitaque quisquis es, mirere, quod adhærescens Jesu Christo Servatori meo, eum arctè teneam, complectar & exosculer, ut qui pro peccatis meis justo Dei judicio satisfecerit patiendo & moriendo, & æternam mihi vitam promeritus sit.
units.tr: Therefore, whoever you are, do not wonder that I cling to Jesus Christ my Saviour, hold him tightly, embrace and kiss him, since he, by suffering and dying, made satisfaction for my sins by the just judgment of God, and has merited for me eternal life.

units.la: ETENIM.
units.tr: FOR.

units.la: 1. Est MEDIATOR noster æter-num fœdus gratiæ suâ morte sanciens, qui semet ipsum redemtionis pretium pro nobis dedit.
units.tr: 1. Our MEDIATOR is the eternal covenant of grace, ratifying it by his death, who gave himself as the ransom price for us.

units.la: 2. Est RECONCILIATOR noster, quem ipse Deus constituit placamentum per fidem in sanguine ejus,
units.tr: 2. He is our RECONCILER, whom God himself set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood,

units.la: 3. Est vere ac proprie REDEMTOR noster, qui suo pretioso sanguine nos redemit, & per eum effusum nos à ventura irâ liberavit.
units.tr: 3. He is truly and properly our REDEEMER, who redeemed us with his precious blood, and by that blood poured out freed us from the wrath to come.

units.la: 4. Ipse sustulit INIQUITATES nostras, quas ipsi Deus, ut Sponsori nostro, imposuit, in corpore suo super li-gnum.
units.tr: 4. He took away our INIQUITIES, which God laid upon him, as our Surety, when he bore them in his body on the tree.

units.la: 5. Ipse pro nobis factus PECCATUM, & Maledictum pro peccatis nostris expiandis est vulneratus, afflictus, passus & denique mortuus.
units.tr: 5. He was made SIN for us, and was wounded, afflicted, suffered and at last died as a Curse, to expiate our sins.

units.la: 6. Ipsius sanguine in remissionem peccatorum effuso, peccata nostra EXPIANTUR, à peccatis nos abluimur[?] & emundamur.
units.tr: 6. With his blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins, our sins are EXPIATED; we are washed and cleansed from our sins.

units.la: 7. Ipse est summus noster PONTIFEX, qui seipsum pro nobis obtulit & sanctificavit, atq; ita purgatione peccatorum nostrorum per seipsum facta in cœlo pro nobis intercedit.
units.tr: 7. He is our great PRIEST, who offered and sanctified himself for us, and so, having effected the purging of our sins by himself, intercedes for us in heaven.

units.la: 8. Ipse ideo traditus & mortuus est, ut peccata nobis propter mortem ejus REMITTI, & justitia coram Deo consistere valens, restaurari queat.
units.tr: 8. He was therefore delivered up and died, so that, through his death, our sins might be REMITTED to us, and we might be restored, able to stand righteous before God.

units.la: 9. Ipse Agnus ab origine mundi mactatus carnem suam pro mundi vita dedit, ejusq; mortis virtus pervenit ad eos etiam, qui ante ipsius incarnationem vixerunt.
units.tr: 9. He, the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, gave his flesh for the life of the world, and the virtue of his death reached even those who lived before his incarnation.

units.la: 10. Ipsius obedientia J u s t i constituimur, quatenus illa nobis per fidê ad justitiam imputatur.
units.tr: 10. By his obedience we are constituted JUST, inasmuch as that obedience is imputed to us for righteousness through faith.

units.la: 11. Ipse à Deo nobis SERVATOR datus, nos maledictos peccatores justi-tiæ Dei, punitionem ob peccata requirenti, suâ morte satisfaciendo, sal-vos fecit.
units.tr: 11. Given to us by God as SAVIOUR, he saved us, the cursed sinners, by satisfying with his death the justice of God, which requires punishment for sins.

units.la: 12. Ipse denique ex patris decreto morti traditus est, non quod ipse esset peccator, sed HOSTIA pro peccato nostro, & SPONSOR pro nobis peccatoribus, & ita moriendo pro peccatis nostris satisfecit. Huic nostro Sponsori & sponso sit gloria & honor in omnem seculorū omni-um sempiternitatem, Amen.
units.tr: 12. Finally, by the decree of the Father he was delivered to death, not because he was a sinner himself, but as the HOST for our sin and the SURETY for us sinners; and so by dying he made satisfaction for our sins. To this our Surety and Bridegroom be glory and honour for all the everlasting ages of ages, Amen.

units.la: SECUNDA LIBRI PARS, CAPUT I.
units.tr: SECOND PART OF THE BOOK, CHAPTER I.

units.la: Socinianorum Refutatio. CAPUT I. PROPVGNATIO MERITI & Satisfactionis IESU CHRISTI contra id, quod dicitur, nullam satisfactionem pro peccatis necessariam: DEUM semper peccata voluisse remittere absque satisfactione: iustitiam Dei nobis non perennitibus satisfieri non posse.
units.tr: Refutation of the Socinians. CHAPTER I. DEFENCE OF THE MERIT AND SATISFACTION OF JESUS CHRIST against the claim that no satisfaction for sins is necessary: that God has always been willing to forgive sins without satisfaction: that the justice of God cannot be satisfied for us by anything but perpetual...

units.la: SENTENTIAM hanc nostram de Merito & satisfactione IESU CHRISTI certam [?] hactenus & demonstratam Adversarii non erubescunt appellare absurdam, continentem execrabiles errores, detestandam, ac penitus rejiciendam: quod ut persuadeant, rationes quasdam, quibus ipsi compulsi nostrae sententiae refragantur, in medium plausibili quadam ratiocinatione producunt, quas brevi examine, pro modulo meo, ad fidei mea dei meae & aliorum confirmationem, discutere fert animus, salutis meae & gloriae Jesu Christi studiosus.
units.tr: Our opponents are not ashamed to call this doctrine of ours concerning the merit and satisfaction of Jesus Christ, though so far certain and demonstrated, absurd, containing detestable errors, to be abhorred, and utterly to be rejected. To persuade people of this, they bring forward in the open some arguments, by which they are driven to oppose our position, with a certain plausible reasoning; and I, being zealous for my own salvation and for the glory of Jesus Christ, feel moved to examine them briefly, according to my ability, for the confirmation of my faith, of my God, and of others.

units.la: CAPITIS I. SECTIO I.
units.tr: Chapter I, Section I.

units.la: Si nulla omnino satisfactio pro peccatis ex parte Dei est necessaria, doctrina de satisfactione & merito Christi inane est figmentum.
units.tr: If no satisfaction at all for sins is necessary on God's part, the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction and merit is an empty fiction.

units.la: Atqui ex parte Dei nulla omnino satisfactio est necessaria. Hoc ita probatur: Si Deus & iure potuit, & benigne voluit nobis nostra condonare peccata, nulla vera pro illis satisfactione ab ulla persona ullo modo accepta, certe nulla omnino satisfactio pro peccatis nostris est & fuit necessaria.
units.tr: But on God's part no satisfaction at all is necessary. This is proved thus: If God both can by right and is graciously willing to forgive us our sins, without any true satisfaction for them being accepted from any person in any way, then certainly no satisfaction at all for our sins is or was necessary.

units.la: Atqui Deum iure potuisse nobis nostra condonare peccata, nulla pro ipsis vera satisfactione accepta demonstratur.
units.tr: But that God could by right forgive us our sins, without any true satisfaction being accepted for them, is shown as follows.

units.la: Primo sic: Si Deus est omnium omnino dominus, & de iure suo quantum velit, remittere potest, vera pro peccatis satisfactione non accepta, illa nobis condonare iure suo potest.
units.tr: First, thus: If God is Lord of all things without exception, and can remit as much of his own right as he wishes, then, without a true satisfaction being accepted for sins, he can by his right forgive them to us.

units.la: Atqui Deus in hominibus vel puniendis vel absolvendis, non tanquam iudex aliquis statuendus est: qui de alieno iure agat, cuius non licet a legum praescripto recedere, sed tanquam Dominus & Princeps, cuius sola voluntas; cum de ipsius ipsius iure tantum agatur, omnium rerum est, & perfectissima norma.
units.tr: But God, in punishing or absolving men, is not to be regarded as some judge who acts by another's right, whose prescribed laws he may not depart from, but as Lord and Prince, whose will alone governs. Since the matter concerns only his own right, it belongs to him, and he is the most perfect rule of all things.

units.la: Jam unicuique de jure suo, quantum velit, remittere licet. Quod si igitur quilibet homo jure potest injurias sibi illatas libere condonare, & quamvis maximè possit, eas tamen minimè ulcisci, nec solùm id facere-ju-re potest, sed etiam ob eam ipsam causam laudibus in cœlum tollitur: An eo jure & potestate Deum privare audebimus? Et quis est, qui nesciat delicta nostra, debita sive æs alienum, quod cum Deo contraxerimus, in divinis literis appellari, & propterea Deum tanquam creditorem nostrum, nos autem ejus tanquam debitores, peccatorum nostrorum respectu constitui? Atqui nullus est creditor, qui debitori suo, vel debiti partem, vel unius versum debitum, nulla satisfactione acceptâ, condonare summo jure non possit.
units.tr: Now it is lawful for each person to remit as much of his own right as he wishes. If therefore any man can by right freely pardon injuries done to him, and, though he could most fully avenge them, can in no way avenge them, and not only may he do this by right but for this very reason is raised to heaven with praise, shall we dare to deprive God of that right and power? And who does not know that our sins, our debts or what we owe, which we have contracted with God, are called debts in the divine writings, and that therefore, with respect to our sins, God is set up as our creditor and we as his debtors? But no creditor exists who cannot, by the highest right, remit to his debtor either part of the debt or a single item of it, without any satisfaction having been accepted.

units.la: Respondetur per distinctionem.
units.tr: The reply is made by distinction.

units.la: Debitum aut lædit honorem, debitoris, aut non lædit, Si non lædit ejus honohonorem, magno cum augmento honoris potest sine ulla compensatione emitti; ut cum Rex aliquis servo suo emittit debitum aliquot millium florenorum. Hoc debitum ut non laedeat Majestatem Regis, ita salva Majestate remitti potuit.
units.tr: A debt either injures the honour of the debtor or does not. If it does not injure his honour, it can be discharged with a great increase of honour and without any compensation, as when some king remits to his servant a debt of several thousand florins. Since this debt does not injure the king's majesty, it could be remitted with his majesty intact.

units.la: Si vero debita laedant honorem & Majestatem creditoris, ejusque naturae & gloriae ex diametro adversentur, certè non possunt sine satisfactione, libero quodam ductu voluntatis, remitti. Alia autem debita sunt peccata; utpote, quae aeternae voluntatis divinae regulam infringunt, eíque adversantur: ita ut salva Dei justitia & rectitudine, sine poena expiari non possint.
units.tr: But if debts injure the honour and majesty of the creditor and are diametrically opposed to his nature and glory, then certainly they cannot be remitted without satisfaction, by a free movement of the will. Sins, however, are debts of another kind: they break the rule of the eternal divine will and oppose it, so that, if God's justice and rectitude are to remain safe, they cannot be expiated without punishment.

units.la: Hinc adeò est, quod quidam distinguant debitum in Externum & Internum. Externum debitum dicunt civile illud, ad quod bona tantum fortunae contingunt, non autem bona ipsa interiora, sive virtutem ejus, cui debetur, & tale affirmant remitti posse salva justitia sine satisfactione. Internum debitum vocatur, quod pertinet ad virtuvirtutem internam, & normam justitiae ejus cui debemus; Sic nimirum peccata commissa ab Angelis & hominibus, sua natura comparata sunt, ad laedendam Dei virtutem internam, sive aeternam illam voluntatem, quae est lux Dei. Itaque Deus haec remittere non potest sine satisfactione.
units.tr: Hence some distinguish debt into external and internal. They call that civil debt external, which is owed only in respect of goods of fortune and not of the inner goods themselves, or of the virtue of the one to whom it is owed; and they affirm that such a debt can be remitted, with justice preserved, without satisfaction. A debt is called internal when it pertains to the inner virtue and the rule of justice of the one to whom we owe it. Thus sins committed by angels and men are, by their nature, such as to injure God's inner virtue, that is, that eternal will which is the light of God. Therefore God cannot remit these without satisfaction.

units.la: Justitia enim, ajunt, Deo ita est essentialis & immutabilis, ut poenas creaturis per benignitatem remittere non possit, nisi justitiae huic satisfiat. Quippe justitia Dei sit ex perfectione Dei & immutabili voluntate, quae legi ita conjuncta est, ut necesse sit aut legem voluntatis Divinae servari, aut omnes creaturas in nihilum redigi; quia creaturae sunt aliquid extra Deum, sine quo Deus esse potest.
units.tr: For justice, they say, is so essential and immutable in God that he cannot remit punishments to creatures out of kindness unless this justice is satisfied. Indeed, the justice of God arises from the perfection of God and his immutable will, which is so joined to the law that it is necessary either that the law of the divine will be kept or that all creatures be reduced to nothing, because creatures are something outside God, and God can exist without them.

units.la: Voluntatis autem lex & integritas est in Deo ita, ut sine ea Deus esse nequeat nec possit Deus contra seipsum dispensare, ut peccata remittat sine satisfactione pstitā justitiae.
units.tr: The law and integrity of the will are in God in such a way that without them God could not be, and God cannot act against himself by dispensing so as to remit sins without a satisfaction made to his justice.

units.la: Potest tamen Deus per benignitatem suam simul & sapientiam reperire modum aliquem, quo justitiae ipsius satis-fiat. fiat, etiamsi creatura, quæ peccavit, satisfacere non potest.
units.tr: Yet God, by his goodness and wisdom together, can find some means by which his justice is satisfied, even if the creature which sinned cannot make satisfaction.

units.la: Ego quidem fateor, Deum habere potestatem in nō utendo iure suo, quia plerumq; nobiscum summo jure non agit, & quod alioqui facere posset, (puta hos vel illos delinquentes punire) sæpius ex gratia facere omittit. Fateor & hanc potestatem niti absoluto Dei dominio, quod habet in omnia. Nullus enim Domin[?] simpliciter jus suum persequi tenetur, dummodo nulla cujusquam injuria in ipsa proprii juris remissione implicetur. Itaque Deus tam liberè miseretur, quorum vult, quàm liberè, quos vult, indurat, quia semper licet illi de suo facere, quod vult.
units.tr: I indeed grant that God has the power of not using his right, since for the most part he does not deal with us by strict right, and often out of grace omits to do what he could otherwise do (for instance, punish these or those offenders). I grant too that this power rests on God's absolute dominion over all things. For no lord is simply bound to pursue his right, provided that no injury to anyone is involved in the very remission of his own right. Thus God has mercy as freely on whom he wills as he hardens whom he wills, since it is always lawful for him to do with his own what he wills.

units.la: Interim dico & sentio, Deum punire non posse immerentes, si qui essent; imò nec resipiscentes, quotquot sunt: nec contra potest absolvere peccatores impoenitentes, quamvis & justos interdum graviter affligat, & peccatores poenitentes à reatu semper absolvat. Etenim fieri non potest, ut Deus contra suam ipsius voluntatem semel definitam, nedum contra suam ipsius na-turam, quicquam jure statuat. Qua de re paulo post.
units.tr: Meanwhile I say and hold that God cannot punish the undeserving, if there were any, nor indeed the penitent, however many there are; nor, on the other hand, can he absolve impenitent sinners, although he sometimes afflicts even righteous men severely, and always absolves penitent sinners from guilt. For it cannot happen that God should decide anything by right against his own will once fixed, still less against his own nature. On this more will be said shortly.

units.la: Sic igitur Statuo, liberrimam Dei potestatem locum habere in iis omnibus & solis, quae perfecto ipsius dominio subjacent. At talia non sunt, quae naturaliter ipsi Deo insunt: de quibus idcirco aliter statuere non potest, quam fert absolutae illius naturae necessitas. Sic non potest Deus quidquam agere jure, quod ipsius sapientiae, aut bonitati, aut justitiae repugnet; nec potest ea nolle aut omittere, q; naturaliter vult aut facit, &c. Quia nulla facultas, nullus item actus, ferri potest, extra objectum sibi adæquatum[?].
units.tr: I therefore lay down this: God's most free power has its place in all those things, and only those, which lie under his perfect dominion. But such things are not those which naturally inhere in God himself; concerning these he cannot decide otherwise than the necessity of that absolute nature requires. Thus God cannot do anything by right which would be repugnant to his wisdom, goodness or justice; nor can he refuse or omit what he naturally wills or does, and so on, because no faculty, and likewise no act, can be carried beyond its adequate object.

units.la: Deinde eadem Dei potestas non-imminuitur, etiamsi dicamus, Deum nunc quaedam ex hypothesi facere jure non posse, quae alias absolute loquendo, supremae ipsius potestati subjecta sunt. Sicut ergo vitam aeternam credentibus non potest denegare, postquam illis hanc se daturum promisit, quam alioqui donare illis nullo jure te-neba[?]ebatur: Sic etiam iis, quos certò & [?]solutè[?] se punituruum minatus est, poe-nam remittere non potest, quam alio-ui[?] infligere non tenetur. Quoniam & promissio & comminatio DEI ginit obligationem: Illa quidem respectu solius DEI certo aliquid futurum sseverantis: illa vero tum respectu Dei afferentis, tum respectu hominis, acceptantis & consentientis. Deniq; impossibile est DEUM ullâ ratione à praescripto justitiæ aut veritatis unquam aberrare.
units.tr: Further, that same power of God is not diminished even if we say that God now cannot, by hypothesis, do certain things which, speaking absolutely, are otherwise subject to his supreme power. Just as he cannot deny eternal life to believers after he has promised to give it to them, which otherwise he was under no right obligation to give, so too he cannot remit the penalty to those whom he has certainly and absolutely threatened to punish, which otherwise he is not bound to inflict. For God's promise and his threatening both create obligation: the former with respect to God alone, as affirming that something will certainly come to pass; the latter both with respect to God, who asserts it, and with respect to man, who accepts it and consents. Finally, it is impossible for God in any way ever to depart from the prescription of justice or truth.

units.la: SECUNDO igitur sic arguunt: Si justitia illa quæ punitionem requirit ob peccata, non est propriétas in Deo residens, sed effectum liberæ voluntatis Dei, sicut & oppositæ est misericordia: Deus nobis jure potest peccata ignoscere absque præstita illi satisfactione. At quod antecedit, verum, probatur sic.
units.tr: SECONDLY, then, they argue thus: If that justice which requires punishment for sins is not a property residing in God, but an effect of his free will, just as its opposite, mercy, is, then God can by right forgive us our sins without satisfaction being rendered to him. But the antecedent is true, and is proved thus:

units.la: 1. Si justitia illa resideret in Deo, nunquam ne minimum quidem delictum cuiquam condonaret. Nihil enim unquam fecit aut facere potest Deus, quod qualitatibus, quæ in ipso residet, adversatur. Vt cum in Deo sapientia & æquitas resideat, nihil unquam insipienter, nihil intque facere potest, aut facit. At sæpe Deus peccata condonat hominibus.
units.tr: 1. If that justice resided in God, he would never pardon even the least offence to anyone. For God never did, and never can do, anything that is opposed to the qualities which reside in him: as, since wisdom and equity reside in God, he never does or can do anything foolishly or unjustly. But God often pardons sins to men.

units.la: 2. In Deo sunt pugnantia contraria. Atqui justitia punientes peccata, & misericordia condonans peccata, sunt contraria pugnantia. Punire enim delicta & condonare, sibi invicem adversantur.
units.tr: 2. In God there are contraries which are opposed. But the justice which punishes sins and the mercy which pardons sins are contrary and opposed. For to punish offences and to pardon them are mutually hostile.

units.la: 3. Ea quae in Deo residunt, terminum nullum habent, simul stare possunt, & inter se magnitudinis respectu sunt prorsus aequalia. Atqui haec justitia punientes peccata, & Misericordia condonans habet terminum. Punitio enim & condemnatio non est infinita. Stare simul non possunt, sed altera alteram tollit. Et una ab altera magnitudine superatur, quia Deus dicitur tardus irae, & multus misericordiae. Exod. 34. 6.
units.tr: 3. Those things which reside in God have no limit, can exist together, and are altogether equal to one another in greatness. Yet this justice, which punishes sins, and this mercy, which pardons sins, have a limit. For punishment and condemnation are not infinite. They cannot stand together, but the one destroys the other. And one is surpassed by the other in magnitude, because God is said to be slow to anger and abundant in mercy. Exod. 34. 6.

units.la: Concludendum igitur est, inquam illi [?], nullam in Deo justitiam esse, quae omnino peccatum puniri debere dicet, & cui ipse renuntiare non possit, sicut nulla in eo est misericordia, quae peccatoribus ignoscendum esse omnino statuat; & cui voluntas divina quodammodo obsequi debeat. Ergo nihil est, propter quod Deus liberè, cui velit, nullâ satisfactione acceptâ, peccata jure condonare non possit, non minus, quàm eum, qui deliquit pro suo arbitratu punire.
units.tr: It must therefore be concluded, I say to them [?], that there is no justice in God which would declare that sin must altogether be punished, and which he himself could not renounce, just as there is no mercy in him which decides that sinners must altogether be forgiven, and to which the divine will must in some way yield. Therefore there is nothing on account of which God, freely and without any satisfaction received, cannot justly pardon sins to whomever he wishes, no less than he can punish the one who has offended according to his own pleasure.

units.la: EXAMEN.
units.tr: EXAMEN.

units.la: 1. Justitia Dei ꝑprie dicta, est omni- nō [?]naturalis Dei proprietas, per quam se in Natura & omni actione sua jus ac recte esse intelligitur; sicut, Misericordia Dei, quatenus Clementem in ipso affectum seu perpensionem miseris succurrendi significat, in ipso Deo residet, & proprietas, vis & virtus quaedam. Et quia in Deo utraq; est, utraq; etiam infinita est. Atque licet [?]concedamus, justitiam punientem peccata, & Misericordiam ea condonante, utramq; scilicet esse liberrimæ Dei voluntatis effectum: tamen satisfactionem pro peccatis, ad condonanda ea, non esse ullo modo necessariam, non concedimus.
units.tr: 1. Justice in the proper sense is a natural property of God entirely, through which he is understood to be right and just in his nature and in all his actions. Likewise, the mercy of God, insofar as it signifies in him the affection or inward feeling of compassion for helping the wretched, resides in God himself, and is a property, power and a certain virtue. And because both are in God, both are also infinite. And although we grant that justice punishing sins and mercy pardoning them are both, namely, the effects of the most free will of God, nevertheless we do not grant that satisfaction for sins is in any way necessary for pardoning them.

units.la: Necessitas enim satisfactionis, de qua hic agitur, est HYPOTHETICA, propter immutabile decretum DEI. Neq; enim sine impietate affirmari potest, Deum, utpote immutabiliter constantem, tum in promissionibus, tum in comminationibus suis, (uti dicitur Malach. 3. 6. Ego Jehova non mutor. Jac.1. 17. Apud Deum non est transmutatio, aut conversionis obumbratio,) posse huic justitiæ renunrenunciare, quâ ut iustis praemia promisit, sic peccatoribus punitionem comminatus est. Levit. 18. v. 5. 19. Sicut[?] servabitis statuta mea, & iudicia mea, homo qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis: Ego Iehova. Quis[?] vero fecerit aliquam ex omnibus abomina-tionibus istis, utiq; exscindetur anima, quae illa fecerint, è medio populi sui. Genes. 2, 17. Qui cunq; die comederis de ligno isto, morte morieris. Deut. 27. 26. Maledictus, qui non præstiterit verba legis huius, faciendo ea, & dicet totus populus, Amen.
units.tr: For the necessity of satisfaction, which is the subject here, is HYPOTHETICAL, arising from the unchangeable decree of God. For it cannot be affirmed without impiety that God, who is immutably constant both in his promises and in his threats (as it is said in Malachi 3. 6: I, the LORD, do not change; James 1. 17: With God there is no variation, nor shadow of turning), could renounce this justice by which he promised rewards to the righteous and threatened punishment to sinners. Lev. 18. 5, 19: You shall keep my statutes and my judgments, which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the LORD. But whoever commits any of these abominations, that soul shall surely be cut off from among its people. Gen. 2. 17: In the day that you eat of that tree, you shall surely die. Deut. 27. 26: Cursed is he who does not establish the words of this law by doing them. And all the people shall say, Amen.

units.la: Et qui fieri unquam potest, ut iustus ille Deus contra suam ipsius voluntatem semel definitam, nedum contra suam ipsius naturam, quicquam iure statuat? Genes. 18. v. 25. Absit à te, ut facias tale quippiam, morti tradendo iustum cum iniusto, ut ita sit iusto sicut iniusto: absit à te, an iudex totius terra nō exerceres ius? Exod. 34. v. 6. 7. Transiens Iehova ante faciem ejus inclamavit: Iehova, Iehova, Deus fortis, misericors & gratiosus, longanimis & multum benignitatis ac fide: custodiens benignitatem millibus, condonans iniquitatem & defectionem, & peccatum: & qui nullo pacto non absolvit fontem, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, & in filios filiorum, & in nepotes ac abnepotes. Ezech. 18 4, [illegible, ~3 letters]rima, qua peccaverit, ipsa morietur. Nam qui erit iustus & exercebit ius ac iustitiam, &c.
units.tr: And how can it ever happen that that just God should decree anything by right against his own will once determined, much less against his own nature? Gen. 18. 25: Far be it from you to do such a thing, to slay the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous would be as the wicked: far be it from you! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? Exod. 34. 6, 7: And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed: The LORD, the LORD God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and who by no means clears the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and fourth generation. Ezek. 18. 4: The soul that sins, it shall die. For he who is just and does judgment and righteousness, etc.

units.la: Iustus hic omnino vivet, dictum Domini Iehovæ. Quod si quis genuerit filium effractorem, effusorem sanguinis, &c. qui fecerit omnes abominationes, non vivet, sed omni-no morte afficietur.
units.tr: He who is just shall surely live, says the Lord GOD. If he begets a son who is a robber, a shedder of blood, etc., who does all these abominations, he shall not live, but shall surely be put to death.

units.la: 2. Omnino iustitia illa specialis, quæ dicitur Retributiva, in Deo est, quæ exigit, ut unicuique secundum opera sua redatur[?], nempe ut piis & Deo obedientibus promissum præmium donetur; impiis autem & Deo rebellib. constitutum supplicium infligatur. 2. Thessal. 1. v. 6. Iustum est apud Deum retribuere iis afflictionem, qui pios affligunt, piis vero qui affliguntur, relaxationem. Est Iustitia in Deo, per quam ex mera benignitate pietati merces constituta persolvitur. In exercenda misericordia etiam iustus est Deus.
units.tr: 2. Certainly that special justice which is called retributive is in God, which requires that to each one should be rendered according to his works: namely, that the promised reward be given to the pious and obedient to God, and that the punishment appointed be inflicted on the impious and rebellious against God. 2 Thess. 1. 6: It is a righteous thing with God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to give rest to you who are troubled. There is a justice in God by which the reward established for piety is paid out from pure kindness. In exercising mercy also, God is just.

units.la: Est etiam iustitia in Deo, per quam impiis ac impœnitentibus debita supplicia tandem irrogantur: ne videlicet divina benignitas & patientia impune semper contemnantur. At non valet: Si justitia est in Deo, cujus vi peccata puniuntur, non est misericordia in Deo, cujus vi condonantur peccata: Sicut nec hoc: Ergo nulla unquam peccata remittuntur.
units.tr: There is also a justice in God by which the due punishments are at last inflicted on the impious and the impenitent, so that the divine kindness and patience may not always be despised with impunity. But the argument does not hold: If there is justice in God, by whose power sins are punished, there is no mercy in God, by whose power sins are pardoned; nor does this: Therefore no sins are ever remitted.

units.la: Justitia enim irrogat poena ob peccata iis, quibus illam comminata est; & Misericordia condonat peccata illis, quibus condonare ex gratia promisit. Utrumq; postulat justitiæ & æquitatis divinæ ratio. Sicut hoc consequens est: Si in Deo est æquitas, nihil iniqui facit: sicet-iam consequitur: Si in Deo est justitia, nihil injusti unquam facit.
units.tr: For justice inflicts punishment for sins on those to whom it has threatened it, and mercy pardons sins to those to whom it has promised pardon out of grace. The reasoning of divine justice and equity requires both. Just as this follows: If there is equity in God, he does nothing unjust, so too this follows: If there is justice in God, he never does anything unjust.

units.la: 3. Fieri non potest, ut ipsæ naturales DEI proprietates verè sint inter se contrariæ: proinde proprie dicta Misericordia & justitia in Deo, non sunt pugnantes qualitates. Quòd autem aliquando solet Misericordia justitiæ opponi, id etiam eatenus fieri concedimus, quatenus per Misericordiam non ipsum naturalem miserendi affectum, sed liberum gratiosæ voluntatis effectû: Item justitiæ nomine non æquitatem ipsam, sive rectitudinem Dei, sed iram seu vindictam Dei, quæ similiter ut ef-sectus sectus consideratur, intelligimus. In quam sententiam inquit Deus Ezech. 8. v. 18. Faciam in furore meo, non parcet oculus meus, non miserebor, &c. Ubi furorem Misericordiæ opponit. Sic Ierem. 13. 14. & cap. 16. 5. 6. Quo sensu Apostolus etiam benignitatem et severitatem inter se opponit, Roman. 11. 22.
units.tr: 3. It cannot be that the natural properties of God themselves are truly contrary to one another; therefore justice and mercy in God, properly speaking, are not opposing qualities. But that mercy is sometimes wont to be opposed to justice, we also grant that this happens so far as, by mercy, we understand not the natural affection of compassion itself but the free effect of a gracious will; and likewise, by the name of justice, we understand not equity or rectitude itself in God but the wrath or vengeance of God, which is similarly considered as an effect. To this effect God says in Ezek. 8. 18: I will act in fury; my eye shall not spare, nor will I have pity, etc. Where he opposes fury to mercy. So in Jer. 13. 14, and chap. 16. 5, 6. In this sense the Apostle also opposes goodness and severity to each other, Rom. 11. 22.

units.la: 4. Certum etiam, ea, quæ in Deo sunt, esse infinita, sicut ipse Deus est infinitus, adeoque omnes proprietates & virtutes Dei proprias esse interminatas ac infinitas: Ipsam vero peccatorum condonationem & punitionem esse terminatam ac finitam, ut effecta benignæ & justæ voluntatis divinæ, seu ipsius Misericordiæ & Justitiæ infinitæ ac æternæ.
units.tr: 4. It is also certain that the things which are in God are infinite, just as God himself is infinite; and so all the proper properties and virtues of God are unbounded and infinite. But the pardoning and punishing of sins themselves are limited and finite, as effects of the kind and just will of God, or of his mercy and justice, which are infinite and eternal.

units.la: At, Si causa est infinita, numquid etiam infinita ejus sunt effecta? an non ex infinita potentia procedit infinitus actus ac effectus externus?
units.tr: But if the cause is infinite, are its effects not also infinite? Does not an infinite external act and effect proceed from an infinite power?

units.la: Nequaquam potest esse causa infinita, cujus effecta non sunt infinita: dicitur enim illa infinita, propter potentiam, qua causari potest infinitam. Infinitæ causæ, infinita agendi potentia, infinitus quærendi modus. Etsi nihil infinitum faciat. Sic Misericordia & Justitia proprie dicta in Deo sunt & manent infinitæ, quia potentia earum in Deo infinito infinita est, at non illius vel huius, illud vel hoc effectum necesse est infinitum.
units.tr: A cause cannot be infinite whose effects are not infinite: for it is called infinite on account of the power by which it can cause what is infinite. An infinite cause has infinite power of acting, an infinite manner of seeking, although it does not make anything infinite. Thus mercy and justice properly speaking are and remain infinite in God, because their power in the infinite God is infinite; but it is not necessary that this or that effect, of this or that kind, be infinite.

units.la: Per justitiam igitur vindicantem pro justa sua voluntate punit peccata impiorum, sicut & quibus minatus est, quomodo & quando vult. Per Misericordiam ignoscentem pœnas peccatorum condonat & tollit, sicut & quibus promisit, pro misericordia sua voluntate.
units.tr: Through justice, therefore, which avenges, God punishes the sins of the impious according to his just will, as and to the extent that he has threatened, in what manner and at what time he wills. Through mercy, which pardons, he remits and removes the punishments of sins, as and to whom he has promised, according to his merciful will.

units.la: §. Diversitas respectus tollit omnem oppositionem. Condonatio & punitio peccatorum secundum idem, ad idem & eodem tempore intellecta, se tollunt, at horum diversitate incidente stare simul possunt. Ut Misericordia & Justitia, ita peccatorum nostrorum condonatio & punitio optime in salutis nostræ negotio conspirant, & declarata conspiciuntur in diversis subjectis, CHRISTO & nobis.
units.tr: §. A difference of respect removes all opposition. Pardon and punishment of sins, understood in the same respect, toward the same object and at the same time, cancel each other; but with this difference of respect intervening, they can stand together. As mercy and justice do, so the pardon and punishment of our sins agree most well in the business of our salvation, and are seen declared in different subjects: in CHRIST and in us.

units.la: Exercet Deus justitiam suam, puniendo peccata nostra, in CHRISTO spononfore[?] ac redemtore nostro ; Exer-cet idem & declarat suam misericordi-m, condonando seu à nobis auferen-o peccatorum poenas, adeoq; nostri [?]iferendo, in nobis miseris peccatori-us & debitoribus. Eum, qui non no-it peccatum, fecit peccatum, ut nos sfemus[?] justitia in eo. 2. Cor. 5.
units.tr: God exercises his justice by punishing our sins in Christ, our surety and redeemer; and the same God exercises and displays his mercy by remitting to us the penalties of sins and by bearing them himself, so that he deals with us as wretched sinners and debtors. "He who knew no sin, he made to be sin for us, that in him we might become the righteousness of God." 2 Cor. 5.

units.la: TERTIO sic opponunt. Si falsum est, delinquentibus deberi punitionem ob peccata, falsum quoque est, punitione illa justitia divina satisfieri debere.
units.tr: Thirdly, they object as follows: "If it is false that punishment is owed to offenders for their sins, then it is also false that divine justice must be satisfied by that punishment."

units.la: At prius verum. Delinquentes quidem optimo jure puniuntur: verum ea punitio non ipsis, sed Reipubl. (cujus interest sontes puniri, & eam ob causam, ut puniantur, lege cavit) debetur. Haec si juri suo renuntiare velit, & eo se ipsam privare, cum sibi ipsi nemo injuriam facere possit, nulli injuriam facit.
units.tr: But the first statement is true. Offenders are indeed punished by the best right, but that punishment is owed not to them but to the commonwealth, whose interest it is that the guilty be punished, and which for that reason has enacted by law that they be punished. If the commonwealth is willing to renounce its right and deprive itself of it, it does no injury to anyone, since no one can do an injury to himself.

units.la: Hoc sensu accipiendum, quod dici solet: justitia est, suum cuique tribuere, nempe, nulli non dandum, quod ad ipsum non pertinet, & ad ejus commodum atque utilitatem spectat.
units.tr: This is how the saying commonly given should be understood: "Justice is giving each his due," namely, that one should give to no one what does not belong to him and does not regard his advantage and benefit.

units.la: Neque ea sententia Mala & poenas complectitur, quæ jure alicui debeantur. Ergo nec Deus injustum aliquid facere censendus est, si sibi ipsi, dum contra suam legem committentibus parcit, suum non tribuit, quia nemini quicquam præterea adimit.
units.tr: Nor does that saying embrace evils and penalties that are owed to someone by right. Therefore, "God is not to be judged to do anything unjust if, in sparing those who commit offences against his law, he does not give himself what is his due, since he takes nothing from anyone else."

units.la: EXAMEN [?]
units.tr: EXAMINATION

units.la: Si Retributiva justitia in Deo est, ut paulo ante monstratum est, per quam justum est apud Deum obedientibus decreta præmia distribuere, contumacibus decretas pœnas infligere; utique punitio peccatoribus contumacibus debetur, tum quia Deus lege cavit, & pœnam comminatus est, ut qui execratur facientes iniquitatem, tum quia ipsi contumaces sua iniquitate punitionem illam promeriti sunt, ut sibi debitam. Et cum dicitur, suum cuique tribuendum, non debitum bonum ac commodum tantum, sed etiam debitum pœnæ Malum intelligi debet: nec Deus cum sit constanter verax, justæ suæ promissioni, neque justæ suæ comminationi, (prout vel promisit, vel minatus est) renuntiare poterit, cum seipsum negare non possit. Audiamus potius Apostolum 2.
units.tr: If retributive justice is in God, as was shown a little earlier, by which it is just before God to distribute the rewards decreed for the obedient and to inflict the penalties decreed for the contumacious, then certainly punishment is owed to stubborn sinners, both because God has laid this down by law and threatened the penalty (since he abhors those who do iniquity), and because by their own iniquity the contumacious have deserved that punishment as due to themselves. And when it is said that "each should be given his due," what is due must be understood not only as the good and advantage, but also as the evil of penalty. Nor, since God is constantly truthful, can he renounce his just promise or his just threat (whichever he has made or uttered), since he cannot deny himself. Let us rather hear the Apostle, 2 Thess. 1.

units.la: Thes.[?] 1. Quare manifestum est judicium justi edicis Dei, ut digni habeamini regno Dei, pro quo etiam patimini. Siquidem JUSTUM est apud Deum, vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, afflictionem: Vobis vero, qui affligimini, relaxationem nobiscum.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 1: "Therefore it is a manifest token of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer; since it is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled rest with us."

units.la: Attendamus illud: JUSTUM est apud Deum. Dei justa natura, quam nunquam negat, & cui non renuntiat, arguit Deum Justum judicem totius mundi, ut inde concludatur, non modo piis convenientibus praemiis ornandos, sed etiam injustos, meritis poenis afficiendos. Rom. 2. Judex ille justi judicii reddet unicuique secundum Opera ipsius: iis quidem qui perseverant boni operis gloriam, & honorem & immortalitatem, id est, iis qui quaerunt vitam aeternam: iis vero, qui sunt contentiosi et qui veritati quidem non obtemperant, sed obtemperant injustitia (reddetur) excandescentia & ira, oppressio et angustia, adversus omnem animam hominis perpetrantis malū. Hic utiq; suum cuiq; tribuitur, at malis malū, ut bonis bonum.
units.tr: Let us attend to that phrase: "it is a righteous thing with God." The just nature of God, which he never denies and never renounces, shows God to be the just judge of the whole world, so that it follows that he will adorn the pious with fitting rewards, and afflict the unjust with deserved punishments. Rom. 2: "That judge of righteous judgment will render to each according to his works: to those who by patient continuance in well-doing seek glory, honour and immortality, eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth but obey unrighteousness, indignation and wrath, tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that does evil." Here indeed each is given his due: to the evil, evil; to the good, good.

units.la: Si inquiunt, suum cuiq; tribuendum; bo-nis praemia, malis poena, nec debita remitti, nec injuria condonari jure possunt.
units.tr: "If," they say, "each is to be given his due, rewards to the good and punishment to the evil, then neither what is owed can be remitted nor an injury lawfully forgiven."

units.la: Connexum hoc falsum. Suum cui-que tribuendum, prout lex & aequitas postulat. Illa postulant a nobis caritatem & mutuam condonationem, quia Deus nos dilexit & nobis condonavit ex gratia. Ex gratia autem condonavit propter Christum, qui ipsi a nobis persolvit.
units.tr: This consequence is false. Each is to be given his due as law and equity require. These demand of us charity and mutual forgiveness, because God loved us and forgave us out of grace. But he forgave out of grace on account of Christ, who paid the debt on our behalf.

units.la: In foro Dei, suum cuiq; tribuitur, ut Deus unicuiq; & decrevit & promisit, vel comminatus est. Omnis enim promissio gratiae & comminatio poenae habet annexam conditionem, a qua dependet retributio. Spectetur hic Sponsor Christus, hominis restipulatio, Fides vel infidelitas: & justus Deus in omnibus operibus suis collaudatur.
units.tr: In God's court each is given his due in the way that God has both decreed and promised to each, or threatened. For every promise of grace and threat of penalty has an attached condition, on which the recompense depends. Here let Christ the Surety be considered, the man's counter-stipulation, faith or unbelief; and the just God is praised in all his works.

units.la: Si inquias: concedo, comminationem ad solos impoenitentes peccatores pertinere, cum resipiscentibus liberalis peccatorum condonatio passim in scripturis offeratur. Nec ego reclamo, sed hoc urgeo.
units.tr: "If you say: I grant that the threat pertains only to impenitent sinners, since generous remission of sins is everywhere offered in the Scriptures to those who repent." I do not object, but I press this point.

units.la: Interim memineris, veram resipiscentiam esse donum Dei salvatis proprium, quippe quod ex formula foederis illis solis contingit, quos jam in gratiam recepit Deus. Jerem.31.v.18.19.
units.tr: Meanwhile, bear in mind that true repentance is a gift proper to the saved, since by the form of the covenant it falls only to those whom God has already received into favour. Jer. 31.18, 19.

units.la: Castigasti me, ut castigarer tanquam vitulus non assueeffusum; converte me, ut convertar, quia tu es Iehova Deus meus.
units.tr: "You have chastised me, and I was chastised like a calf not accustomed to the yoke; turn me, and I shall be turned, for you are Jehovah my God."

units.la: Nam postquam conversus fuero, poenitebit me, & postquam ostensum fuerit mihi, applaudam femori (dolens gravissimè) erubesco, etiamque suffundar rubore, quod sciam opprobrium puerilitia mea. & v.33.34.
units.tr: "For after I was turned, I repented; and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh; I am grieved greatly, and I am ashamed, and I blush, because I bear the reproach of my youth." And v. 33, 34.

units.la: Nam hoc illud est foedus, quod pangam cum domo Israelis: Post dies illos, dictum Iehova, indam legem meam mentibus[?] eorum, & cordibus[?] eorum inscribam eam: & ero eis Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus.
units.tr: "For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel: after those days, says Jehovah, I will put my law in their minds, and write it in their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people."
