So Scripture says: that we have been redeemed by the blood of the Lamb, healed by his stripes, redeemed by him from the curse of the law; that, sins having been purged by his blood, he entered in through his own blood and obtained eternal redemption, and that the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all our sins.

units.la: Haec igitur CHRISTI JESU satis-factio illud ipsum est & manet, quod nobis imputatur ad justitiam, seu q; est nostra justitia coram Deo, ad vitam aeternam, de qua re postea fusius.
units.tr: This satisfaction of Christ Jesus is therefore that very thing which is imputed to us for righteousness, or which is our righteousness before God unto eternal life, concerning which I will speak more fully afterwards.

units.la: Certè ipse horresco, cum lego, hac ratione, ex hac nostrâ sententiâ Deum summae iniquitatis & pravitatis, supremâ cum impietate accusari: Imò Deum hac ratione extremae inscitiae ac fa-tuitatis per turpissimam atq; indignis-simam blasphemiam & contumeliam insimulari,
units.tr: Truly I shudder when I read that, by this reasoning, on our view, God is accused of the utmost iniquity and perversity, with supreme impiety; indeed God is charged, by this reasoning, with extreme folly and foolishness, through the most shameful and unworthy blasphemy and insult.

units.la: Quì verò sic, ô homo? Si enim inq;[?] Misericordiam erga humanum genus exercuit, & bonitatem ac liberalitatem suam nobis commendare voluit: Deus: cur prorsus gratuito, quidem potuit (non autem potuit, ut jam stultum) scelera hominibus non condonavit? Sin vindictam & severitatem suam in injurias ulciscendis, & delictis puniendis, ad sui nominis gloriam offendere statuit, cur non eos ipsos ulcisci[?] & supplicio afficere aggressus est, qui deliquerunt, & ejus Majestatem laserant?
units.tr: But how so, O man? For if, he says, he exercised mercy towards the human race and wished to commend his goodness and liberality to us, why could God not simply and freely forgive men's crimes, if he was able to (or, if he was not able, which is now foolish to say)? But if he decided to display his vengeance and severity in avenging wrongs and punishing offences, for the glory of his name, why did he not set about punishing and afflicting those very persons who committed the offences and wounded his majesty?

units.la: Audisti rationem; quia impunitiq; dimittuntur, credunt in filium Deum Sponsorem suum, qui pœnas ipsorum peccatis debitas, ultro in se sustulit, & luit, adeoq; pro ipsis satisfecit, & re-piscunt. Ex parte itaq; Dei, justitiæ jus respondet nostri sponsoris satisfa-ctio. Ex parte nostra, postulato Dei, respondet per gratiam ipsius in fœdere promissam, fides & obedientia ejus.
units.tr: You have heard the reasoning: because they are released unpunished, they believe in God's Son, their Surety, who of his own accord took upon himself and paid the penalties due to their sins, and so satisfied for them, and they repent. On God's side, therefore, the satisfaction of our Surety answers to the right of justice. On our side, to God's demand there corresponds his faith and obedience, promised in the covenant through his grace.

units.la: II. Non posse corporalem pœnam nisi ab eo ipso exigi, qui peccavit, pro-batur testimonio ipsius Dei, Ezech. 18. Ubi multis verbis declarat, semper esse {a}[?] quitates filiorum in patribus, nec patrum in filiis punire, si filii similes patrum scelestorum nō sunt. Anima, inquit Deus, quæ peccaverit, sa morietur, Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, neq; pater portabit iniquitatem filii: Iustitia iusti super eam erit: & impietas impii super eum erit. Eandem sententiam legimus criptam, Deut. 24. 16. Ergo nihil est absurdius, quam filium Dei portare iniquitates nostras.
units.tr: II. That a bodily penalty can be exacted only from him who sinned is proved by the testimony of God himself, Ezek. 18. There he declares at length that it is always the case that the iniquities of the fathers are not to be punished in the sons, nor the sons' in the fathers, if the sons are not like their wicked fathers. The soul, says God, that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. We read the same sentiment written in Deut. 24. 16. Therefore nothing is more absurd than that the Son of God should bear our iniquities.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: RESPONSE.

units.la: Ne quaso, dicas absurdum & impium, quod Spiritus Dei totidem fere verbis (sed a te, immane, quantum con-ortis!) per Jesaiam, per Joannem Baptistam, per Paulum & Petrum Apostolos asseruit. Et noveris, hic satis esse, si eadem natura, quæ peccavit, satisfecit.
units.tr: I beg you, do not call it absurd and impious, for the Spirit of God has affirmed it in almost the same words (but, monstrous man, how much you have distorted them!) through Isaiah, through John the Baptist, and through the apostles Paul and Peter. And you should know that here it is enough if the same nature which sinned has made satisfaction.

units.la: Et sicut iure peccata parentum in filiis, qui vitia illorum imitantur, vindicantur, uti videre est Exod. 20. 5. sic iure Deus in Filio suo Sponsore nostro Voluntario peccata nostra vindicavit. Rom. 5. dicitur: Christus cum adhuc nullis viribus essemus, suo tempore pro IMPIIS mortuus est.
units.tr: Just as the sins of parents are rightly avenged on the children who imitate their vices, as may be seen in Exod. 20. 5., so God has rightly avenged our sins in his Son, our voluntary Surety. Romans 5 says: Christ, while we were still without strength, died at his appointed time for the ungodly.

units.la: Enimvero vix pro iusto quispiam moriatur; nam pro eo, qui sit ipsi utilis, forte aliquis etiam mori sustineat. Co-mendat autem suam caritatem erg[?] nos Deus, quod cum adhuc essemu[?] peccatores, Christus ꝑ nobis mortuu[?] sit. Justificati igitur ejus sanguine, ser-vabimur nunc multo magis per eumal[?] ira. Gal. 4. 4. Postquam venit plenum tempus, emisit Deus Filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum legi obnoxium, ut eos, qui legi erant obnoxii, redimeret, ut adoptionem accipere[?]. 2. Cor. 5. 21. Reconciliamini Deo: Fecit eum (Deus) ut qui non novit peccatum, pro nob[?] peccatum (satisfactio.peccati) esset, ut nos fieremus[?] justitia Dei in eo. Hæc autem Deus, eo modo, ut jam dictum est, feci[?] ideo, ut temperamentum quoddam justitiæ & misericordiæ ad gloriam suam ederet. Rom. 3. 26. Justificamur gratis, per gratiam ejus, per redemtionem factam in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus, ut esset placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam justitiam suam, per remissionem peccatorum præcedentium; ex Dei tolerantia, ad declarandam justitiam suam præsenti tempore: ut sit ipse justus, & justificans eum, qui est ex fide Jesu. JESU.
units.tr: Indeed, scarcely would anyone die for a righteous man; for one who is useful to him, perhaps someone might even dare to die. But God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Being justified therefore by his blood, we shall now be saved much more through him from wrath. Gal. 4. 4. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made subject to the law, to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive adoption. 2 Cor. 5. 21. Be reconciled to God. He made him, who knew no sin, to be sin (the satisfaction for sin) for us, that in him we might become the righteousness of God. Moreover, God did this in the manner already stated, so that he might display a certain temperament of justice and mercy to his glory. Rom. 3. 26. We are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness, for the remission of previous sins, through the forbearance of God; to declare his righteousness at the present time: that he himself may be just, and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus. JESUS.

units.la: Etsi igitur poena corporalis non po-test transferri in alium INNOCENTEM, pse nolit; nec forte etiam possit eam sustinere: transferri tamen potest in illum[?], qui & SPONTE SE OFFERT, satis potens est ad eam sustinendam; præsertim[?] si jam ante ex optimo judi- cio ad hoc ipsum munus sit de- natus. Ast Christus Sponsor noster ipsum sponte obtulit, Heb. 10. f. Chri- stus ita alloquitur Patrem: Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti: corpus autem aptasti mi- hi, &c. Tunc dixi: Ecce adsum (in volumine li- bri scriptum est de me) ut faciam ô Deus, volun- tatem tuam. cap. 9. 19. Seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo. Joh. 10. 17. Ego pono animam meam, nemo tollit eam à me (scilicet invito) sed ego pono eam à meipso.
units.tr: Although, then, bodily punishment cannot be transferred to another who is INNOCENT, if he is unwilling, and perhaps could not even bear it, it can nevertheless be transferred to one who VOLUNTARILY OFFERS HIMSELF and is strong enough to bear it, especially if he has already been appointed to this very office by the best judgment. But Christ our Surety offered himself willingly. Heb. 10. f. Christ thus addresses the Father: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me, etc. Then I said, Behold, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me) to do your will, O God. ch. 9. 19. He offered himself without blemish to God. Joh. 10. 17. I lay down my life; no one takes it from me (namely against my will), but I lay it down of myself.

units.la: Christus etiam satis potens fuit ad œnam nostram sustinendam, ut lievebit ex argumento Adversariorum sequente. Et quidem ex optimo Patris Consilio ad hoc redemtionis munus fuit destinatus. Pet. 1. Agnus ille immaculatus Christus, cujus pretioso sanguine redemti sumus, præordinatus quidè ante jacta mundi fundamenta, patefactus vero ultimis temporibus. Et passim ipse dicit, se a Deo Patre missum venisse in mundum[?] In Christum igitur poena illa corporalis transferri potuit.
units.tr: Christ was also strong enough to bear our punishment, as will be clear from the following argument of the Adversaries. Indeed he was appointed to this office of redemption by the best counsel of the Father. 1 Pet. 1. That spotless Lamb, Christ, by whose precious blood we have been redeemed, was foreordained indeed before the foundation of the world, but was made manifest in the last times. And everywhere he himself says that he came into the world sent by God the Father. Therefore that bodily punishment could be transferred to Christ.

units.la: III. Hanc caussam opponunt, nobis non pereuntibus, divina justitia vere peccatis nostris satisfieri nullo pacto potuerit[?].
units.tr: III. They raise this objection: if we are not to perish, the divine justice could in no way truly have been satisfied for our sins.

units.la: Vera n. satisfactio est plena debiti persolutio.
units.tr: True satisfaction is the full payment of a debt.

units.la: Vnusquisq; autem nostrum mortem aeternam divina iustitia debebat.
units.tr: Yet each one of us owed eternal death to divine justice.

units.la: Vnusquisque igitur nostrum, nisi nos ipsi facere volebamus, alium habere debuisset, qui pro ipso mortem aeternam subiret: Verum id fieri poterat, cum omnibus hominibus generaliter, si Deus summo iure uti voluisset, aeterna mors eunda[?] esset. Quomodo enim posset quis corporalem poenam, praesertim vero mortem, pro alio solvere, quam ipsemet debeat?
units.tr: Each one of us, therefore, unless we ourselves were willing to do it, ought to have had another who would undergo eternal death in his place. But this could have happened for all men in general only if God had wished to use his supreme right, so that eternal death would be exacted. For how could anyone pay bodily punishment, especially death, for another, when he himself owes it?

units.la: Vnum autem quempiam, qui morti aeternae utpote qui nihil deliquisset, minime obnoxium in ventus[?] fuerit, pro omnibus satisfacere potuisse plane ridiculum est cogitare, nedum asserere.
units.tr: But that one man alone, who had committed no offence and was in no way liable to eternal death, could make satisfaction for all, is plainly ridiculous to think, let alone to assert.

units.la: Nam perinde est, ac si quis diceret, unum, qui nihil ipse debeat, et centum tantummodo aureos nummos habeat, quos dare posset pro innumeribus aliis, qui singuli aureos nummos centum debeant, posse satisfacere, cum vix pro uno tantum vere satisfaciendi habeat facultatem. Nemo enim plus, quam unam mortem aeternam subire potest, etiamque pro alio pendere.
units.tr: For it is just as if someone were to say that one man, who owes nothing himself and has only a hundred gold coins, which he could give for countless others, each of whom owes a hundred gold coins, could make satisfaction, when he scarcely has the ability to truly satisfy for one alone. For no one can undergo more than one eternal death, or pay for another as well.

units.la: Vnum i[illegible, ~4 letters]
units.tr: One [illegible]

units.la: Cur aliquis tantum ex omnibus fortasse hac ratione servari poterat. RESPOSIO.
units.tr: Why could not someone have been saved in this way, perhaps, alone out of all? ANSWER.

units.la: Non tam unitate, quam dignitatem ejus personæ, quæ pro nobis satisfecit, non nos spectare oportet, ut appareat, non ex parte, sed plenissimè dissolutum esse totum debitum nostrum. Tanta enim est virtus & potetia Mediatoris nostri, Filii Dei, ut ei tyrannis peccati & Satanæ resistere nō possit: cum tamē potentia Satanæ & vis peccati tanta sit, ut adversus illam nulla virtus humana, imò nec angelica quidē, aliquid præstare possit.
units.tr: It is not so much the unity as the dignity of that person who satisfied for us that we ought to consider, so that it appears that our whole debt has been dissolved, not in part but most fully. For so great is the power and might of our Mediator, the Son of God, that the tyranny of sin and of Satan cannot resist him; and yet the power of Satan and the force of sin are so great that no human virtue, nor indeed even an angelic one, could accomplish anything against them.

units.la: Christus enim quia verus Deus & homo est, ad nos redimendum habuit & jus proprietatis, & jus ꝓpinquitatis.
units.tr: For Christ, since he is true God and man, had both the right of ownership and the right of kinship to redeem us.

units.la: Proprietatis in nos jus habet Christus tanquam verus Deus. Nisi certè verus Deus esset, hoc modo Servator noster non esset. Necesse quidem est, ut coram Deo inveniatur ꝓportio inter peccatū & peccati pœnam. Atqui si infinita est DEI Majestas, quæ peccato offenditur, peccatum quoque pœnam infinitam meretur: Is igitur, qui pœnam tanquam homo luit, fuit quoque infinitus Deus, & cum nulla vis tanta esset, sive angelica, sive humana, quae ponderi intolerabilis irae Dei par esse potuerit.
units.tr: Christ has the right of ownership over us as true God. Unless he were truly God, he would not be our Saviour in this way. It is indeed necessary that before God a proportion be found between sin and the punishment of sin. But if the majesty of God, which is offended by sin, is infinite, then sin also deserves an infinite punishment. He therefore who paid the punishment as man was also infinite God; and since no power, whether angelic or human, was so great as to be able to match the weight of God's intolerable wrath.

units.la: Christus itaq; non homo tantum, sed verus Deus exstitit, qui Diabolo, peccatis, morte ipsa profligatis, gloriosè ut victor resurrexit. Et quia in-comprehensibilem bonitatem suam patefacere voluit, noluit duntaxat sui morte peccatum nostrum aequare, sed longè etiam superare. Ut si Adami contumacia nos perterrefacit, iustitia IESU CHRISTI nos multò magis confirmet, & vitam in IESU CHRISTO speremus meliorem eâ, quam in Ada-mo perdidimus, tanto inquam meliorem, quanto CHRISTUS Adamo praestat.
units.tr: Christ, then, was not only man but true God, who, having overthrown the devil, sins and death itself, rose gloriously as victor. And because he wished to reveal his incomprehensible goodness, he chose not merely to equal our sin by his death, but to far surpass it. So that if the disobedience of Adam terrifies us, the righteousness of Jesus Christ may strengthen us all the more, and we may hope in Jesus Christ for a better life than we lost in Adam; better, I say, by as much as Christ excels Adam.

units.la: Propinquitatis deinde persona Re-conciliatrix Christi jus habet, ut verus homo. Cûm enim DEUS sit summè iustus, & homo propter peccatum sit ipsius irae naturâ obnoxius, necesse fuit aliquem vere hominem exsistere, in quo, ruinâ istâ instauratâ, genus humanum D E o reconciliaretur. Homo tenetur implere omnem illam iustitiam, quam Deus requirit. Filius itaq; Dei homo factus, impleta omni iustitiâ, Deo acceptus fuit. Ceteri homines cooperti peccatis, Dei maledictioni sunt obnoxii: Hic vero integer & nulla peccati labe infectus, ut D E o pro nobis posset satisfacere, se puram & incontaminatam hostiam seu victimam obtulit Deo.
units.tr: Next, by the person of kinship, the Reconciler has the right as true man. For since God is supremely just, and man, on account of sin, is by the very nature of God's wrath liable to it, it was necessary that someone truly man should exist, in whom, the ruin having been restored, the human race might be reconciled to God. Man is bound to fulfil all that righteousness which God requires. The Son of God, made man, therefore, having fulfilled all righteousness, was acceptable to God. Other men, covered with sins, are liable to God's curse; but he, whole and untainted by any stain of sin, that he might be able to make satisfaction to God for us, offered himself to God as a pure and unspotted sacrifice or victim.

units.la: Atqui ita Mediator noster inter Deum & nos, ipse Deus omnipotens, &c. & homo purissimus, pretium redemptionis ac semetipsum obtulit sacrificium propitiatorium Deo Patri, qui jus condemnationis in nos habuit. Ex personæ itaq; dignitate, pretii & victimæ, adeoque satisfactionis dignitas æstimari debet.
units.tr: Thus our Mediator between God and us is, indeed, almighty God himself, etc., and most pure man, and offered himself as the price of redemption and as a propitiatory sacrifice to God the Father, who held the right of condemnation over us. From the dignity of the person, therefore, and of the price and the victim, and thus the dignity of the satisfaction, must be estimated.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: PROPUGNATIO MERITI ET SATISFACTIONIS Jesu Christi, contra id, quod dicitur, Christum non potuisse poenas nobis debitas persolvere: non potuisse Christo peccata nostra imputari: Meritum Christi pugnare cum gratia Dei, & studium sanctimoniae impedire.
units.tr: THE DEFENCE OF THE MERIT AND SATISFACTION OF JESUS CHRIST, against what is said: that Christ could not pay the penalties owed by us; that our sins could not be imputed to Christ; and that the merit of Christ conflicts with the grace of God and hinders zeal for holiness.

units.la: Si jam ex verbo Dei esset convictus, nullam omnino satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris ex parte Dei esse necessariam, ipsumq; Deum semper voluisse resipiscentibus condonare peccata, absq; ulla interveniente alicujus Mediatoris satisfactione, & nobis non perennibus justitiae Dei satisfieri nullo pacto posse; quid facerem, si mihi firmis rationibus demonstraretur, ex S. literis, Christum poenarum, quas nos ex lege Dei tenebamur subire, solutione, divina justitia pro nobis satisfacere non potuisse; nostra peccata Christo non potuisse imputari; Et denique Meritum ac Satisfactionem Christi cum gratia Dei pugnare, & studium sanctimoniae ex animis hominum aut prorsus tollere, aut saltem labefactare? Vires itaque sequentium trium argutiarum exploremus.
units.tr: If I were already convinced from the Word of God that no satisfaction at all for our sins was necessary on God's part, that God himself had always wished to pardon the sins of those who repent, without any intervening satisfaction by some Mediator, and that justice could in no way be satisfied for us, who are not everlasting; what would I do if it were shown to me by solid arguments from the holy Scriptures that Christ, by bearing the penalties which we were bound to undergo under the law of God, could not satisfy divine justice on our behalf; that our sins could not be imputed to Christ; and finally that the merit and satisfaction of Christ conflict with the grace of God and either utterly remove, or at least weaken, zeal for holiness in the minds of men? Let us therefore examine the strength of the following three subtleties.

units.la: CAPITIS II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: SECTIO I.
units.tr: SECTION I.

units.la: SI Christus pro nostris peccatis Deo plenissime satisfecit, potuit poenas, quas nos ex lege Dei subire tenebamur, perferre et persolvere. At non potuit. Quia aeternam mortem subire non potuit, passus mortem temporariam.
units.tr: If Christ fully satisfied God for our sins, he could have borne and paid the penalties which we were bound to undergo under God's law. But he could not. For he could not undergo eternal death, since he suffered only temporary death.

units.la: I. Poena, quam unusquisque nostrum propter delicta sua pendere tenebatur, mors est aeterna. Hanc profecto Christus non subiit, sed si eam subiisset, universa salutis nostrae & liberationis a peccatorum poena, spes & ratio funditus eversa fuisset. Imo si jam Christus non resurrexisset, vana, ut inquit Paulus, effet Evangelii praedicatio, & nos adhuc essemus in peccatis nostris. Et tamen si idcirco nos servasset Christus, quod poenas nostris peccatis debitas ipse sustinuisset, & cuius rei fides facienda fuisset: eum nunquam resurgere, sed in morte perpetuo manere oportuisset.
units.tr: I. The penalty each of us was bound to pay for his offences is eternal death. Christ certainly did not undergo this; but if he had, all our hope and reasoning about our salvation and deliverance from the punishment of sin would have been utterly overthrown. Indeed, if Christ had not risen, the preaching of the Gospel would be vain, as Paul says, and we would still be in our sins. And even if Christ had saved us because he had borne the punishments owed to our sins, and if the proof of this had to be given, he would have had to remain in death forever and never rise.

units.la: EXAMEN.
units.tr: EXAMINATION.

units.la: Etsi Christus aeternam mortem non sensit, sed passio eius fuit temporaria; non tamen hinc sequitur, cum pœnas nostris peccatis debitas non persolvisse, nec ideo satisfecisse.
units.tr: Although Christ did not feel eternal death, but his suffering was temporary, it does not follow from this that he did not pay the penalties owed to our sins, nor that he therefore did not make satisfaction.

units.la: Hæc enim temporaria Passio & Mors Christi, si non præponderat, certe æquivalet æternis nostris suppliciis. Tanta quippe est dignitas passionis & mortis Christi, ut sit pretium sufficiens pro redemptione generis humani. Idque ex his concurrentibus in Christo causis.
units.tr: For this temporary passion and death of Christ, even if it does not outweigh our eternal punishments, certainly equals them. The dignity of Christ's passion and death is so great that it is a sufficient price for the redemption of the human race. This follows from the following causes which concur in Christ.

units.la: PRIMA causa est spontanea obedientia filii ad mortem usque crucis. Philip. 2. Satisfactoria enim non fuisset Christi passio, nisi fuisset voluntaria. Hinc Apostolus Roman. 5. v. 19. ait: Sicut per inobedientiam unius peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita per unius obedientiam justi constituuntur multi. Loquitur autem, ut Theophylactus dicit, de obedientia mortis CHRISTI, per quam obedi-entiam morte contrita, ex mortis su-mus erepti condemnatione.
units.tr: The FIRST cause is the voluntary obedience of the Son, even to the death of the cross. Phil. 2. For Christ's passion would not have been satisfactory unless it had been voluntary. Hence the Apostle says in Rom. 5:19: As by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one many will be made righteous. He speaks, as Theophylact says, of the obedience of Christ's death, by which obedience, his death having been broken, we were rescued from the condemnation of death.

units.la: Secunda causa, quod Christus non tantum sponte sua se obtulerit, ad nos redimendum, adeoque ejus humiliatio & mort r mors fuerit plane voluntaria: Sed quod[?] ipse etiam summe innocens pas- us est, tanquam qui peccatū non fecit, & in cujus ore dolus non inventus est. Talis enim decebat nos pontifex, pi- us, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, cui nō esset necesse pri- mum pro propriis peccatis, deinde pro populi peccatis offerre. Quoniam ita- que passus est justus ꝑ injustis jure pre- tiosus ad redemtionem censetur san- guis ejus, tanquam Agni immaculati & incontaminati. 1. Pet. 1.
units.tr: The second cause is that Christ not only offered himself of his own accord to redeem us, so that his humiliation and death were entirely voluntary, but that he, being most innocent, also suffered, as one who had done no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found. For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, harmless, undefiled, separated from sinners, who did not need first to offer for his own sins and then for the sins of the people. Therefore, since he, the just one, suffered for the unjust, his blood is judged precious for redemption, as that of a lamb without blemish and without spot. 1 Pet. 1.

units.la: Tertia omnium maxima est, quod mors Christi non fuerit meri & nudi hominis, quamvis innocentis & justi, sed fuit ejus, qui fuit verus Deus & homo in una eadēmq; persona. Atq; hæc immensa personæ hujus dignitas facit, ut ἀνήλωτον[?] hoc sanguinis & mortis ipsius, licet temporarium, si duratio spectetur; immensi tamen vigoris sit, ad servandum in perpetuum eos, qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum.
units.tr: The third and greatest cause is that the death of Christ was not that of a mere and bare man, however innocent and just, but of him who was true God and man in one and the same person. And this immense dignity of the person makes this blood and death of his, although temporary if its duration is considered, of immense power to keep forever those who come to God through him; it is ἀνάλωτον [inexhaustible].

units.la: Si enim sanguis taurorum (Heb. 9.) & hircorum, & cinis juvencæ, asperges inquiinquinatos, sanctificat ad carnis puritatem; quanto magis Sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum aeternum, seipsum obtulit incul-patum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram a mortuis operibus, ad serviendum Deo vivo. Paulus dicit Actor. 20.
units.tr: For if the blood of bulls (Heb. 9.) and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on the unclean, sanctifies to the purity of the flesh; how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works, to serve the living God. Paul says this in Acts 20.

units.la: Deum proprio sanguine ecclesiam suam redemisse, non quod Deitas carnem & sanguinem habeat, (quippe Deus Spiritus est) sed ista, quae mortem pro nobis oppetiit, simul Deus & homo est: Atque ita sanguis hic vere dicitur, & est sanguis Dei: ejus proinde summa praestantia & dignitas est. Has causas conjunctim sumtas, vim ingentem passioni & morti Christi tribuisse, quis inficias ibit?
units.tr: That God redeemed his Church with his own blood (Acts 20:28) does not mean that the Deity has flesh and blood (for God is Spirit), but that he who suffered death for us is at once God and man; and so this blood is truly called, and is, the blood of God, and its supreme excellence and dignity is therefore his. Who will deny that these causes, taken together, have given great power to the passion and death of Christ?

units.la: Deinde ex eo, quod Christus potenter & gloriose ex mortuis resurrexit, nos constare affirmamus, eum pro nobis satisfecisse, & satisfaciendi vim habuisse.
units.tr: Next, from the fact that Christ rose from the dead powerfully and gloriously, we affirm that it is established that he made satisfaction for us and had the power to satisfy.

units.la: 2. Verùm hoc negant Adversarii: Si ex Christi, inquiunt, resurrectione constat ipsum satisfecisse pro peccatis nostris, id constat, aut quia per resurrectionem declaratus fuit aeternus Deus, aut quia reipsa demonstravit ista sua resurrectione, morte sua peccata nostra plane & plene expiata esse.
units.tr: 2. But the adversaries deny this: If it is established from Christ's resurrection that he made satisfaction for our sins, this is established either because by the resurrection he was declared to be the eternal God, or because by his resurrection he really showed that our sins were fully and completely expiated by his death.

units.la: {*} — ut utrumq; falsum. Ergo ideo potius resur- exit, ut nos immortalitatis inde spem concipien- tes, ab iniquitatibus nostris ad Deum, ea ratio- ne, qua ipse Christus jusserat, converteremur.
units.tr: {*} — since both are false. Therefore he rather rose again so that, conceiving from this the hope of immortality, we might turn from our iniquities to God, in the manner which Christ himself had commanded.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Conclusio ista neq; nihil neq; totum dicit. Spem quidem confirmari nostrā Christi resurrectione, & eadem nos commonefieri, ut à morte peccatorum per Christum resurgamus ac justitiæ vivamus, large concedimus.
units.tr: This conclusion is neither wholly wrong nor wholly right. We readily concede at large that our hope is confirmed by Christ's resurrection, and that we are thereby reminded to rise from the death of sin through Christ and live in righteousness.

units.la: Assumtio verò, quod falsum dicere non erubescit, hoc nos, & quidem utrumq; verissimū esse ex ipso Dei verbo demonstramus, nihil facientes futiles aliorum subtilitates. Verè Christus resurrexit, partim <bl>ppter</bl> seipsum, partim propter nos.
units.tr: As for the assumption, which they are not ashamed to call false, we show from God's own word that both parts are entirely true, without making futile subtleties of others. Christ truly rose, partly for himself and partly for us.

units.la: 1. Propter seipsum, hoc est, ad asserendum suam gloriam. Hanc enim resurgendo asseruit maximè apud eos, quibus jam tum nota erat ignominiosa ejus mors, quatenus resurgendo demonstravit, se fuisse & doctorem veracem, quippe qui hoc ipsum prædixerat: omnipotentem Dei filium. Rom. 1,4.
units.tr: 1. For himself, that is, to assert his own glory. For by rising he asserted it most of all before those to whom his shameful death was already known, since by rising he showed that he had been a true teacher, as he had himself foretold this, and that he was the omnipotent Son of God. Rom. 1:4.

units.la: Christus declaratus est (alii: definit[?]) filius Dei potenter, secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, ex resurrectione mortuorum, id est, exeo, quòdre-surrexit à mortuis.
units.tr: Christ was declared (others: defined[?]) the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, that is, by the fact that he rose from the dead.

units.la: Quòd verò negatur, Christum seipsum excitavisse potentiâ suâ divinâ, licet efficientia resurrectionis in scriptura plerumq; tribuatur Patri; tamen id fit contra scripturam, quæ eandem & ipsi Christo tribuit. Joh. 10. 18. & cap. 2. 19. &c.
units.tr: As for the denial that Christ raised himself by his own divine power, although the efficacy of the resurrection is in Scripture mostly ascribed to the Father, this is nevertheless done against Scripture, which ascribes it also to Christ himself. John 10:18; and ch. 2:19, etc.

units.la: Jesus igitur Christus Filius Dei unigenitus assumsit carnem, in eáque conversatus est inter homines, passus est tanquam maleficus: At idem justus seu innocens declaratus est per naturam divinam, cujus vi corpus suum in sepulcro incorruptum conservavit, & tertio die à mortuis resurrexit.
units.tr: Jesus Christ, therefore, the only-begotten Son of God, assumed flesh and lived among men in it, and suffered as a malefactor. Yet the same Christ was declared just or innocent by his divine nature, by whose power he preserved his body incorrupt in the sepulchre, and on the third day rose from the dead.

units.la: II. Propter nos quoq; resurrexit, ad promovendam nostram salutem, per confirmationem nostri non tantum in spe immortalitatis, & caritate vitæ innocentis, sed etiam Fidei de remissione peccatorum, quatenus resurgendo à mortuis reipsâ demonstravit, testatúmque fecit, quod morte suâ omnia ostra peccata, quæ ut Sponsor in se susceperat, expiaverit, pròq; illis judicio Dei satisfecerit. 1. Corint. 15. 17. Si Christus non est excitatus, inanis est fides vestra; adhuc estis in peccatis vestris.
units.tr: II. He also rose for us, to advance our salvation, confirming us not only in the hope of immortality and in love of an innocent life, but also in faith concerning the remission of sins. By rising from the dead he really demonstrated and attested that by his death he had expiated all our sins, which he had taken upon himself as Surety, and had made satisfaction to the judgment of God on their behalf. 1 Cor. 15:17. If Christ has not been raised, your faith is empty; you are still in your sins.

units.la: Ergò cum Christus sit excitatus, se-quitur credentes non amplius esse in peccatis suis, nec fidem eorum inanem esse; nempe fidem, quâ credunt peccata sua per mortem Christi esse expiata. Roman. 4. v. ult. Qui (nempe Jesus) traditus est propter delicta nostra (scilicet exp-iandos suâ morte) & excitatus est propter iustificationem nostri (scilicet testificandam, quòd nimirum illa facta sit per sanguinem ipsius. Confer cap. 5. 9.) Actor.13. postquam Apostolus ex Psal. 18. osten-disset, Jesum esse Christum, ut qui incorruptus excitatus sit à mortuis, subjungit: Notum ergo sit vobis, fratres, quòd per hunc vobis remissio peccatorum annunciatur. Huc pertinet quòd Petrus dicit: Bonam conscientiam Deum interrogare per resurrectionem Jesu Christi, de quo dicto supra satis.
units.tr: Therefore, since Christ has been raised, it follows that believers are no longer in their sins, and their faith is not empty; namely, the faith by which they believe their sins to have been expiated through the death of Christ. Rom. 4, last verse: who (namely Jesus) was delivered up for our offences (namely, to be expiated by his death) and was raised for our justification (namely, to be attested, since it was indeed effected through his blood; compare ch. 5:9). Acts 13: after the Apostle had shown from Ps. 18 that Jesus is the Christ, as one who was raised from the dead incorrupt, he adds: Be it known to you therefore, brethren, that through this man the remission of sins is announced to you. To this pertains what Peter says: the good conscience asks God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, about which saying enough has been said above.

units.la: 3. Si daretur, inquiunt, CHRISTUM semel se mortem æternam pro nobis, non tamen esset [?]. retur, Christum pœnarum pro peccatis nostrũ persolutione, Deo satisfacere potuisse, siquidem uno aliquo tantum, non pro innumerabilibus aliis eam gustasset. Nonne, ajunt, id quod unusquisq; nostrum propter delicta sua pati tenebatur, infinitum quiddam erat? Nonne mortem æternam, & sic tempore numquam finiendā pœnam, quilibet ex nobis pendere tenebatur? Etsi ad summum illud divinæ severitatis jus, ut hîc faciendum videtur, rem expendere velimus; ne pœnam ut tempore non definitam, sic pretio infinitam pendere tenemur, cum Deum, rem infiniti pretii offenderimus? Quod si infinitatem temporis, cui jure obnoxii non essemus, quippe quorum delicta temporaria fuissent, loco infinitatis pretii, quam debebamus, sed solvendo non eramus, in unoquoq; nostrũ successisse dicamus: cur vicißim pretii infinitatem pro temporis infinitate, si ab hoc reatu per pœnarum solutionem, ab alio pro nobis faciendam, liberandi sumus, unusquisq; nostrum, quando per se non potest, per alium solvere nõ teneretur? Infinitas igitur pretii, pro uno quopiam persolvi potuisset, & unum tantummodo ex nobis ejus vi, à mortis æternare-[?]atu liberari. Quia quilibet ex nobis perse eam pretii infinitatem debebat. Quare totidem pretii infinitates exsistere opus fuisset, quot nos sumus, non unicam tantum, si omnes id per alium solvendo quod nos debebamus, eo nexu liberandi fuissemus. Hæc & alia pluribus subtilibus futilita-tibus nobis objiciunt.
units.tr: "Even if it were granted," they say, that Christ had once for all tasted eternal death for us, he could not nevertheless have satisfied God by paying the punishments for our sins, if he had tasted it for only one, and not for innumerable others. Is it not, they ask, something infinite that each of us was bound to suffer for his own offences? Was not each of us bound to pay eternal death, and so a punishment never to be ended in time? Even if we wish to weigh this against the supreme right of divine severity, as seems to be done here: are we not bound to pay a punishment that is infinite in price, not merely unlimited in time, since we have offended God, a being of infinite worth? But if we say that the infinity of time, to which we would not have been liable by right, since our offences would have been temporary, took the place, in each of us, of the infinity of price that we owed but could not pay; why then, conversely, if we are to be freed from this guilt by the payment of punishments made by another on our behalf, would not each of us, since he cannot pay by himself, be bound to pay through another? Therefore an infinity of price could have been paid for one person, and by its power only one of us freed from the guilt of eternal death, since each of us by himself owed that infinity of price. Wherefore there would have needed to be as many infinities of price as there are of us, not just one, if all of us were to be freed by that bond, by another paying what we owed. These and many other subtle trifles they object to us.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: RESPONSE.

units.la: Satis est, quicquid etiam rationabi-liter dici queat, quod pro nobis PAS-SUS est DOMINUS GLORIÆ, & DEUS BENEDICTUS in secula[?]. A-ctor. 20.28. Deus sanguine suo redemit Eccle-siam. Hic Deus infinitus uno actu omnē illam infinitate præstare potest. 1. Cor. 2. 8. Dominum gloriæ crucifixerunt, non purum & merum hominem. Rom. 9. v. 5. Fuit quidem Christus, qui pro nobis est passus, ex Iudaeis[?], secundum carnem, sed est etiam supra omnes Deus laudandus in secula.
units.tr: It is enough that whatever can reasonably be said is this: the LORD OF GLORY, and the BLESSED GOD for ever, suffered for us. Acts 20.28: God redeemed the Church with his own blood. Here the infinite God is able by one act to render satisfaction of infinite value. 1 Cor. 2.8: They crucified the Lord of glory, who was not a bare and mere man. Rom. 9.5: Christ indeed, who suffered for us, came from the Jews according to the flesh, but he is also God over all, blessed for ever.

units.la: Hic per SPIRITUM æternum se obtulit Deo. Heb. 9. 14. Hinc vis purga-tis sanguinis Christi pendet, primum ab excellentia divinæ naturæ Christi. Obtulit enim se per SPIRITUM æter-num; Postea a sanctitate naturæ suæ humanæ: obtulit enim se inculpatum Deo. Ergo nos redemtos esse pretioso sanguine Christi tanquam agni inculpati & incontaminati, dicit Petrus.
units.tr: Here he offered himself to God through the eternal SPIRIT (Heb. 9.14). From this the cleansing power of Christ's blood depends: first, on the excellence of Christ's divine nature, for he offered himself through the eternal Spirit; and second, on the holiness of his human nature, for he offered himself without blemish to God. Therefore Peter says that we were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.

units.la: Quare hinc fieri dicimus, ut propter dignitatem personæ patientis & morientis, & simul infinitum pretium perpessionum Christi, Omnes CHRISTO DATI, TANQUAM unum cum ipso CORPUS CONSTITUENTES, passi & mortui censeantur, & quidem morte æterna, idèo quia ille UNUS DEUS BENEDICTUS in secula est mortuus. 2. Cor. 5. 14[?].
units.tr: Hence we say that, on account of the dignity of the person who suffered and died, and at the same time the infinite value of the sufferings of Christ, all who were given to Christ, as one with him, constituting his body, are counted as having suffered and died, and indeed with an eternal death, because that ONE BLESSED GOD for ever died. (2 Cor. 5.14.)

units.la: Hoc statuimus, Si unus pro omnibus mortuus fuit, nempe, hos omnes fuisse mortuos: & illum pro omnibus mortuum esse, ut qui vivunt, posthac non sibi vivant, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit.
units.tr: We maintain this: if one died for all, then all were dead; and he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who died and rose again for them.

units.la: In uno igitur hoc nostro Mediatore & Spósore[?], censemur nos omnes mortui, ut qui omnium nostrum personam gessit, non secus ac si ipsi tam diram mortem pro peccatis nostris oppetissemus, ut vitam recuperaremus in eo, qui propter vitam mortuus est. Hinc non male judicavit, si modo recte intellexit, Caiphas Pontifex maximus, cum dixit Johan. 11. Non cogitatis conducere nobis, ut unus homo moriatur pro populo, & tota gens non pereat.
units.tr: In this one Mediator and Bridegroom of ours, therefore, we are all counted dead, since he bore the person of us all, just as if we ourselves had undergone so dreadful a death for our sins, so that we might recover life in him who died for the sake of life. Hence Caiaphas the high priest did not judge badly, if he understood rightly, when he said (John 11.50): You do not consider that it is better for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.

units.la: Hæc igitur temporaria passio Dei, cum sit passio VERI & ÆTERNI DEI, æquivalet, imò præponderat, æternis & infinitis omnium nostrum, pro quibus is ille passus & mortuus est, suppli-is.
units.tr: This temporary suffering of God, therefore, since it is the suffering of the TRUE and ETERNAL GOD, is equivalent to, indeed outweighs, the eternal and infinite punishments of all of us for whom he suffered and died.

units.la: 4. Objicitur: Certum est, inquiunt, nulla alia ratione posse vim istam infinitam, iis, qua passus est Christus, attribui, nisi ita aeternum Deus sit. Sed Christus non potuit, quatenus aeternus Deus, quidquam pati. Ergo infinitam vim ejus perpessionibus tribuendam nihil momenti habet, quod Christus aeternus Deus sit. Neque enim satis est, Christum si passus fuit, aeternum Deum fuisse: nisi eatenus, quatenus aeternum Deus est, fuerit passus.
units.tr: 4. It is objected: It is certain, they say, that this infinite power cannot be attributed to the sufferings Christ underwent by any other means than if God were eternal in this way. But Christ, as eternal God, could not suffer anything. Therefore the fact that Christ is the eternal God has no weight in ascribing infinite power to his sufferings. For it is not enough that Christ, if he suffered, was the eternal God, unless he suffered in so far as he is the eternal God.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: RESPONSE.

units.la: Divina natura in se quidem est ἀπαθὴς[?], fieri enim nequit, ut immutabilis Deitas ac essentia Dei lacereturac patiatur, ut immortalis divinitas moriatur. Passio interim & mors fuit personae, quia persona illa quae passa est, Deus est & Homo, quae persona proprie passa & mortua est, in ea natura, quae pati & mori potuit. Ideo Paulus personae respectu dicit, Deum sibi acquisivisse Ecclesiam sanguine suo (ineptissimum vero est, quod dicunt, Deum non respicere personam; ideoque nec personam filii ad hanc passionem & satisfactionem ordinari.) Respectu autem humanæ naturæ, Petrus inquit, Christum passum esse carne. Et Epist. ad Heb. 2,14. dicit Filium Dei participem fuisse carnis & sanguinis, ut per mortem eum destrueret, qui mortis habebat imperium.
units.tr: The divine nature in itself is indeed impassible [ἀπαθής], for it cannot happen that the immutable Godhead and the essence of God should be torn or suffer, or that the immortal divinity should die. Yet suffering and death belonged to the person, because the person who suffered is God and Man, and this person properly suffered and died in that nature which was able to suffer and die. Therefore Paul, speaking with respect to the person, says that God acquired the Church for himself with his own blood. (It is most absurd, however, what they say, that God does not regard the person, and therefore the person of the Son is not appointed to this suffering and satisfaction.) With respect to the human nature, Peter says that Christ suffered in the flesh. And in the Epistle to the Hebrews 2.14 it says that the Son of God shared in flesh and blood, so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death.

units.la: Etsi igitur passio & mors propria est carnis, secundum naturam: ad λόγον[?] tamen pertinet secundum personam, quia & verbi & carnis una est persona. Hinc jam passio & mors Christi perfecta & accepta est Deo, quia, ut dictum est, voluntaria obedientia filii præstita mandato patris: humiliavit enim seipsum, obediens factus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: deinde quia est infiniti meriti, ejus quippe hominis, qui verus est Deus.
units.tr: Although, therefore, suffering and death are properly of the flesh according to its nature, yet they pertain to the Word [λόγος] according to the person, because the Word and the flesh are one person. Hence the suffering and death of Christ are now perfect and acceptable to God, because, as has been said, they were voluntary obedience of the Son rendered to the command of the Father; for he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Then, too, because it is of infinite merit, since it is the merit of that man who is true God.

units.la: Neq; sane refert, quod Divina Chri-sti natura vim aliquam perpessionibus Christi compatiendo, h. e. eo quod & ipsa cum carne sua sit excruciata, lacerata, perfossa, ppella[?] in se, conciliare nō potuerit: quoniam satis est eam & voluisse hanc passionem & morte assum-tæ carnis, & carnem patientem ac morienientem fustentasse, & deniq; persona-iter ei unitam & communicatam ma-isse[?], dum illa pateretur ac moreretur.
units.tr: Nor indeed does it matter that the divine nature of Christ could not bring some power to the sufferings of Christ by suffering with them, that is, by being itself tortured, torn and pierced together with its flesh. For it is enough that it both willed this suffering and death of the assumed flesh, and sustained the suffering and dying flesh, and finally that it was personally united to and communicated with that flesh while it suffered and died.

units.la: V. Ipsa (regerunt) divina natura, hoc est, ipse Deus est, cui satisfaciendum erat. Et cum iterum aliam in ipsa essentia diuina personam pa-tris[?] esse, aliam personam filii, & patri potuisse a filio satisfieri, nec tamen aliquid, quod satisfactionem persolutionem satisfaciendam adversetur, committi. Dicite inquiunt illi, Nonne ipsius filii persona non minus, quam Patris satisfaciendum fuisse affirmatiue[?]? Si filius patri satisfecit, quis ipsi filio, quod ipsi debetur, solvet? Nemo autem potest sibi ipsi satisfacere.
units.tr: 5. The divine nature itself, they reply, that is, God himself, is the one to whom satisfaction had to be made. And since there is in the divine essence itself one person of the Father and another person of the Son, and satisfaction could be made to the Father by the Son, and yet nothing is committed that would be contrary to a satisfaction rightly rendered. Tell us, they say, is not the person of the Son himself to be satisfied no less than the Father? If the Son has satisfied the Father, who will pay to the Son himself what is owed to him? No one, however, can satisfy himself.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Satisfactio hic est, si eadem sit Patris & Filii & Spiritus S. voluntas. Ac proinde cum pater sibi judicavit esse satisfactum, simul etiam filio & Spiritui sancto fuit satisfactum. Futile hoc est adversariis, qui dicunt, in vera satisfactione habere rationem non voluntatis, sed rei ipsius. Sed mecum considerent illud, quod ipse Deus in Christo sibi mundum reconciliaverit, & fecerit eum, qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum, 2. Corinth. 5. Atqui ita quoddammodo suam ipsius ira placaverit. Quid quod Iesa. 59. verf. 16. 17. sic legamus: QUUM ITAQUE DEUS VIDIT NUL-LUM ESSE VIRUM, ET OBSTUPUIT NULLUM ESSE INTERVENTOREM (id est) hominem ullum pium, qui pos-set intercedere ad servandam Eccle-siam, nisi idem fuisset Deus) SALUTEM [?]tulit ei (nimirum viro, qui neq; seipsum poterat sistere coram Deo, neq; pro alte-ro intercedere, sed jam erat in peccatis mortuus, Eph. 2. 1.) BRACHIUM IPSIUS (id est, Christum Dei potentiam & sapientiam, 1 Cor. 1. 24.) ET JUSTITIA IPSIUS (idem Christus, qui factus est nobis a Deo sapientia, & justitia, sanctificatio & redemtio, 1 Cor. 1. 30.) hac FULCIVIT eum. Nam (ipse Christus intervē-tor noster Regnū Satanæ potestatem-que tenebrarū debellaturus) INDUIT JUSTITIAM QUASI LORICAM (ut ad Eph. 6. 14. 17.) ET GALEAM SALUTIS CAPITI SUO: INDUIT INQUAM, VES-TIUM ULTIONIS INDUMENTUM, ET AMICIVIT SE ZELO QUASI PALLIO, Sed satis sit, cum semel rationi infanti-enti nunquā alias satisfiat.
units.tr: Satisfaction takes place if the will of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is the same. Accordingly, when the Father judged himself satisfied, satisfaction was at the same time made to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. This is a weak argument for our opponents, who say that true satisfaction has regard to the thing itself and not to the will. But let them consider that God himself reconciled the world to himself in Christ, and made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, 2. Corinth. 5. Indeed, in a sense, he thereby appeased his own wrath. What is more, let us read Isa. 59. vers. 16. 17. as follows: "AND WHEN HE SAW THAT THERE WAS NO MAN, AND WAS ASTONISHED THAT THERE WAS NO INTERCESSOR" (that is, no godly man who could intercede to save the Church, unless he were God himself), "HE BROUGHT SALVATION TO HIM" (namely to the man who could neither present himself before God nor intercede for another, but was already dead in sins, Eph. 2. 1.), "HIS ARM" (that is, Christ, the power and wisdom of God, 1 Cor. 1. 24.) "AND HIS RIGHTEOUSNESS" (the same Christ, who was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, 1 Cor. 1. 30.) "UPHELD HIM." For Christ himself, our intercessor, who was to overthrow the kingdom of Satan and the power of darkness, "PUT ON RIGHTEOUSNESS AS A BREASTPLATE" (as in Eph. 6. 14. 17.) "AND A HELMET OF SALVATION ON HIS HEAD. HE PUT ON, I SAY, THE GARMENTS OF VENGEANCE, AND WRAPPED HIMSELF IN ZEAL AS IN A CLOAK." But let this be enough, since reasoning of that childish kind is never otherwise satisfied than once for all.

units.la: CAPITIS II. SECTIO II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. SECTION II.

units.la: SI Christo peccata nostra imputari non potuerunt, vana est satisfactionis ejus persuasio. At nostra peccata Christo a Deo imputari non poterunt, nisi ut sibi imputarentur: ommeritum fuerit, quod dicere est blasphemum.
units.tr: If our sins could not be imputed to Christ, then the belief that he made satisfaction is empty. But our sins could not be imputed to Christ by God, unless they were imputed to him as though he had deserved them. That would be blasphemy to say.

units.la: Pugnat cum natura Dei, aliena peccata innocentissimo imputare. Ne Patris quidem peccata filio imputat, nisi filius patrem imitetur. Illud etiam quod dicitur Exod. 20. Deuter. 5. Deum punire peccata parentum in filiis, ita conciliatur cum eo, quod scriptum est Ezechiel 18. Duo igitur, ut aliena peccata alicui imputari queant, conjunctim necessario requiruntur. Unum est, illum, cui imputari debent, ei cujus peccata imputanda sunt, ita conjunctum esse, ut propter solam ipsam conjunctionem, particeps illius delictorum esse videatur. Alterum est ipsum quoque peccasse, & illius scelera imitatum fuisse: alioqui iniquissima ea imputatio censenda esset.
units.tr: It is contrary to the nature of God to impute the sins of others to the most innocent. He does not even impute a father's sins to a son, unless the son imitates his father. The saying in Exod. 20 and Deut. 5, that God visits the sins of the parents upon the children, is reconciled with what is written in Ezek. 18 in this way. Two things are therefore necessarily required together, for the sins of others to be imputed to someone. The first is that the person to whom they are to be imputed is so joined to the one whose sins they are that, by that union alone, he seems to share in that person's offences. The second is that he himself has also sinned and imitated that person's crimes. Otherwise such imputation would be judged most unjust.

units.la: Cum Deus Sodomam destruere vellet, Abrahamus ad Deum sic ait: Absit à te, ut facias rem talem ut mori faciat justum cum impio, sitq; justus sicut impius. Absit, inquâ àte: nunquid judex universa terra non faciet judicium? Iniquum igitur censetur apud Deum, ut justus una cum impio affligatur. Cum igitur duo illa simul juncta in alienis peccatis imputandis requirantur, in Christo autè non fuisse appareat, quid quæso detestabilius fieri potuisset, quam illi aliena peccata imputare? Christus nō modo aliorum turpia scelera imitatus non est, sed sanctissime semper, & innocentissime vixit. Cum ipsis vero scelestis hominibus ea sola ratione conjunctus fuit, quod & ipse homo fuit, alioqui à peccatoribus segregatus.
units.tr: When God was about to destroy Sodom, Abraham said to God: Far be it from you to do such a thing, to slay the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous would be as the wicked. Far be it from you; shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? It is therefore considered unjust before God that the righteous should be afflicted together with the wicked. Since, then, those two things joined together are required for imputing the sins of others, and it appears they were not present in Christ, what, I ask, could be more detestable than to impute to him the sins of others? Christ not only did not imitate the shameful crimes of others, but lived always most holy and most innocent. He was joined to wicked men by one reason only, that he too was a man; otherwise he was separated from sinners.

units.la: 2. Huc accedit, quod potest quidem Deus jure, si velit, ei peccata non imputare, cui merito imputari possent. De suo enim jure quilibet, quantū velit, decedere potest. Sed nemini jure aliena peccata imputare potest Deus, cui immerito imputari non possint. Peccatorum enim alienorum imputa-tio, tio, apud Deum non ex eorum nume-ro est, quæ à sola ipsius voluntate pen-dent: sed ad alia etiam relationem ha-bet, & in ipsa non de Deus tantum, sed de alternis quoq; jure agitur.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, God can indeed rightly, if he wishes, not impute sins to one to whom they could justly have been imputed, for anyone can give up his own right as far as he wishes. But God cannot rightly impute the sins of others to anyone to whom they could not be imputed without desert. For the imputation of others' sins before God is not among those things that depend on his will alone. It has a relation also to other things, and in it there is question not only of God's right but also of the right of the other party.

units.la: Ut igitur Deus neminem punit eam solam ob causam, quia sic velit, sed etiam, quia sic puniri meretur: Sic nemini imputat peccata aliena, quia simpliciter ita velit; sed quia is, ut sibi imputentur, commeritus fuerit. Et quemadmodum, ut quis verè puniri pos-sit, non satis est, quod ipse puniri velit, nisi delictum aliquod commiserit (Relativa enim sunt pœna & delictum; ita ut ubi delictum non est, ibi pœna esse nullo modo possit.) Sic ut alicui aliena peccata verè possint imputari, non satis est ipsum ita velle: nisi imputationis antecedens alia digna causa subsit, &c.
units.tr: Just as God punishes no one for the sole reason that he so wills, but also because the person deserves to be punished, so he imputes the sins of others to no one simply because he so wills; rather, because that person has deserved that they be imputed to him. And just as, for someone to be truly punished, it is not enough that he wishes to be punished, unless he has committed some offence (for punishment and offence are correlative, so that where there is no offence, punishment cannot in any way exist), so, for the sins of others to be truly imputed to someone, it is not enough that God so wills, unless some worthy cause lies before the imputation, and so on.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: REPLY.

units.la: 1. Idem sane tecum affirmare non dubitarem, si rationis & justitiæ ductum sequi tantum vellem, nisi ipsum Dei Verbum aliud mihi oftendedo, mere[?] traheret. Vide mihi, prodeat jam unus[?] ille Iesaias proponátq; mihi vates vaticinium illud de Christo indubitatu[?] celebratissimum cap. 53[?]. quomodo nō possum nō fidem ei adhibere toties di-centi, Conjecta[?] in eum peccata ac iniquitates[?] nostras CHRISTUM portasse. v. 7: sicinque[?] veruntamen infirmitates nostras tulit, & dolores nostros portavit; nos autem astimavimus plagis affectum, percussum Dei, & afflictum.
units.tr: 1. I would certainly not hesitate to agree with you, if I wished only to follow the guidance of reason and justice, were it not that the Word of God itself draws me another way. Look: let that one Isaiah now come forward and let the prophet set before me that prophecy about Christ, most famous and beyond doubt, in chapter 53. How can I not give faith to him, when he says so often that he laid upon him our sins and iniquities, that CHRIST bore them? Verse 7: Yet he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows; but we esteemed him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.

units.la: Hic audio duo, 1. Commendari beneficium Christi, q; ipse peccatorum nostrorum pœnas in se transtulerit. 2. Perversum Judæorum judicium de Christi passione reprehendi, quasi Propheta exclamet: Non est, Oves eaci[?] hominum, cum summa Christi infirmitas, exinanitio, ignomi-niosissimaq; passio vobis offendiculo fit: infirmitas enim illa, quam in ipso conspicitis, ea ipsa vobis est; & a nobis ab ipso suscepta, eamque infra causa & induit & pertulit.
units.tr: Here I hear two things: 1. The benefit of Christ is commended, that he himself transferred the punishments of our sins onto himself. 2. The perverse judgment of the Jews concerning Christ's passion is rebuked, as if the prophet cried out: Do not, O men, be offended, when you see the great weakness, humiliation and most shameful passion of Christ. For that weakness which you behold in him is yours; he took it up from us and bore it in our place and on our account.

units.la: Merito igitur admiror tantũ Chri-sti beneficium, quod ipse nostra pecca-ta fecerit sua peccata, ut ipse suam ju-stitiam faceret nostram justitiam, & id persolveret, quod nobis solvendum, uodque debita noftra in fe diffolven- a fufceperit, ut nos ab ipforum obli- atione liberi effemus. Credo itaq; CHRISTUM NOSTRAS infirmita- s tulisse, & noftros dolores portasse.
units.tr: I therefore rightly marvel at so great a benefit of Christ, that he made our sins his own, so that he might make his righteousness ours, and that he bore in himself what was to be paid by us, so that he might set us free from their bond. So I believe that CHRIST bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows.

units.la: 2. Pergit Propheta verf. 8. Ipse autem vulneratus est propter prævaricationes noftras, tritus est propter iniquitates noftras; Caftiga- tio pacis noftræ fuper eum eft, & propter livo- rem ejus fanitas facta eft nobis.
units.tr: 2. The prophet goes on in verse 8: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed.

units.la: Hic audio exponi veram, falutarémque afflictionū & vulnerum CHRISTI auffam, nimirum noftras prævaricationes, & iniquitates: adeoq; CHRI- STUM pro nobis paffum, & fua paf- fione nobis pacem cociliaffe omnémque felicitatem nobis acquisiviffe. Ille at nos cum DEO pacem haberemus, caftigatus eft, & nos cum DEO, ideóque reconciliati fumus, quia Chriftus noftræ pacis comparandæ pretium perfolvit.
units.tr: Here I hear that the true and saving cause of Christ's afflictions and wounds is explained, namely our transgressions and iniquities; and so that Christ suffered for us, and by his passion procured peace for us and gained all happiness for us. He was chastised while we were at peace with God, and we are reconciled to God, and therefore we have been reconciled, because Christ paid the price to obtain our peace.

units.la: Livor itaq; ipfius noftra fanitas eft, vulnera & plagæ ejus, funt falutaria noftrorum morborum pharmaca.
units.tr: His bruises, therefore, are our healing; his wounds and stripes are the saving remedies of our diseases.

units.la: Quid ni igitur credā, paffione & morte Chrifti peccata noftra effe expiata eo quod nostros dolores portaverit, ipsi scilicet à Deo imputatos.
units.tr: Why then should I not believe that our sins were expiated by the passion and death of Christ, because he bore our sorrows, which were imputed to him by God?

units.la: 3. Vers. 9. Omnes nos, sicut pecus erravimus, quisque in viam suam nos convertimus: JEHOVA autem conjecit in illum iniquitatem seu poenam omnium nostrum.
units.tr: 3. Verse 9: We all, like sheep, have gone astray; each of us has turned to his own way; but JEHOVAH has laid on him the iniquity or punishment of us all.

units.la: Hic iterum duo audio: 1. Nostram miseriam in eo sitam, quod omnes via mandatorum DEI longè deflexerint & caecum Naturae corruptae dudum secuti, à recta salutis via alienati sint, 2. Immensam erga nos miseros Dei Patris misericordiam, quod iniquitates NOSTRAS, hoc est, poenas INIQUITATIBUS nostris meritas Christo filio suo impu-ture, quia eas in unigenitum filium conjicere, & traducere dignatus est: quia audio expresse Deum fecijsse, ut incurrat in eum poenam OMNIUM nostrum, quod aequipollet huic: trajecit, traduxit, transtulit eum poenam omnium nostrum.
units.tr: Here again I hear two things: 1. Our misery, which lies in this, that all of us have strayed far from the way of God's commandments and, following the blindness of corrupted nature long ago, have been alienated from the right way of salvation. 2. The immense mercy of God the Father toward us wretched men, in that he deigned to lay our iniquities, that is, the punishments deserved by our iniquities, upon his Son, to impute them to him, and to transfer them to the only-begotten Son. For I hear expressly that God has caused the punishment of us all to fall upon him, which is equivalent to this: he cast, transferred, and carried upon him the punishment of us all.

units.la: Cur itaque non statuam peccata nostra super Christum à Deo injecta fuisse & illi ut nostro vadi & sponsori imputata, ut nos ab illis liberi & immunes essem, qui respiciimus & in eum credimus?
units.tr: Why then should I not hold that our sins were laid by God upon Christ and imputed to him as our surety and bondsman, so that we who look to him and believe in him might be free and immune from them?

units.la: Vere itaque sic Christus factus est pro nobis PECCATUM, id est, victima peccatorum nostrorum expiatrix.
units.tr: Truly, then, Christ was made for us sin, that is, the victim who expiates our sins.

units.la: Verf. 11, Ex coarctatione & judicio sublatus est; generationem ejus, quis enarraturus est? quia succisus est ex terra viventium, propter praevaricationem populi mei plaga fuit ei.
units.tr: Verse 11: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; who shall declare his generation? For he was cut off from the land of the living; for the transgression of my people was he stricken.

units.la: Hic rursus audio certam & salutarem causam, cur Christus tam dura, tamque probrosa perpessus sit, nempe praevaricationem & plurima peccata populi Dei, quae hic in eum fecerat incurrere. Passus itaque Christus est, non sua, sed nostra causa, quae passus est. Audio vero hic Deum ipsum loquentem & causam perpessionum Christi explicantem, quasi dicat: Ipse nullam ob causam aliam ita plagis afflictus est, quam propter populi mei praevaricationem. En igitur Christum, in quem transtulerat Deus nostras iniquitates, poenas a nobis meritas & nobis ferendas, ipsum luentem. En inaestimabilem Dei bonitatem sic Ecclesiam suam amplectentem, ut proprio filio non pepercerit.
units.tr: Here again I hear the certain and saving cause why Christ suffered such hard and shameful things, namely the transgression and the very many sins of the people of God, which he here caused to fall upon him. Christ therefore suffered, not for his own cause, but for ours. But I hear here God himself speaking and explaining the cause of Christ's sufferings, as if he were saying: He was afflicted with stripes for no other reason than the transgression of my people. Behold, then, Christ, upon whom God had laid our iniquities, the punishments deserved by us and due to be borne by us, himself paying them. Behold the inestimable goodness of God, embracing his Church in such a way that he did not spare his own Son.

units.la: Verf. 13 Jehova autem voluit conterere eum eum & ægrotare fecit: quandoquidem exposuit animam suam in sacrificium, videbit semen, pro-longabit dies: Voluntas Jehovae per manum ejus prosperabitur.
units.tr: But the LORD was pleased to crush him; he has put him to grief: when his soul has made an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days; the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand.

units.la: Hic disertis & expressis verbis audio Prophetam docere, quod Deus Pater peccata nostra in filio suo sit persecut', & justis pœnis punierit, eo quod ipse filius coram Deo Patre suo nostro nomine obtulerit, ut nos ejus damnatio-ne à nostris peccatis absolveremur, & jus filiorum Dei consequeremur.
units.tr: Here the prophet teaches, in plain and explicit words, that God the Father punished our sins in his Son with just penalties, because the Son himself offered himself before God his Father in our name, so that by his condemnation we might be absolved from our sins and attain the right of the sons of God.

units.la: Hic observo primum, luculentū in-effabilis Dei Patris erga nos amoris te-stimonium, quod pœnam nobis debitā in filium trajecerit. Legitur enim in contextu: At JEHOVA delectatus est conterere eum, q.d. Deo patri mirifice placuit, quod filius ejus ad nos redimendos se vadem & sponsorem ipsi Deo statuerit, quodq; homo fieri, formam servi suscipere, & pro peccatis nostris justas pœnas luere, atque ita homines ad Deum suum adducere voluerit. Hæc gratiosa filii Dei voluntas patri usque adeo placuit, ut ipsum illa, nova quadam itia oblectarit. Verbum enim CHA-EZ, proprie significat Bene volu-gratum habuit Christum, scilicet loco ftro, atterere & contundere.
units.tr: Here I observe first the clear testimony of the ineffable love of God the Father toward us, in that he laid upon his Son the punishment we owed. For the context reads: But the LORD was pleased to crush him; that is, it pleased God the Father wonderfully that his Son should undertake to be surety and guarantor before God for our redemption, and that he should become man, take the form of a servant, pay the just penalties for our sins, and thus be willing to bring men to their God. This gracious will of the Son of God so pleased the Father that it delighted him with a certain new kind of joy. For the verb CHA-EZ properly means to be well pleased with, to hold in favour, and so, in place of the Christ, to crush and bruise. [חָפֵץ]

units.la: Deinde noto inæstimabilis Chri-Jesu dilectionis erga nos argumen-tum, quod ille semetipsum nobis redi-endi pretium statuerit, & horribile ei judicium, quod nos omnes manebat, ne in se susceperit. Ait enim Propheta: Siquidem exposuit animam suam in sacri-ficium, quod & ita legi potest: Quoniam ipsa ejus exposuit sempiternam sacrificium pro delictis.
units.tr: Next I note the proof of the inestimable love of Christ Jesus toward us: that he set himself up as the price of our redemption, and took upon himself the dreadful judgment that hung over all of us. For the prophet says: When he has made his soul an offering for sin; which may also be read thus: "Because his soul has laid itself down as a lasting sacrifice for transgressions."

units.la: Hebræa Syntaxis id exigere dicit, quia vox THASIM est tertiæ per-næ fœminini generis, ea ergo, cum alio nomine, quam ANIMA suam convenientiam in constructione habere non debet: Secundæ personæ masculini generis, hic esse nequit, quia hic nullum nomen est, cum quo construi possit. Accusativus etiam sæpe apud Hebræos intelligitur, cum eadem persona vel res & agens & patiens est.
units.tr: Hebrew syntax demands this, since the word THASIM is the third person feminine, and so, with a noun other than ANIMA ("soul"), it ought not to agree in construction. The second person masculine cannot be meant here, since there is no noun in the passage with which it could be construed. The accusative is also often understood among the Hebrews when the same person or thing is both agent and patient.

units.la: Notæ ASCHAM licet sæpe quodlibet peccatum in genere significet: aliquoties tamen pro victima, quae pro peccato expiando immolatur, accipitur.
units.tr: The word ASCHAM, though it often signifies any sin in general, is nevertheless sometimes taken for the victim which is slain to expiate sin. [אָשָׁם]

units.la: Videre igitur hinc licet, quod Christus sua libera voluntate se DEo Patri victimam pro peccatis nostris obtulerit. Haec cum sint emphatica & valde manifesta, quem non commoveant?
units.tr: From this it may be seen that Christ, by his own free will, offered himself to God the Father as the victim for our sins. Since these things are emphatic and very plain, whom would they not move?

units.la: 6. Verf. 14, Propter laborem anima sui videbit, & satiabitur: Cognitione sui iustifi-bit iustus servus meus multos, quia iniquitatum ipse portabit.
units.tr: 6. Isaiah 53:11: He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied; by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, for he shall bear their iniquities.

units.la: En iterum: Justus servus Dei Christus cognitione sui justificabit multos: quare? quia iniquitatum eorum portabit. Litte-ra enim Vau, hic particula caussalis est, quoties oratio ab effectu ad caussam traducitur. Multorum igitur justificatio arguitur portatione & sublatione peccatorum eorum, qui justificantur, facta autem a Christo pro nobis contrito & contuso.
units.tr: Behold again: the righteous servant of God, Christ, by his knowledge shall justify many. Why? Because he shall bear their iniquities. For the letter Vau here is a causal particle, whenever the sentence passes from effect to cause. The justification of many is therefore grounded in the bearing and removal of the sins of those who are justified, and this was accomplished by Christ, who was crushed and bruised for us.

units.la: 7. Deniq; verf. 15. Propterea partem dabo ei cum multis, & cum robustis dividet spolia[?]; eo quod effudit in mortem animam suam, cum sceleratis annumeratus est; Nam ipse pec-catum Multorum pertulit, & pro defectoribus intercessit. Hic toties audio CHRISTVM su-[?]am animam, ad nos redimendos, effla-tuámq; vitam ad nos seruandos prom-indere, paratissimū fore. Dicit enim P[?]ropheta, quod ipse Christus animam suam in [?]ortem profuderit. Deinde vaticinatur, Iudaeos Christum probrosissimo mor-[?]s genere esse occisuros, dum illum in-[?]er duos sceleratos in cruce suspendi procuraturi sint. Et cum sceleratis numer-[?]itus est, habet textus. Deniq; Christum nihilominus pro sua ineffabili er-[?]a miseros peccatores bonitate, officio [?]o fungi non desiturum sed multorū eccata perlaturum, & pro defectori-us intercessurum. Quid igitur ambi-[?]am? Certè Christus volens propter nostra peccata omnes illas plagas ac-cepit, omnibus probris nō sua, sed no-stra caussa affectus est. Nostra itaque peccata ipsi imputata adhuc statuo.
units.tr: 7. Finally, Isaiah 53:12: Therefore I will give him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he poured out his soul unto death, and was numbered with the transgressors; for he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors. Here I hear again and again that Christ was ready to pour out his soul to redeem us and to lay down his life to save us. For the prophet says that Christ poured out his soul unto death. Then he foretells that the Jews would put Christ to death in the most shameful manner, by arranging for him to be hanged on a cross between two criminals. The text says: "and he was numbered with the transgressors." Finally, for his unspeakable goodness toward wretched sinners, Christ nevertheless would not cease to perform his office, but would bear the sins of many and make intercession for the transgressors. What, then, am I to doubt? Surely Christ, willingly, on account of our sins, bore all those blows; he was afflicted with all those reproaches not for his own cause but for ours. I therefore still maintain that our sins were imputed to him.

units.la: II. Respondeo igitur ad splendidū & speciōsum illud objectum; Totum illud verum esset, si Christus nudus homo, non autem simul æternus & verus Deus esset. Neque enim commeritus erat Christus aliqua antecedente culpa, ut peccata nostra ipsi imputarentur. Neque solet Deus cuiquam imputare aliena delicta, nisi ille quodammodo fuerit istorum particeps: nimirum quando agitur de iis qui nec possunt, nec debent proprium illud Mediatoris officium sustinere. Ac licet dicamus, Christo imputata esse nostra peccata; non tamen exigimandum est hic agi de jure alicujus, qui sit extra Deum, quum constet Deum ipsum nos sibi reconciliasse, atque ita filium suum (qui idem est cum Patre Deus) fecisse pro nobis peccatum, imo fecisse pro nobis exsecrationem, ut nos justitiam & salutem aeternam consequeremur. 2. Corinth. 5. 21. Galat. 3. 13. de quibus supra.
units.tr: II. To that splendid and specious objection I reply: all of that would be true if Christ were a mere man, and not at the same time eternal and true God. For Christ had not deserved, by any prior fault, that our sins should be imputed to him. Nor is it God's habit to impute the offences of others to anyone unless that person is in some way a partner in them; namely when it concerns those who neither can nor ought to undertake that proper office of the Mediator. And although we say that our sins were imputed to Christ, we must not think that this concerns the right of someone outside God, since it is certain that God himself reconciled us to himself, and so made his Son (who is one God with the Father) to be sin for us, indeed to be a curse for us, so that we might obtain righteousness and eternal salvation. 2 Corinthians 5:21. Galatians 3:13, which were discussed above.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: SECTIO III.
units.tr: SECTION III.

units.la: Unde horrenda sequuntur absurda, id ipsum absurdum esse necesse est.
units.tr: Hence horrible absurdities follow, and it must be that the absurdity itself is so.

units.la: Atqui ex sententia illa inveterata de Merito & satisfactione horrenda sequuntur absurda. Quod ita probatur:
units.tr: But from that long-standing opinion about merit and satisfaction, horrible absurdities follow. This is proved as follows:

units.la: I. Absurdum id est, quod seipsum ever-tit, & secum pugnat.
units.tr: I. That is absurd which overthrows itself and contradicts itself.

units.la: Satisfactio Christi asserta cum Dei gratia, qua justificamur & condonantur nobis peccata, mutua pugna seipsum evertit.
units.tr: Christ's satisfaction, asserted together with the grace of God by which we are justified and our sins are forgiven, overthrows itself by mutual conflict.

units.la: Pugnat enim Meritum Christi cum Gratia illa Dei. Siquidem Gratia nisi omnibus nobis gratuita statuatur, gratia dici non potest. Rom. ii. 6. Quod si per gratiam, jam non ex operibus: alioqui gratia jam non est gratia. Sin ex operibus, jam non est gratia: alioquin opus jam non est opus.
units.tr: For Christ's merit conflicts with that grace of God. Indeed, grace cannot be called grace unless it is held to be free for all of us. Rom. 11. 6: But if it is by grace, it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is of works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Per gratiam Dei & particula GRA-TIS in S. literis excluduntur nostra Merita, non CHRISTI: unde dicimur summo pretio a Christo redemti, ut recte dicere possimus, nos meritis & operibus justificari, quia Christi Meritis & operibus justificamur. Non igitur merito Christi tollitur vel obscuratur gratia Dei, imo ab ea dependet. Et quae subalterna sunt, non pugnant, ideoque nihil obstat, quo minus gratuita sit condonatio peccatorum ex mera Dei gratia, & simul interveniat Christi meritum, quod Dei gratiae subjicitur.
units.tr: By the grace of God and the word GRATIS in the Holy Scriptures our own merits are excluded, not Christ's. For this reason we are said to have been redeemed by Christ at the highest price, so that we may rightly say that we are justified by merits and works, because we are justified by the merits and works of Christ. Therefore the grace of God is not taken away or obscured by the merit of Christ; rather, it depends on that grace. Things that are subordinate do not conflict, and so nothing prevents the forgiveness of sins from being free, from the pure grace of God, while at the same time Christ's merit intervenes, which is itself subject to the grace of God.

units.la: Hinc toties apud Paulum reperitur, nos justificari GRATIS, id est, ejus gratia per redemtionem factam in JESU Christo. Hinc ab eodem fides & vita æterna, DONUM DEI dicitur, idq; in Christo Domino nostro, ut iis verbis excludat omnia operum merita, tanquam directè pugnantia cum gratia Dei.
units.tr: Hence in Paul we so often find that we are justified freely, that is, by his grace, through the redemption made in Jesus Christ. Hence the same apostle calls faith and eternal life the GIFT OF GOD, and this in Christ our Lord, so that by these words he excludes all merits of works, as directly contrary to the grace of God.

units.la: Instant: Cum infinitis S. scriptura locis dicatur, totum salutem nostram pendere à gratia et Misericordia Dei; si eadem illa salus adscribatur merito & satisfactioni Christi, sequitur eodem tempore, & de eadem re prædicari posse maximè pugnantia.
units.tr: They press: Since Scripture says in countless places that our whole salvation depends on the grace and mercy of God, if that same salvation is ascribed to the merit and satisfaction of Christ, it follows that at the same time things most contradictory can be predicated of the same matter.

units.la: RESPONSIO.
units.tr: ANSWER.

units.la: Tum verum id esset, si merita Christi gratiæ Dei è diametro opponerentur.
